#5819. The Zombie Engine: How Brussels Bureaucrats Are Breathing False Life Into Combustion

If you poured rapeseed oil into a combustion engine and declared it a “zero-emission vehicle,” you would be laughed at. But in the EU Parliament, this fiction is being drafted into law.

If you poured rapeseed oil into a combustion engine, watched toxic exhaust billow from the tailpipe, and declared it a “zero-emission vehicle,” you would be laughed at. Yet inside the corridors of the European Parliament, this exact fiction is being drafted into law.

Under heavy pressure from the fossil fuel lobby and legacy carmakers, EU lawmakers are preparing to endorse a bizarre new regulatory beast: the VEEF, or “Vehicle Exclusively running on Eligible Fuels.” In plain English, these are standard combustion-engine cars promised to run exclusively on liquid biofuels or e-fuels. In exchange for that promise, Brussels plans to grant them a legal tailpipe emission score of zero.

It is regulatory alchemy at its worst. Cloaked in the seductive language of “technological neutrality,” this proposal creates an escape hatch for an obsolete technology, all while setting up ordinary European drivers for an expensive logistical nightmare.

It is just another desperate tactic to extend the life of the combustion engine by any means possible.

To understand the absurdity of the biofuel car, look at what actually happens in the engine. It’s still the exact same combustion. A piston firing on biofuels produces the same toxic cocktail of nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, and fine particulates that has choked European cities for decades. Labeling these cars “zero-emission” launders the pollution through a regulatory loophole and continues to foster emission-induced pathology.

Nor does it save the climate. The average biofuel blend available today delivers a modest 20% to 40% emissions saving compared to fossil fuels. When you factor in the indirect land-use change of first-generation crop biofuels ploughing up forests to grow food for engines, crop-based biofuel cars actually emit 23% more greenhouse gases than a standard petrol car.

Biofuel cars are being sold to the public under the guise of affordability, yet running them is punishingly expensive. Hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO) biodiesel costs around €13 per 100 kilometers to run, compared to roughly €7 for an equivalent electric vehicle. Pushing drivers toward these cars locks households into volatile, high fuel costs at the exact moment renewable electricity prices and battery costs are tumbling.

Then comes the phantom fuel problem. Europe possesses a strictly limited supply of biofuels. The continent produces only enough advanced petrol biofuel to power roughly one million cars.

The Parliament’s compromise envisions allowing food-crop fuels until 2032, before shifting new biofuels models to run strictly on advanced wastes and residues from 2033 onward. But because sales skew heavily toward petrol while advanced biofuels skew toward diesel, the arithmetic collapses immediately. If carmakers sell one million petrol VEEFs cumulatively, European biofuel supplies would run dry immediately. Millions of drivers would be left with nowhere to fill up.

How does Brussels propose to stop a driver from pulling up to a regular pump and filling their “zero-emission” car with cheaper fossil petrol?

Through a bureaucratic and technical monster. The proposals require that manufacturers install complex onboard systems to ensure fuel exclusivity: fuel sensors, tamper-proof hardware, and engine-throttling software to strand your car if the wrong liquid is detected. Pumps would require cryptographic digital handshakes with the car’s chassis number to authorize a fill-up. On top of that, it could require two separate, parallel, continent-wide pump networks; one for pre-2033 crop fuels, another for post-2033 advanced fuels.

For an EU Commission committed to deregulation and “simplification,” this is pure loophole-hungry nonsense.

Naturally, the industry knows this. The fuel-combustion lobby is already quietly pivoting to their real goal: “mass balancing.” Under this proposal, carmakers wouldn’t need to put pure biofuels into your tank at all. Instead, by using the standard blended biofuel mix of today, they could manufacture “virtual” clean cars, allowing them to keep selling dirty combustion engines while selling fewer electric vehicles.

This is not just a technical Eurocrat debate, it is an industrial fork in the road. More than €200 billion has already been committed to building Europe’s electric vehicle and battery supply chain. That capital was deployed on the promise of a clear, stable regulatory path to zero emissions by 2035.

While China dominates the global battery supply chain and electric vehicle sales surge worldwide, European policymakers are entertaining a bizarre scheme to keep 19th-century technology on life support.

The VEEF loophole solves no climate target or air pollution, helps no driver, and builds no clean industry. It is simply a regulatory Trojan horse designed to buy legacy polluters a few more years of business-as-usual. When the vote arrives, lawmakers must slam the door shut on this costly diversion.

If you are looking for a terrifying Halloween costume, a zombie combustion engine masquerading as zero-emission is about as scary as it gets.

#5818. Op-ed: Plug-in solar expands access to renewables, but needs a strong safety framework

By Michael Becker, Global Business Director, Energy Storage/Energy & Power, CSA | October 29, 2026

Access to plug-in solar is becoming increasingly available across North America. As more consumers explore technologies such as balcony solar and plug-in photovoltaic (PIPV) systems, these emerging solutions have the potential to make renewable energy more accessible and support broader participation in the energy transition. Solar remains one of the most accessible and promising renewable energy tools being added to the grid, and plug-in solar products may help expand that access to consumers who have traditionally faced economic barriers to participation.

As adoption grows, however, products designed to be convenient and accessible must still be treated as electrical products that interact with a building’s infrastructure. Product design, connectors, wiring, system integration and installation practices all play an important role in safety and performance. Expanding access and maintaining confidence in emerging technologies are complementary goals, and achieving both will require continued attention to the frameworks that support responsible deployment.

Clear safety standards, code-compliant installation practices and appropriate regulatory requirements will be essential to helping ensure that innovation can reach more consumers safely and responsibly. Solar-related issues are often associated not with the panels themselves, but with connectors, wiring and improper installation practices. A major misconception is that consumers can simply purchase a solar panel with a standard plug and connect it to a household outlet. Responsible deployment of PIPV systems depends on several complementary elements working together: products evaluated to appropriate safety standards, compliance with the National Electrical Code (NEC), qualified installation practices, and applicable state and local requirements.

No single element alone can provide the framework needed to support broad and responsible adoption.

An important emerging component of that framework is UL 3700, which is helping establish a product-safety benchmark specifically for plug-in photovoltaic systems. UL 3700 can provide manufacturers with a clearer benchmark for product development and evaluation, while giving regulators greater confidence as they consider how plug-in PV should be addressed within electrical codes and regulatory frameworks. Continued industry involvement in the development of UL 3700 will also be important as the standard evolves toward broader consensus and adoption. At the same time, UL 3700 is only one part of the overall approach. It does not replace NEC compliance, qualified installation practices or applicable state and local requirements that govern the deployment of electrical systems.

Emerging safety benchmarks are already moving from concept to practice. CSA has certified a microinverter to UL 3700, providing an early example of how the standard can be applied to products entering the market. The certification demonstrates how a consistent benchmark can be applied as new technologies enter the market, while helping support confidence among regulators, manufacturers and consumers as plug-in solar continues to develop.

The regulatory landscape for PIPV continues to evolve, with proposed changes to the NEC, state laws and local codes and ordinances aimed at facilitating the safe installation of these systems. As the industry works to establish appropriate requirements, keeping standards, codes and regulatory frameworks aligned with technological advancement will be critical to supporting the growth of PIPV products. Well-aligned requirements can help create a pathway for innovation while maintaining consistency in how emerging technologies are evaluated and deployed.

Technology itself continues to advance rapidly. Improvements in inverter technology are helping make solar more affordable while enabling greater integration of renewable energy into the grid. As inverters become more energy-dense and cost-effective, they can help lower the overall cost of PV systems and support broader adoption. New inverter capabilities can also provide valuable grid-support functions that help integrate more renewable resources and contribute to a more flexible and resilient electric grid. As these technologies evolve, standards, codes and regulatory requirements must continue evolving alongside them so that innovation and deployment can advance together.

Ultimately, greater accessibility brings greater responsibility. As plug-in solar technologies become easier for consumers to adopt, the safety frameworks that support them must keep pace with innovation. By developing appropriate product standards, maintaining NEC-compliant installation practices, utilizing qualified installers and advancing state and local requirements alongside technological progress, the industry can help expand access to renewable energy while maintaining the confidence of consumers, manufacturers, regulators installers and other stakeholders.

The statement “A major misconception is that consumers can simply purchase a solar panel with a standard plug and connect it to a household outlet.” is, in and of itself a misconception. If the plugin systems are safely designed, that is exactly what they are meant to prov ide the consumer–a solar panel with a plug they can connect to a household outlet. The fact that several millions of such systems have already been plugged in around the world without incident amply demonstrates their safety. All the hand-wringing about safety seems to be originating with existing vested interests that stand to loose significant revenues built on the existing over-complicated and over-regulated systems.

Helpful safety framing. One practical reader check is to separate product evaluation from deployment permission: UL 3700 does not replace NEC compliance, installation instructions, or state/local and utility rules, and effective dates vary by state. PluginForSolar.com maintains a U.S. state-by-state guide plus exact-system readiness checks so readers can verify those layers before buying.

#5817. Rethinking the outage map for a multi-hazard world

For many, fall means sweater weather and all things pumpkin spice. For utilities, these months have other, less festive sides. Hurricane season, wildfire season and the start of the heating season all converge in the same 8-12-week window.

Hurricane season may be quieter this year, thanks to El Niño, but data shows climate change has intensified Atlantic hurricanes. Meanwhile, fall is peak wildfire season, particularly in California, when Santa Ana winds kick up. And the northern half of the country is switching furnaces back on after months of inactivity. Individually, these are known risks utilities plan for. Layered together, they're a bigger threat.

Because of this, utilities are starting to ask more of their outage maps, moving beyond "when will my power be back on?" to "what's happening around me?" Maps are becoming less of a status tracker and more of a situational awareness tool.

For decades, utility outage maps told customers when their power would be back on, along with repair status and outage cause. That’s still valuable, but outages aren’t the only thing causing sleepless nights. Hazards now stack and planned maintenance often lands in the same week and region as storms, wildfires and seasonal gas-related risk.

Historically, customers pieced this information together from disconnected sources like text alerts, county web pages, weather apps and wildfire trackers. Now, hazard layers bring it together in one place, drawing on GIS, OMS and weather feeds.

This shift isn’t just about the growing frequency and overlap of hazards. It also reflects rising customer expectations for self-service, with the map as their first stop before the call center.

During a crisis, utility customers want access to whichever channel responds fastest and most clearly. If the utility’s map can’t deliver, their next stop is usually the already strained call center.

Utilities say they want the same thing. Chartwell's 2024 benchmark survey found that 77% named reducing call center and crew impacts as a strategic objective and 93% named satisfying customers as a strategic objective. The stakes are real. Annual call center cost is $20-40 million for a typical two-million-customer utility fielding two to three million calls a year.

What does this look like in practice? During a major winter storm, Rappahannock Electric Cooperative added richer hazard context to its outage map, adding outage polygons to outline affected areas and damage photos to explain long restoration times. The result: 500,000+ views in two days and an average session time of approximately 12 minutes, well above the global benchmark of 2.5 minutes. This shows customers used the map as a primary source, not a quick check-in.

It wasn’t an outlier. During a major multi-state storm, outage maps across affected utilities drew 9.78 million views in three days. Mobile traffic climbed from 75% to 86%, as customers checked and rechecked maps from their phones. Every customer who self-serves on the map is one less person tying up phone lines.

Visibility upgrades only matter if everyone can benefit. Language, disability and access barriers mean some customers still get left behind in a crisis. Addressing these challenges means making map information clear and in actionable language across all channels.

Text, email and voice reach different populations in different ways. During Hurricane Idalia, opt-in data to alerts showed just that: text and email led at 45.3% and 40.3%, respectively, with voice trailing at 14.4%, underscoring the value of offering multiple channels, delivered in language customers can actually act on.

Channel reach is only half the equation; plain language is the other. Most utilities are still catching up. Very few have fully simplified their messaging or removed jargon. The message needs to be clear to work.

Uptime and map refresh rates still matter, but next-gen outage maps will be judged on more than restoration times. As storms, wildfires and gas risks pile up alongside planned maintenance, utilities need to keep every customer informed, not just report on uptime. That means investing in multiple communication channels. As the Idalia data shows, each channel reaches a different slice of the customer base and no single channel is enough alone.

Treating hazard visibility, communication equity and channel diversity as one problem, not three, is what builds trust.

#5816. She Had a Life-Threatening Reaction After Sex

— Partner's antibiotic use likely triggered anaphylaxis after intercourse

A young woman with a known allergy to penicillin had a severe allergic reaction immediately after intercourse with her husband, who was taking amoxicillin.

The case underscores the fact that sexual contact can lead to mucosal exposure to beta-lactams in bodily fluids, and trigger anaphylaxis in those with allergies, Cassim Akhoon, MBChB, of King's College Hospital in London, and colleagues wrote in BMJ Case Reports.

The lesson is that unprotected sexual intercourse can be a route of transmission and cause significant allergic reactions in a partner, Akhoon told MedPage Today. "At the moment, including allergy specialists I've spoken to in the U.K., this is not something people are mindful of, nor counselling people on when they're being given a diagnosis of a drug allergy."

After this case, he counsels patients with allergies of the risk for transfer if their partner is taking penicillin, "and it's better to use protection or abstain during those times."

It's unclear whether other drugs or even foods might be transmitted in the same way, but reactions have been reported to another antibiotic, and in one case, walnuts. "We don't know enough to be able to give precise answers about which ones can, but it's enough evidence to say that some can, and it is something we need to start getting data on," he said.

Reports of anaphylaxis related to beta-lactam transfer during sexual contact are rare, the authors wrote. The case reported here is "an episode of anaphylaxis, tightly linked to a partner taking amoxicillin, supported by subsequent positive skin prick testing to amoxicillin, and a clinical course that argues strongly against seminal plasma hypersensitivity."

In this case, paramedics were called when a young woman in her 20s had sudden onset of generalized pruritic or itching, widespread urticaria or hives, and angioedema, swelling affecting her throat and tongue. Onset occurred 5 minutes after ejaculation by her partner during vaginal intercourse.

She had a prior history of penicillin allergy after having a systemic reaction to treatment with amoxicillin/clavulanic acid 5 years earlier. That reaction started only 10 minutes after her first dose, with generalized urticaria, lip angioedema, and hypotension that caused a loss of consciousness, requiring treatment in the emergency department.

Another time, she developed urticaria while crushing amoxicillin to give to her dog. Although she had not had formal allergy testing, she was prescribed a 300-μg epinephrine autoinjector due to the high risk of exposure to beta-lactams through her occupation as a student nurse.

So, in the current case, she was able to self-administer epinephrine prior to arrival of the paramedics. Once they arrived, she was found to be hypotensive, with a blood pressure of 88/56 mm Hg, and tachycardic, with a heart rate of 115 beats per minute, and have an audible wheeze on chest auscultation. They administered an additional 500 µg of intramuscular epinephrine, and transported her to the emergency department, where she was treated for anaphylaxis.

That day, she hadn't knowingly ingested beta-lactam antibiotics, and reported no new foods or medications. Her partner, however, had started taking oral amoxicillin in a dose of 500 mg, three times per day, and had taken the last dose approximately 6 hours before intercourse.

"The temporal relationship to ejaculation during the partner's antibiotic course, together with subsequent tolerance of antibiotics, led clinicians to suspect seminal transfer as the most likely exposure route," they wrote.

After observation for a minimum of 6 hours, the patient was discharged with additional autoinjectors, and a referral to specialist allergy services, the authors noted. One year later, serum-specific IgE to penicillin determinants and amoxicillin was negative, but skin prick testing showed sensitization to amoxicillin, they added.

The report also includes the perspective of the patient, who expressed concern about the reaction of the paramedics, nurse, and physician at the emergency department to the idea she had not herself taken the amoxicillin, when she had a known penicillin allergy. "This was incredibly frustrating to have to explain multiple times and not feeling believed," she said.

#5815. Eugene Becomes 5th Oregon City to Adopt Home Energy Score Requirement

Energy Audits Support Emissions Reductions and Energy Efficiency Upgrades

Eugene, Oregon — In a 6-1 vote on Wednesday, October 28th, the Eugene City Council adopted the Residential Energy Performance Disclosure Requirement ordinance, a policy commonly referred to as a Home Energy Score requirement. The vote places Eugene among four other Oregon cities, Portland, Hillsboro, Milwaukie and Bend, that have similar Home Energy Score ordinances. The vote comes in the midst of a larger trend of cities adopting a variety of policies to aid community members navigating home retrofits and efficiency upgrades as support for building electrification grows in Oregon, and nationwide in the face of efforts to undermine existing climate policy at the Federal level.

“We applaud the City Council for taking this common sense step and establishing a home energy score requirement in Eugene. This policy will ensure that home buyers have the information that they need to make informed choices when making what is often the most important financial decision in their lives,” said Bethany Cotton, Conservation Director with Cascadia Wildlands. “The vote is an important step forward to tackling building emissions, reducing energy costs, and meeting the City’s Climate Recovery Ordinance goals to reduce emissions by 50% by 2030.”

The adoption of the ordinance is the first major step from the City to reduce building emissions since the Ninth Circuit’s April 2023 decision on the Berkley building electrification requirement, which invalidated the City’s February 2023 residential building electrification ordinance. The passage of this policy in Eugene also marks more than 1 million Oregonians living in a jurisdiction with a Home Energy Score disclosure policy, representing nearly 1 in 4 Oregon residents (24.4%).

“The Ninth Circuit’s disastrous decision in 2023 set Eugene, and cities across the region, back for years on climate action and energy efficiency. While this policy is just a small step, it is a critical signal that the City is ready to begin moving decisively to regaining lost time and transitioning away from polluting fossil fuels,” said Dylan Plummer, Deputy Director of the Sierra Club’s Clean Heat Campaign. “We look forward to supporting Eugene and other local governments to continue to push the ball forward on common sense policies to require building decarbonization.”

The ordinance requires that a home energy score assessment be conducted and posted when a home is listed for sale. These assessments review the average energy cost of a home, evaluating existing appliances, heating systems, windows, doors and insulation, as well as the climate emissions associated with the home, and score the house’s energy use on a scale of one to ten. The reports include recommendations for how to improve a home’s energy efficiency and reduce emissions, and include key information about existing incentives and subsidies at the local, state and federal level.

“Eugene Water and Electric Board customers can access significant incentives to support home electrification and energy efficiency including zero interest loans and cash subsidies for weatherization and heat pumps for space and water heating. Sadly, these programs are deeply underutilized because many folks are not aware they exist,” said Meredith Tufts, Coalition Coordinator with the Fossil Free Eugene Coalition. “The Home Energy Score requirement will ensure that every new home owner has the information they need to take advantage of these programs to reduce their energy bills and climate pollution.

#5814. Utilities need to become project developers. Are they ready?

Load growth is no longer an abstract number in an electricity market report or forecast; it’s a reality. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), U.S. electricity load will increase nearly 2 percent in 2026 and 2.5 percent next year, driven by large loads like data centers and manufacturing as well as increased electrification of transportation and building heating and cooling. To put that number in perspective, annual load growth between 2005 and 2019 was about 0.1 percent, meaning the next two years will see nearly 50 times the growth that the industry experienced in the last 15 years.

Rapid load growth changes nearly everything for utilities, from how they plan and invest to how they engage and communicate with customers. Load growth is also compelling many utilities to do something they haven't done at this scale and pace before: develop their own generation. “Utilities are used to designing and building a gas plant once every five or 10 years, and then they would contract via PPAs (power purchase agreement) everything else,” said Alex Pope, Manager of Power Development Portfolios 1898 & Co. “But the systems utilities have in place to self-develop generation projects were never built to handle the volume necessary to meet the demand and timelines of today’s customer needs.”

As PPAs and BTAs (Build-Transfer Agreement) alone become insufficient to close the generation and load gap, many utilities that recognize the need to build more projects themselves face an important question: how do we start? One avenue is to focus inward and develop the internal expertise and resources needed to move projects from concept to commercialization—everything from land acquisition and permitting to financing, regulatory approvals, procurement strategies, and construction.

While this approach gives utilities complete control over the development of new generation, it also has meaningful challenges. One significant hurdle is the need to either augment the teams responsible for each phase of a successful new project or completely build from scratch. “You may have to quadruple your internal team of environmental specialists because you need to be pushing multiple projects forward,” Pope said. “The challenge is that everyone is trying to hire for these project-related roles and competition is stiff.”

Beyond adding personnel, what utilities also find is that the underlying internal processes and coordination needed to efficiently develop a large pipeline of generation projects simply don’t exist. Creating that necessary foundation involves hard choices about responsibilities and collaboration that inevitably take time that utilities don’t have if they are to meet this historic moment of load growth.

There’s another option, one that leverages existing utility expertise without requiring a vast expansion of staff. That option is to bring in a partner like 1898 & Co. to work alongside utility staff, increase their impact across projects, provide industry lessons and best practices from other utility peers, and act as the connective tissue between departments that need to collaborate for generation projects to move forward efficiently.

The rationale for the partnership is simple: utilities already have exceptionally capable people to handle environmental review, land rights, interconnection, regulatory approvals, and other aspects of project development. What utilities often lack, however, is a foundational infrastructure to ensure their internal teams work together rather than at cross-purposes across a large portfolio of projects in simultaneous development. This is necessary when utilities are trying to expand their self-development capacity from one or two projects per decade to a large and growing portfolio. “Their groups are industry best at what they do,” said Pope, who works directly with major utilities across the country to bolster the utility’s self-development capabilities. “But what they did was suited for one thermal project every five years. It was never set up to handle the throughput of what they’re being asked to do right now.”

1898 & Co.’s partnership approach is intentionally flexible, designed to supplement a utility’s existing self-development capacity and expand it to align with its goals and strategies. For example, Pope says some utilities start with development transfers, in which a third-party developer brings a shovel-ready project, and the utility completes due diligence before moving forward. This offers a lower-risk way to better understand the demands of self-development before attempting a larger portfolio of self-originated projects.

Other utilities have embraced full self-development, choosing to outsource only the capital-intensive step of land acquisition while keeping the rest of project management in-house. Utilities like Xcel Energy and DTE Energy, with support from 1898 & Co, leverage a blend development-transfer, self-development, PPA, and BTA structures to avoid putting all their eggs in one basket. No matter what model a utility chooses, Pope says 1898 & Co. provides a “single source of truth” across a portfolio of projects. This is possible because 1898 & Co. screens potential sites, manages due diligence, helps steer overall strategy, tracks deliverables, and coordinates across environmental, permitting, interconnection, and land rights teams. That combination of coordination and analysis ensures that a utility’s internal specialists, consulting partners, and selected EPC firms can all work together as one cohesive self-development team.

The financial rationale for pursuing a partnership that enhances a utility’s self-development is also compelling. 1898 & Co.’s services not only help investor-owned utilities keep up with the demands of their customers but also create strong shareholder value in the process.

Ultimately, though, what matters is whether a partnership approach allows utilities to function as high-volume generation project developers. In a recent all-source request for proposals (ASRFP), 1898 & Co. supported over 60 gigawatts of generation projects for its utility clients. Of those, 22 gigawatts were then bid in competitive RFPs. The result: 10 gigawatts won.

#5813. Exelon eyes $8B in energy storage, partly to address PJM supply crunch

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

President and CEO Calvin Butler said the grid operator isn’t adding generation fast enough, but the utility’s plan to invest in energy storage and transmission can help address the issue.

Exelon utilities could spend $3 billion to $7 billion building 1.5 GW to 3.5 GW of regulated energy storage, not including a $1 billion, 500-MW project already proposed for New Jersey, company officials said Friday during an earnings call.

“With regulated storage, we have certainty that projects get built, and control over when and how they're deployed,” Robert Kleczynski, Exelon’s CFO, said during the call. “We view utility-owned storage as one option alongside competitive development, not a replacement for it.”

Customers would benefit from the projects through lower capacity prices and the flow-through of investment tax credits, which would ease the assets’ effect on electricity rates, he said.

Three states where Exelon utilities operate — New Jersey, Maryland and Delaware — allow them to own energy storage facilities to bolster grid resiliency, Kleczynski noted.

Atlantic City Electric’s 500-MW project, developed with Invenergy, would be the largest battery installation in the PJM Interconnection and is expected to provide more than $700 million in net benefits to customers, he said. Exelon expects the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities to make a decision on the proposal late in the first quarter next year, according to Kleczynski.

PJM isn’t moving fast enough to add generation onto its system, which is the biggest issue facing consumers in the grid operator’s Mid-Atlantic and Midwest footprint, according to Calvin Butler, Exelon president and CEO.

Two key PJM initiatives — its backstop capacity procurement plan and its Interim Resource Adequacy Service proposal — have been delayed by only partial approvals by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

“Neither proposal would have solved the reliability and affordability challenges facing our customers, but both represented important steps forward,” Butler said.

However, adding energy storage and transmission can help address the issue, according to Butler. Exelon’s current capital expenditure plan calls for investing $16.3 billion on transmission through 2029, and the Chicago-based company sees opportunity for $12 billion to $17 billion in transmission spending beyond that plan, including on infrastructure for large loads.

Exelon’s “high-probability” large load additions remained flat at 11 GW — with 9 GW in Commonwealth Edison’s service area in northern Illinois and 2 GW in the Mid-Atlantic region, the company said.

Its future pipeline slipped to 23 GW — 14 GW with ComEd and 9 GW in the Mid-Atlantic — from 25 GW last quarter.

On the financial front, Exelon’s third-quarter income fell to $729 million, down from $875 million in the same period last year, partly due to higher writeoffs related to a rate case, and higher storm and interest expenses. Third-quarter revenue jumped to $7.3 billion from $6.7 billion in the year-ago period.

Not including one-time factors, third-quarter adjusted income increased to 87 cents/share from 86 cents/share in the third quarter in 2025.

In a note, Jefferies equity analyst on Friday said the earnings results and the potential spending on storage and transmission, in addition to Exelon’s $41.7 billion capital expenditure plan, were “favorable.”

However, the analysts warned that regulatory uncertainty in 2027 dampens the outlook and may offset any incremental earnings from new capital expenditures.

Exelon has close to 11 million customers through its six utility subsidiaries —  Atlantic City Electric,  Baltimore Gas and Electric,  ComEd,  Delmarva Power &  Light,  PECO Energy Co.  and Potomac Electric Power Co.

#5811. DTE utility program funded a 132-MW Michigan solar project

DTE Energy’s 132-MW Fish Creek Solar Park near Sheridan, Michigan, is now operational. The $268 million development was fully funded by customers who voluntarily participate in DTE’s MIGreenPower program. The solar park can generate enough energy to power approximately 30,000 homes.

“Our customers expect us to keep the lights on and keep bills as affordable as possible, and bringing new generation like Fish Creek online is part of how we deliver on that commitment,” said Matt Paul, president and COO of DTE Electric. “Fish Creek adds more Michigan-made energy to our system while supporting local jobs, generating new tax revenue and delivering lasting benefits for the communities that helped make this project possible.”

Fish Creek will generate tax revenue, supporting regional infrastructure, such as schools, first responders, road maintenance and veteran and senior citizen services. The solar park also created hundreds of local jobs during construction and will provide participating landowners with supplemental income.

In addition, Bushnell and Evergreen townships each received $330,000 through Michigan’s Renewables Ready Communities Award, a grant available to local governments that host large-scale renewable energy projects. The townships plan to invest the funding in town hall and fire station renovations, along with other community improvements.

Fish Creek is part of DTE’s broader plan to meet Michigan’s growing energy needs with a mix of resources. DTE currently has 20 wind parks and 37 solar parks across Michigan, which together generate enough clean energy to power nearly 1 million homes. DTE’s 2026 Integrated Resource Plan includes an additional 15 GW of renewable energy by 2042.

Billy Ludt is managing editor of Solar Power World and currently covers topics on mounting, inverters, installation and operations.

#5809. Mitsubishi Electric seeks to expand North American grid foothold

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

In August, the Japanese conglomerate said it would spend $1.4 billion to buy PCI Energy Solutions, whose platform manages about 60% of U.S. power generation.

On Friday, Mitsubishi Electric reported a 20% year-over-year revenue increase in its utility-facing business segment as it prepares to launch an electrical components joint venture with fellow industrial firm ABB and acquire an energy management software provider to boost its exposure to North American wholesale power markets.

On Aug. 20, the Japanese conglomerate said it would spend $1.4 billion to buy PCI Energy Solutions. PCI supports utilities, independent power producers and other wholesale market participants in bulk power trading and settlement, generation and transmission operations, supply-demand planning and risk management, Mitsubishi Electric said.

About 60% of U.S. power generation is managed by PCI’s platform, according to Mitsubishi Electric.

The transaction, which is expected to close by the end of 2026, will help the combined company manage a North American bulk power system transformed by rising renewable energy generation, expanded use of distributed energy resources, greater power market volatility and a broad increase in electricity demand, Mitsubishi Electric said.

“These developments are increasing demand for advanced energy management and optimization solutions capable of supporting integrated forecasting, scheduling, trading, risk management, settlement and operational decision-making,” the company said.

Mitsubishi Electric’s Infrastructure segment houses most of the firm’s work for utilities and heavy power consumers. It took in 379.7 billion yen in the second quarter of the 2027 fiscal year, up from ¥316.4 billion in the second quarter of fiscal 2026, according to financial figures released Friday.

The company’s fiscal year runs from April 1 to March 31.

Both of the Infrastructure units serving utilities and large power consumers increased their revenue by double-digit percentages, with Public Utility Systems rising by 13% and Energy Systems by 18%. Together, they comprise about 70% of Infrastructure revenues, with the non-utility Defense and Space Systems unit accounting for the remainder.

Public Utility Systems manufactures and markets water treatment controls, communications systems and power supply equipment for large utility users. Energy Systems makes and sells power plant controls, substation equipment, electric transmission and distribution components, power electronics and power supply equipment.

The Public Utility Systems unit drew strength from “large-scale projects in the uninterruptible power supply business outside Japan,” while Energy Systems “saw robust demand …. from the expanded use of renewable energy and increased investments in data centers,” Mitsubishi Electric said.

Transmission and distribution equipment orders were especially robust, the company added.

Mitsubishi Electric’s just-announced partnership with ABB would create a jointly owned subsidiary to manufacture and distribute circuit breakers, electromagnetic switches, controls and uninterrupted power supply systems rated for 5 kilovolt-amperes or less, and to sell “certain high-voltage power distribution control equipment” and smart meters, the Japanese conglomerate said on Oct. 20.

“ABB holds a leading position in the power distribution and control field, and develops power distribution and control solutions by leveraging its technologies and global sales network developed over many years,” Mitsubishi Electric said, adding that rising electricity demand outside Japan necessitates a partner with deeper exposure to international markets.

Mitsubishi Electric expects the ABB transaction to close by October 2027.

In the first half of its 2027 fiscal year, Mitsubishi Electric earned 45% of its revenue in its home market of Japan, according to its second-quarter earnings presentation. Most of the remainder came from China, other parts of Asia, Europe and North America, with roughly equal shares for each, according to a chart provided by the company.

North America, home of Mitsubishi Electric’s Pennsylvania-based electric power products subsidiary, is the conglomerate’s slowest-growing major overseas market so far this fiscal year, according to company figures. North American revenue is pacing about 5% ahead of the same period in fiscal 2026, compared with about 19% for Europe and 34% for China. Japanese revenue is up about 10% so far in fiscal 2027.

#5807. US to install 36% more wind turbines in 2025 than previous year

The United States is expected to add more than 7 GW of wind installations in 2025, a 36% increase over the previous year, and the five-year outlook remains unchanged quarter-over-quarter from previous forecast, according to the “U.S. Wind Energy Monitor” report released by Wood Mackenzie and the American Clean Power Association (ACP).

Amid a challenging market environment, the report shows that the United States is on track to add 46 GW of new wind capacity from 2025 to 2029, with total projected volumes unchanged quarter-on-quarter from previous forecasts. However, timing has shifted, as 2026 and 2027 will deliver significant gains, at 10.7 GW and 12.7 GW, respectively, as more assets advance through the development pipeline.

While Q3 installations came in 23% below forecast at 932 MW, the market has shown progress with 3.8 GW queued for Q4 2025 — representing 52% of the year’s total expected capacity. This back-loaded installation pattern is consistent with typical project-commissioning timelines.

U.S. turbine order intake has rebounded to pre-One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) levels quarter-over-quarter, supported by 2+ GW of firm commitments in Q3, the biggest intake in the region in the last nine months and a 79% quarter-over-quarter increase. However, true visibility remains limited as OEMs increasingly withhold project details and much qualifying “start-of-construction” activity occurs through off-site component manufacturing.

The market will then see a noticeable drop off, as 2029 weakens meaningfully quarter-over-quarter following project cancellations and inactive designations for late-decade capacity, driven by permitting and broader development challenges.

“The U.S. power market is facing mounting strain after a decade of flat demand, with utilities committing to 160 GW of large-load additions. This represents a significant opportunity for wind energy, which benefits from strengthened economic fundamentals and a compelling business case driven by its competitively low LCOE,” said Leila Garcia da Fonseca, director of research at Wood Mackenzie. “However, turbine costs remain elevated due to tariffs and mid-term wind growth will depend on resolving permitting and policy uncertainty.”

Power demand growth through 2029 is expected to average around 3% compared to just 0.7% over the previous decade, with data centers accounting for approximately 59 GW of the 90 GW total peak demand growth. This surge in baseload demand positions wind as a natural fit to meet rising power needs.

The five-year capacity outlook remains unchanged at 39.8 GW of added capacity quarter-over-quarter. The 2025-2027 pipeline is fully committed with all projects having turbine orders in place. More than 60% of the three-year capacity outlook has been commissioned or is under construction.

Activity is led by western states, such as Wyoming, New Mexico and others, that will account for 34% of activity in this time period. Major projects driving the outlook include Pattern’s 3.5-GW SunZia project in New Mexico, which will position the developer as 2026’s top installer, and Invenergy’s 998-MW Towner Energy Center in Colorado, the largest single project expected in 2027.

The market continues expanding geographically, with Arkansas bringing its first utility-scale onshore wind project online through Cordelio’s Crossover Wind.

The repowering market remains strong, as Wood Mackenzie projects that 18 projects will drive 2.5 GW of capacity additions in the next three years.

Wood Mackenzie expects the offshore installation pace to slow in Q4 2025 due to harsh winter weather conditions, pushing remaining capacity into 2026. Despite these near-term adjustments, Vineyard Wind has demonstrated strong execution, connecting 15 turbines in Q3 and delivering 200 GWh through nine months.

“U.S. offshore wind shows diverging momentum,” said Garcia Da Fonseca. “Projects under construction with COD estimated for 2026 continue to hit key milestones, but post-2027 developments face potential delays amid constrained wind turbine installation vessel capacity, driving delays and contract terminations.”

The offshore sector is also experiencing significant financial pressure.

The report highlights that uncertainty around tariffs is a threat to projections. Wood Mackenzie projects that tariffs will drive up turbine costs in 2026, before moderating in subsequent years. In total, U.S. onshore wind capex is projected to increase by 5% through 2029.

“U.S. wind turbine pricing is experiencing unprecedented uncertainty as conflicting market and regulatory forces interact,” said Garcia Da Fonseca. “Domestic manufacturing overcapacity relative to permitted project volumes, particularly after 2028, would normally place downward pressure on prices. Despite this, onshore wind costs are expected to continue rising due to tariff exposure on raw material inputs and subcomponents.”

#5806. Drive Forward or Turn Back? Four Reasons to Vote for a Strong Automotive Package

The coming weeks will be crucial for the future of the EU’s car and van CO₂ standards and Clean Corporate Vehicles Regulation — a choice that will shape Europe’s car market for the next decade.

Driving forward means a competitive, EU-made EV industry and clean and affordable mobility; turning back means locking in energy dependence, industrial decline, and polluting, expensive mobility paid for by citizens and companies.

Households could save €70 a month by switching from petrol to electric. Large companies will save even more. Strong CO₂ standards mean affordable electric cars. Electrifying corporate fleets will speed up supply.

Weak CO₂ standards will delay the moment electric cars cost the same as petrol cars. Citizens are stuck in a fossil fuel trap: diesel already costs €30 extra every time they fill their tank.

Europe is going electric: 38% of new cars sold in August were fully electric. Strong CO₂ standards keep European carmakers in the race. Made-in-EU requirements mean more jobs and investment.

Weak car CO₂ standards and corporate fleet targets means 22 million electric vehicles won’t be built in EU factories (T&E based on ACEA). Clinging to the combustion engine won’t protect jobs or investments from our competitors.

Cars and vans produce 16% of the EU’s CO₂ emissions. A strong automotive package puts them on track, keeping 720 million tonnes of CO₂ out of Europe’s air by 2050.

Weaker rules on cars CO2 standards would add 1.4 billion tonnes of CO2 by 2050. After Europe’s summer of climate disasters, this rollback would threaten our climate objectives and future generations.

Electric cars saved €2.9 billion in oil imports last year alone. The EU is more independent by going electric with locally sourced renewables that strengthen our energy security. Weakening CO2 standards could mean 900 million more barrels of imported oil by 2035.

Giving combustion engines on the road longer will cost Europe €74 billion. Paid by households, straight to oil-rich countries.

#5805. Rising Health Costs, Coverage Changes Worry Older Adults as Election Day Nears

Barbara Weigand could not have prepared more for retirement. She stayed healthy and saved diligently for years.

This year, though, a shoulder surgery and a bladder cancer diagnosis have really tested her finances. She recently withdrew $4,000 from her retirement account to cover medical expenses associated with her cancer treatment.

"On my monthly income, I would not be able to afford my new medical expenses," said Weigand, 83, who lives in North Canton, Ohio. She is currently on a Medicare Advantage plan and was searching for new coverage as Medicare's open enrollment period began in October.

For older adults in the U.S., the rising cost of healthcare is hitting where it hurts most -- their pocketbooks. With Medicare costs, prescription drug prices, and long-term care expenses weighing on household budgets, their concerns could carry significant political weight heading into Tuesday's elections.

Weigand is part of a reliable voting bloc; 83% of voters over age 50 say they're extremely motivated to vote in the midterms, according to an AARP poll conducted in early October. Their concerns over managing healthcare costs put the issue of affordability squarely in the spotlight.

Here are some of their biggest healthcare concerns -- and how Weigand sees them.

THE SITUATION: Open enrollment for Medicare plans began in mid-October, and enrollees are facing a slew of changes that will go into effect in 2027.

During the enrollment period, people are considering higher Part D out-of-pocket caps, the end of temporary federal Part D premium subsidies, and new drug price negotiations. Additionally, in some states, insurers put caps on the number of people who can enroll in Advantage plans, pulling out of markets or eliminating plans that people have come to rely on.

Juliette Cubanski, PhD, MPH, director of KFF's program on Medicare policy, told the Associated Press that the open enrollment period offers enrollees "an opportunity to evaluate the coverage they have and see if there might be better options for them in terms of accessing the care that they need, at possibly a lower cost."

While Weigand is grateful to have the mental acuity to do the research and the spiritual community that she relies on, she worries about other older people who are struggling to plan for the year ahead. "There are so many changes, and a lot of people my age who don't know where to start," she said. "What do they do?"

Worry No. 2: The Affordability of Prescription Drugs

THE SITUATION: The Trump administration has made lowering drug prices a priority in its effort to show Americans that it is tackling soaring costs. Republican President Donald Trump has struck multiple most-favored-nation drug deals with pharmaceutical companies and has launched the discount drug website TrumpRx, among other steps.

In September, his administration said all 50 states would join in on a program set to provide most-favored-nation pricing to some drugs within the Medicaid program, bringing the net price of selected drugs down to prices paid in certain other countries.

Still, the cost of prescription drugs prevents some people from filling prescriptions. A KFF survey from March found that about 4 in 10 U.S. adults say they have not taken their medication as prescribed in the past year due to costs.

Weigand is considering rationing her drugs to save money. "I've been thinking -- if I could just do this every other day rather than every day to make the medicine last longer," she said. "Isn't that sad?"

The KFF report said about 1 in 5 people surveyed had cut pills in half or skipped doses of medicine in the prior year because of the cost.

Worry No. 3: The Costs of Long-Term Support

The costs of receiving long-term care -- whether from spouses, home-care aides, or friends -- have risen steeply for retirees.

An AARP report released Wednesday that examines out-of-pocket caregiving expenses finds that family caregivers are spending nearly 60% more supporting a family member or friend than 5 years ago. They spend an average of $11,508 a year supporting a family member or friend, compared with $7,242 in 2021, according to the report.

"We're already hearing from our members about healthcare affordability -- its prescription drug costs, caregiver costs, co-pays, premiums," said Nancy LeaMond, AARP's executive vice president and chief advocacy officer. "Not only are we trying to help family caregivers with their finances, but also to get them the kind of information they need to help their loved ones."

These worries are top of mind for older people. About one-third of Americans over 50 provide regular care to an adult relative or friend with a health issue or disability, according to a national poll on healthy aging conducted in September 2025 by the University of Michigan.

Worry No. 4: The Solvency of Social Security

The Social Security Administration announced this month that the annual cost-of-living adjustment for older adults and people with disabilities will rise by 3.6% beginning in 2027. That translates to $75 extra per month for the nearly 72 million people who receive monthly Social Security benefits and about 7.3 million beneficiaries who get Supplemental Security Income.

The agency faces an approaching bankruptcy date if a funding shortfall is not addressed by Congress.

The Social Security and Medicare trustees' report from June states that Social Security's combined trust funds, which cover old age and disability recipients, will be unable to pay full benefits beginning in 2034. After that, incoming revenue would cover about 83% of scheduled benefits.

With 2034 not far away, the upcoming Congress will be on the hook to determine how to shore up the program.

Matt Hogan, a partner at the Impact Research polling firm, has this advice to candidates in the closing days of the midterm campaign: "Regardless of party, to make inroads with these voters, Social Security and Medicare should definitely be part of their messaging."

#5803. EVs Sales Are Rising And Another Gasmobile Bites The Dust

The automotive press is practically aflame with rumors that Ford is replacing its Ford Escape crossover SUV with an electric version, also to be named Escape. That has raised quite a ripple across the esoteric field of car-naming. Normally when a model retires, so does the name. The US auto industry is littered with has-beens, wanna-be’s, never-was, and just plain exhausted cars that retired along with their names. Hmmm….perhaps Ford is sending a not so subtle signal about the future of EV sales in the US…

By now, everyone knows that EV sales cratered last fall, after US President Donald Trump and his Republican majority in Congress engineered the “OBBA” tax bill to eliminate federal tax credits for EVs.

Still, EV sales did not actually stop in their tracks, let alone reverse course. A fresh wave of off-lease, used EVs helped keep the momentum up earlier this year, and some automakers (looking at you, Subaru) stayed on track with plans for new EVs in the US.

Plug-in hybrids also factored in as a sort of gateway drug, with Audi CEO Gernot Döllner among those looking forward to strong EV sales in that category.

EV stakeholders must smell blood in the water as Election Day 2026 approaches. With polls indicating that  Trump will lose his chokehold on federal EV policy, news about EVs has been tumbling through the Intertubes over the past several weeks. Among the examples, Slate Auto opened its first showroom in Chicago, and General Motors unveiled its gen-4 EV platform.

Somewhat bizarrely, the Trump administration also contributed to the news cycle with the launch of the new “BattMan” battery collaboration earlier this week. Under the umbrella of the US Department of Energy, BattMan hooks up federal laboratories with academic and private sector partners to push the envelope on next-gen batteries for transportation applications as well as stationary energy storage.

Of course, Tesla also weighed in with its “flying car” stunt, but that was just a stunt. Over in the world of street legal EVs, Ford has been working the publicity machine to gin up interest in the forthcoming Fathom all-electric pickup truck, which is on track for volume production early next year at an MSRP starting at the affordability benchmark of $28,350 with a built-in inverter that cuts the cost of bidirectional charging, too.

The Fathom illustrates how much blood, sweat, and tears go into naming a new car. It’s a mid-sized pickup like the popular Maverick, but Ford went off in a new direction with the Fathom, considering hundreds of options over a months-long naming journey before settling on a maritime-adjacent reference to deep understanding.

The Fathom will be the first EV to roll off Ford’s new “Universal EV” manufacturing platform, and the automaker has indicated that the next vehicle will be a compact SUV. The consensus has settled on something resembling the Escape crossover SUV, all the more so because Ford has been laying plans to retire the gasmobile…but maybe, not the name.

That’s where the ears of the automotive press have pricked up, drawing attention to the Escape landing page that depicts the rear end of a forlorn, rain-splattered Escape heading off into the dustbin of automotive history along with its dual exhaust system.

And, here’s where things get interesting. The text on the landing page simply notes that the Ford Escape is “tapping the brakes,” which has been interpreted as a pausing message, not a forever message.

However, on the same page Ford provides a good reason why the 2026 Escape will not fly. The car is not for sale in California and several other states.

“The 2026 Ford Escape® is not certified for emissions requirements with the California Air Resources Board,” Ford states in a drop-down link. “Therefore, it is not available for purchase by customers intending to register their vehicle in states that have adopted California’s certification requirements for the 2026 model year, specifically California, Massachusetts, Oregon, New York, Washington, and Vermont.”

Ford goes on to suggest two other gas-powered SUVs that are street legal in California-compliant states, the 2026 Bronco Sport SUV and the 2026 Ford Explorer SUV.

So, is Ford really banking on the Escape brand to boost its EV sales in the US? Maybe! In August, the Detroit Free Press summarized a swirl of rumors around the idea of an electric Escape, citing insider sources including a Ford dealer with access to the company’s program codes.

However, in the same report, Reuters cites an inside source who indicated that in 2029, Ford plans to introduce a new entry-level SUV in hybrid and gasoline powertrains.

“At the Las Vegas meeting, the executives, the dealer said, assured dealers that the automaker is committed to hybrid powertrains going forward,” Reuters emphasized.

Hmmmm…so much for an all-electric escape. Back in May, the Canadian Ford dealer MSAFord also raised some questions about an all-electric replacement for the Escape in a blog post (breaks added for readabilty):

“Production of the Ford Escape and Lincoln Corsair ended at the Louisville Assembly plant last December, leaving a giant hole in The Blue Oval’s lineup as it pertains to small crossovers.”

“This is particularly true of the Escape, which disappeared at a time when new vehicle shoppers are increasingly looking for more affordable options, too.

“However, back in December 2022, a report surfaced from AutoForecast Solutions, claiming that the Ford Escape would live on as an all-electric crossover, though it has thus far remained unclear if that plan is intact ever since”

Readers, what do you think? Is half an EV better than none? Full EV sales have yet to surge, but plug-in hybrids have become more popular on the heels of US President Donald Trump’s witless decision to bomb Iran last February.

EREV (extended range EVs) are another halfway-there option that will factor into an uptick in EV sales. The Scout Motors branch of Volkswagen, for example, has stated that EREVs account for the majority of its reservations so far.

Then there’s the pure EV players, including robotaxi stakeholders alongside Slate and Rivian, which is forging ahead with plans to construct a new factory in Georgia.

As for industry leader Tesla, that’s a whole ‘nother can of worms. CEO Elon Musk has earned a fair share of bad publicity in recent years, as depicted in the new “Musk” documentary. However, the film wrapped sometime last year, leaving Musk’s latest hi-jinks for the sequel.

#5801. Electric Hydrofoils Save Energy, But Do They Earn Their Price?

Hydrofoils have an obvious appeal. Lift a boat’s hull clear of the water, reduce drag and move passengers faster while consuming less energy. I’ve written before about the proposed electric hydrofoil ferry between Vancouver, Bowen Island and Gibsons, where floating logs, coastal conditions and uncertain passenger demand make the economics difficult. Hydrofoils have been commercially available for decades, but their operating niche remains narrower than their technical appeal suggests.

A different opportunity emerged when Antwerp pilotage operator Brabo ordered an Artemis EF-12 electric hydrofoil pilot boat in August 2024. The vessel combines electric propulsion with submerged foils and active controls. Artemis has also demonstrated ship-contact manoeuvres using its EF-12 workboat platform, while the EF-12 Pilot design entered sea trials in 2026. The handling benefits are relevant to pilot transfers even when the boat isn’t operating at full speed.

The financial question is whether a hydrofoil can spend enough of its working life taking advantage of its design. Antwerp pilot boats work around locks, docks, ship movements and changing assignments. Reaching a high maximum speed is of limited value when the vessel spends much of its day manoeuvring or travelling through constrained waterways.

I tested that question using a Python-based operating model with synthetic assignments and three hypothetical sets of port-speed permissions. Depending on how much suitable high-speed water was available, the EF-12 spent zero, approximately 6% or approximately 13% of its underway time foilborne. These are modeled scenarios, not measurements of Brabo’s operations or actual Antwerp speed authorizations.

The resulting financial comparison was unflattering to the hydrofoil. In the central case, the EF-12’s modeled fifteen-year discounted cost was approximately €5.32 million, compared with €3.81 million for a conventional diesel tender, a premium of about 40%. Both figures include purchasing new vessels, rather than comparing a new hydrofoil with the marginal cost of keeping an existing diesel boat.

Electric propulsion still brought substantial energy benefits. The hydrofoil’s problem was that lower purchased energy did not compensate for the assumed capital cost and the limited opportunity to operate in its most efficient regime. Its active controls and potential ride-quality benefits remain relevant, but the available evidence did not justify assigning them a financial value.

An alternative electric approach also deserves consideration. Norway’s Moen Marin and Pascal Technologies have developed an air-cavity electric personnel vessel that reduces hull resistance without lifting most of the vessel above the water. It performed better financially than the hydrofoil in the exploratory comparison, although the existing craft was designed for aquaculture work and would require appropriate adaptation and certification before serving as a pilot tender.

The lesson resembles the one I drew from the Vancouver hydrofoil ferry proposal. Hydrofoils can be excellent machines, especially where sustained high-speed passages and suitable sea conditions allow them to exploit their advantages. In congested harbours, their additional complexity and capital cost need much stronger justification.

Different routes, operating permissions and vessel prices could produce different results. For commercial fleet decisions, the relevant benchmark is the work the vessel actually completes and the total cost of providing that service.

#5800. CT Images Facilitate PCI's 'New Era': Planning Before Catheterization

— CCTA-based upstream decision-making claims noninferiority in P4 trial

Coronary CT angiography (CCTA) made it feasible and safe to plan percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) procedures before cardiac catheterization, as shown by the open-label randomized P4 trial.

At 12 months, a CCTA-guided PCI strategy was noninferior to intravascular ultrasound (IVUS)-guided PCI with respect to target vessel failure -- a composite of death from cardiac causes, target vessel myocardial infarction (MI), or ischemia-driven target vessel revascularization -- occurring in 4.1% versus 4.6% of patients, respectively (P<0.001 for noninferiority), reported Carlos Collet, MD, PhD, of the Cardiovascular Research Foundation in New York City.

Additionally, CT guidance resulted in shorter procedures (46 vs 63 minutes) and reduced contrast utilization (150 vs 170 mL).

"P4 supports a CT-based pathway for PCI planning and guidance in selected patients referred to the cath lab ... What we're proposing is moving the PCI planning, not to do it in the cath lab, but basically shift that upstream to read, think, process, share the decision, and then go in the cath lab and treat," Collet concluded at the Transcatheter Cardiovascular Therapeutics (TCT) annual conference hosted by the Cardiovascular Research Foundation.

The P4 manuscript was simultaneously published in the New England Journal of Medicine.

Collet noted the current reliance on making PCI decisions in real time -- everything related to lesion preparation, stent diameter and length, and more -- during the procedure.

"That generates or increases the cognitive load of our brain, when we have to use it to make very complex decisions. So, what if we were to learn from our colleagues in the structural field and start planning PCI interventions? We will be better prepared, perhaps reduce the variability in treatment care, and that will give us an opportunity for shared decision-making with our patients," he said.

Of note, the comparator in P4, IVUS-guided PCI, is associated with a lower risk of adverse clinical events than angiography-guided PCI, but still only provides information after cardiac catheterization has begun.

TCT session discussant Emmanouil Brilakis, MD, PhD, of the Minneapolis Heart Institute Foundation, called P4 a "landmark" trial.

"The study does provide the clinical evidence we need to move to this new era that Dr. Collet alluded to, which is that of planning the procedures before we come to the cath lab," he said. "But there are many steps that we need to achieve to be able to get there. Number one is to have a high-quality scan. The scans in the study were screened and they were very high quality."

"We need to learn how to actually use the CT, how to look at the CT images, and implement them for planning our practices," Brilakis added.

Collet stressed the point that interventional cardiologists should take it upon themselves to look at the CCTA images, and not rely on the reports of the radiologists. "They [radiologists] don't know the details of the techniques that we're using. They don't know the details on when to modify the calcium, bifurcation treatment, etc. So we need to get used to looking at the pictures."

During a press conference, Collet alluded to a rising prevalence of patients undergoing CT scans before a PCI. He noted that the practice is now commonplace in the U.K.; in the U.S., it still varies widely with a national site average of about 10%, he estimated.

"Let us not forget that this requires contrast and radiation for the CT scan," Brilakis cautioned. "Therefore, this needs to be taken into account, and there is also some extra time for the patient to have this procedure."

P4, or the Precise Procedural and PCI Plan trial, was an open-label noninferiority trial that enrolled at 23 centers.

Participants were patients with a clinical indication for coronary revascularization who had undergone CCTA as part of routine clinical care before enrollment in the trial. Entry criteria included having at least one epicardial lesion with a diameter stenosis >70%, a CCTA-fractional flow reserve of ≤0.80, reference vessel diameter 2.5-4.0 mm, and no more than two target vessels.

There were 1,105 individuals randomized to CCTA or IVUS guidance of PCI. To avoid leaving underexpanded stents, Collet and colleagues mandated that the CT arm utilize stent enhancement tools based on angiography.

Median age was 65 years, and 21.7% of the cohort were women. About one in five had diabetes and fewer than 3% a prior PCI. The vast majority had stable ischemic heart disease (about 98%) as opposed to acute coronary syndrome, and the extent of coronary artery disease was mostly one vessel (64%). Average SYNTAX scores were 8 for the CCTA group and 9 for IVUS.

Study authors noted that the burden of coronary calcification was substantial in this cohort, with mean coronary calcium scores of approximately 500, and over 10% of participants judged to have severe calcification.

Participants who ultimately ended up receiving PCI came out to about 93% in both arms.

The investigators reported that beyond the aforementioned primary analysis, CCTA guidance continued to have favorable results when target vessel failure was broken down to its individual components:

Additionally, a per-protocol analysis was consistent with the intention-to-treat analysis.

The noninferiority margin used for the study was an absolute risk difference of 4.5 percentage points. With that met, the investigators proceeded to test for superiority of CCTA guidance, which did not meet significance.

Safety events in P4 did not raise red flags for CCTA-guided PCI. There was no major excess of all-cause death (0.2% vs 0.5% in the IVUS-guided PCI group), bleeding of Bleeding Academic Research Consortium (BARC) type 2, 3, or 5 (1.4% vs 1.3%), or BARC type 3 or 5 bleeding (0.4% vs 0.7%).

However, the P4 trial had lower than expected event rates and is still pending a final 5-year follow-up, Collet acknowledged.

Moreover, among the trial's exclusion criteria were ST-segment elevation MI, left main coronary artery disease, previous PCI in a target vessel, previous coronary artery bypass grafting, and a severely low estimated glomerular filtration rate.

Collet reported that CT planning appeared disproportionately beneficial for patients with the most complex coronary disease. As such, a new trial, P5, is now ongoing, testing the strategy specifically in this population.

#5799. Fuel From Bamboo Costs Just $2.75 Per Gallon

At CleanTechnica, we are passionate champions of the “electrify everything” movement promoted by Tony Seba and Mark Jacobson, among others. However, being realistic, internal combustion engines will continue to play an important role in transportation by land, sea, and air for the remainder of this century and perhaps beyond.

Almost any plant that grows could potentially be turned into a biofuel with a lower emissions footprint than gasoline or diesel. Currently in the US, millions of tons of corn are used every year to make ethanol, which is then blended with gasoline. In theory, the ethanol helps lower emissions, but the reduction, if any, is modest and it decreases fuel economy, so motorist are actually using more fuel than they would if they used ordinary, unadulterated gasoline.

The other part of the equation is that the conversion process itself requires a fair amount of energy and makes its own greenhouse gas emissions, which politicians conveniently choose to ignore. Ethanol, then, is mostly a scam that rewards farmers, but has few other benefits. While the science is sound, the rewards are far less than claimed. However, farmers are an important political group and no one wants to tell them that corn for ethanol is no longer a thing.

Researchers at Worcester Polytechnic Institute think they have found a better way. In a study published September 24, 2026 in the Royal Society of Chemistry journal Sustainable Energy And Fuels, Michael Timko, the head of the chemical engineering department at WPI, and  Timothy Woodard, PhD, claim that bamboo may be the perfect source material for making biofuels. In the published study, they write:

“Corn stover, an agricultural residue widely available in the U.S., has been one of the most studied biomass sources for biofuel production.6 Yet its relatively modest yields and high ash content have created significant challenges for scaling up production. Alternative feedstocks such as switch grass have been explored, but these offer only incremental improvements in performance relative to corn stover, particularly in ash content and growth rate. These limitations highlight the importance of identifying and evaluating less conventional biomass sources that may offer superior attributes for fuel production.

“Bamboo has emerged as a strong candidate due to its rapid growth, high productivity per unit area, and low input requirements. Some bamboo species reach their full height within a few months and mature within four years. Bamboo’s deep root systems improve soil stability, promote subsurface carbon sequestration, and support water conservation. It can also be grown on marginal or degraded land, reducing competition with food crops and offering economic opportunities for rural communities.

“Critically, bamboo also possesses an exceptionally low ash content compared with most lignocellulosic feedstocks, which minimizes inorganic fouling and catalyst poisoning during thermochemical conversion and improves the quality of the resulting biocrude. Furthermore, the presence of ash complicates thermochemical conversion to products, with frequently reported adverse effects on yields.

“The characteristics of fast growth, low fertilizer and water use, and low ash content make bamboo stand out as a promising source of biomass that can achieve economic competitiveness that has not been obtained with other feedstocks. Unfortunately, despite these advantages, bamboo remains largely underexplored as a feedstock for liquid fuel production, especially in thermochemical conversion processes such as hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL).”

Here’s the best part. The researchers believe biofuel from bamboo could be commercially viable at a price of $2.75 a gallon. That’s less than gasoline at the moment and less than half the cost of diesel. What’s more, when compared to diesel, the resulting emissions are up to 26 times lower. So let’s see:  Less than half the cost and only 5 percent of the emissions? Think anyone would take that deal? Oh, you betcha!

Bamboo is a grass, and one of the fastest-growing plants on Earth. Some species grow several dozen inches in a day. Because of this fast growth, the US could make as much fuel from bamboo as it makes ethanol from corn while using only 13 percent as much land.

“I think this research is especially timely and important because fuel prices are high and the transportation sector produces more greenhouse gas emissions in the U.S. than any other,” said professor Timko in a press release. “Bamboo would use different land than we are using for food production, so there is no food versus fuel trade-off. Farmers win, consumers win.

Using bamboo for fuel can reduce greenhouse gasses in two ways, the researchers maintain. First, the process to convert it into biocrude is more efficient than it is for other feedstocks. Second, bamboo itself captures and stores large amounts of carbon both above and below ground.

Unlike annual crops used for many biofuels, bamboo is a perennial grass that can produce large amounts of biomass with relatively low agricultural inputs. Compared with other perennial grasses, bamboo has very low ash content (less than 1% by dry weight), meaning that the conversion process generates negligible waste.

The economic modeling conducted by the researchers indicates that bamboo-based fuel could sell for as little as $2.75 per gasoline equivalent under mature commercial-scale conditions, accounting for the money required to build and operate the fuel plant, suggesting strong economic competitiveness as the renewable-fuel industry expands. Considering the ability of bamboo to store large amounts of carbon in its underground rhizomes, producing fuel from bamboo would generate a greenhouse gas intensity of 3.5 grams of carbon dioxide-equivalent per megajoule of energy, the researchers report.

“The U.S. has enormous land area under cultivation for corn ethanol, a fuel which is often blended into gasoline,” said professor Timko. “Freeing up at least some of that land could allow for more food production and reduce the burden on the environment. Bamboo may eventually offer industry a way to generate low carbon liquid fuels at scale. With further research and development, bamboo could be a compelling option for decarbonization in sectors that are difficult to electrify, including heavy duty transport and aviation fuel supply chains.”

The researchers also point out that bamboo can be cultivated on former industrial land or heavily farmed properties where other crops and vegetation struggle to grow. Their research found the growth rate of bamboo (22–44 tons per hectare per year) “is at least three times that of corn stover and at least twice that of switch grass.

Based on the lowest growth rate, an idealized circular [bamboo] plantation with a 30 mile radius corresponds to an estimated 16.1 million dry tons of biomass per year. Ash content, a critical parameter for processing efficiency and waste generation, was less than 1 percent in bamboo, compared with 4.8–7.3 percent for corn stover and 2.2–11.9 percent for switch grass.

With such data in mind, expect the current US administration to impose a heavy tax on bamboo based biofuel to protect the profits of the oil industry and corn growers. Nothing must be allowed to challenge the hegemony of fossil fuels or the profits of Big Ag. And please don’t tell the head doofus that the WPI research was funded in part by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory and the National Science Foundation. If he found that out, his head might explode!
