#5755. Swarm Of Electric Trucks Coming To US (Battery Swapping Included?)

Tesla CEO Elon Musk famously ditched the idea of EV battery swapping back in 2015 after a brief experiment. That pretty much laid the idea to rest here in the US, but other EV stakeholders soldiered on. The latest example is the Australian firm Janus Electric, which is bringing its Class 8 heavy duty electric truck conversions to North America. Janus offers a battery-as-a-service model that includes both charging and swapping…so, is battery swapping finally coming here to the US?.

Battery swapping for two-wheelers and larger EVs is commonplace in some overseas markets, with industry leader Nio being one example. So far, though, swapping stations for e-bikes are the only sign of emerging activity in the US.

Musk’s opinion aside, a modern battery swapping station can change a spent electric car battery for a fresh one in just a few minutes, or less time than it takes to drive through an automated car wash. On the other hand, considering today’s EV fast charging technology, battery swapping is somewhat less relevant to passenger cars and other light duty vehicles. Access to home charging is another factor that can limit the appeal of driving to a battery swapping station for a refresh.

Electric trucks, though, are another kettle of fish. Every minute counts in the fast paced transportation industry. Waiting in line for an EV charging station to free up is a non-starter, and then there’s the charging time. Even the much-heralded Tesla Semi Class 8 truck can take hours to reach a full charge overnight, though the truck is reported to achieve 60-70% charge in as little as 30-45 minutes at fast charging stations.

The time factor explains why battery swapping for trucks is appearing in overseas markets. The seeds of change have also begun to sprout up in the US, where the the diesel-to-electric conversion field is beginning to offer some opportunities. Last summer, for example, the US startup Revoy (formerly SixWheels) announced a swappable battery retrofit for Class 8 diesel trucks. The retrofit consists of a battery unit inserted between the cab and the trailer, which can be swapped out in a matter of minutes. The unit does not replace the engine, but it reportedly cuts diesel emissions by up to 85%, with a 95% fuel savings aided by regenerative braking.

The US Army is also dipping a toe in the conversion field with “idling kits,” which are batteries powerful enough to run on-board equipment for military vehicles in near silence, without the giveaway noise and heat signature involved in idling the vehicle’s engine. No word yet on whether or not swap-outs will be part of the picture, but the technology pieces are in place.

So much for the current state of affairs. Last week a full diesel-to-electric conversion opportunity suddenly appeared when the Canadian lithium-ion battery specialist Electrovaya announced a new $26 million diesel-to-electric supply agreement with the Janus that leverages Electrovaya’s proprietary “Infinity Battery Technology, a durable system compatible with daily swapping cycles for Class 8 trucks.

The $26 million agreement represents just the initial phase of orders for the US and Canadian markets. “Electrovaya has also agreed to invest approximately $1.4 million in Janus for up to 4.2 million shares, together with up to 6.3 million warrants,” Electrovaya noted, indicating a long term partnership allowing plenty of room for scaleup.

“Janus’s approach converts existing diesel prime movers to battery-electric operation and pairs them with swappable battery packs and Janus Charge & Change Stations, allowing fleets to exchange batteries in minutes rather than wait hours to recharge, and to electrify without the capital cost of purchasing new trucks,” Electrovaya explained (see additional coverage on CleanTechnica  here and here).

Janus’s footprint in North American is still tiny, at 118 truck conversion orders and commitments in the US and Canada combined. However, the firm’s business with Electrovaya should help ramp up the activity. Janus has already begun deliveries to Electrovaya, and Electrovaya has announced a major expansion of its North American manufacturing footprint. The showpiece is a production facility in Jamestown, New York covering lithium-ion battery cells, modules, and packs.  Start of operations is schedule for sometime next year.

With US President Donald Trump’s war in Iran continuing to elevate diesel costs, both Janus Electric and Electrovaya smell an end to the partisan war on EVs that rocked the US market after Trump took office in January of 2025. “Electrovaya’s expanding North American manufacturing capabilities will be important as we scale,” said Janus CEO and Managing Director Ben Hutt in a press statement.

“The investment is a strong vote of confidence in our technology and approach to electrifying heavy transport,” Hutt added.

The CEO of Electrovaya, Dr. Raj Das Gupta, also underscored the potential for rapid scaleup. “Janus has developed a practical solution to one of the major challenges facing heavy transport, enabling diesel-powered trucks to be converted to electric without compromising their commercial operations,” Gupta emphasized.

“Our strategic investment, together with the warrants, aligns us closely with Janus’s long-term growth,” Gupta also explained, with warrants referring to up to 6.3 million in contracts for future stock transactions.

If you’re wondering how much traction Electrovaya and Janus will gain in the US electric truck conversion space, that’s a good question considering Trump’s on-again, off-again trade wars with the upstairs neighbors.

The factory in New York State should help push matters along. As if on cue, over the weekend the White House also signaled that Trump is suddenly willing to call off his tariff dogs, potentially leading to a trade deal with Canda that could help accelerate activity in the US electric truck conversion field, among other areas.

On the other hand, the negotiations are described as achieving an early stage “concept” of a deal, which makes it seem more like a weak effort to gin up voter support for the Republican ticket ahead of Election Day on November 3. The concept of a deal could just as easily de-materialize by the morning of November 4.

Deal or no deal, Trump is scheduled to leave office in January of 2029 at the latest — peacefully this time, one hopes — opening up space for a new era of stability and mutual benefit in US-Canada trade relations.

In the meantime, keep an eye on Electrovaya for more activity in the electrification field, with or without help from the US market. In addition to supplying batteries for electric truck conversion, the company anticipates business in the fields of material handling, robotics, defense, and AI data center infrastructure.

Photo: The Australian firm Janus Electric has hooked up with Canada’s Electrovaya to accelerate the electric truck conversion field in North America, regardless of the sharp U-turn in US electrification policy (cropped, courtesy of Janus).

#5754. Driving A 43-Horsepower Geo Metro Convertible From New York To Los Angeles Looks Really Miserable

The Geo Metro Convertible is one of the silliest cars ever sold in America. The Metro hatchback was already a misfit on American roads, with its microscopic 1.0-liter three-cylinder engine, 1,600-pound curb weight, and $7,000-ish starting price. It was a General Motors rebadge of a Suzuki Swift, and it almost immediately became the butt of every automotive joke. There was no logical reason, then, for any engineer to lop off its roof and turn it into a convertible, but that didn't stop it from happening, and honestly I'm grateful GM sold them anyway. I doubt GM ever imagined that a YouTuber would end up driving one from New York to Los Angeles 34 years after it was built, but that's just what Mitchell Kohrmann did in his latest video.

When new, the Geo Metro convertible was fabled to have 55 horsepower and 58 pound-feet of torque, but Kohrmann was smart enough to dyno test his remarkably clean 1992 Metro convertible before setting off on his cross-continental journey. Before that, though, he gave it a tune-up and fixed the air conditioning — or at least he thought he did... After a 50-second pull, the dyno showed the Metro made 43 horsepower and 53 lb-ft of torque. That's more than enough to complete a 2,838-mile road trip that includes a 10,000-foot climb, right?

I had never seen any of Kohrmann's videos before watching this one, but looking at his other uploads, he's no stranger to long drives, including a 10,050-mile drive to the Arctic Ocean in a Touareg V10 diesel, and a 6,500-mile drive in a V10 Audi S8. Those are both leather-lined luxury cruisers, though, and going from that to a vinyl-topped three-cylinder economy car must feel like quite the downgrade. With just 43 horsepower, Kohrmann ends up keeping the little Metro's gas pedal in contact with the floor a lot more than I expected.

The calamities begin before he even starts his journey, since he realized the Geo's tires may have looked fine at first, but they were utterly ancient, so he had to source some 155/80R13 tires at the last minute. Fortunately he finds some that will fit, and sets off on the drive. Predictably, the drive into and out of Manhattan involves navigating excruciating traffic jams, but once he gets out away from New York, he starts covering more ground.

This video is about 1.5 hours long, and includes lots of POV shots as well as breakdown and repair content and tons of beautiful scenery. Kohrmann initially intended to attempt to beat some sub-1.0-liter engine Cannonball Run record of 48 hours, 9 minutes and 53 seconds that was set in 1964 by a Sunbeam Imp, but he gives up on that after a series of setbacks. Regardless, he still completes the journey in 49 hours, 11 minutes and 18 seconds, after a harrowing journey filled with twists, turns, breakdowns, and hellish traffic jams. I think it's worth a watch. Cheers to you, Mitchell, for following through on what looks like an utterly miserable journey, but a really cool video.

#5753. As Diesel Costs Surge for Farmers & Rural Businesses, Solar Offers a Lifeline

The cost of diesel fuel rose nearly 33% from 2025 to 2026, with some countries experiencing even higher price spikes. For many of the world’s rural farmers, processors, and small businesses, solar-powered equipment offers an attractive alternative.

On a dry hillside in Chamwino, central Tanzania, mango farmers used to watch their trees struggle through the long months without rain. Irrigation was technically possible: A diesel pump could lift water from a nearby borehole. But in practice, fuel was too expensive and too unpredictable for smallholders to run the system often enough. When diesel prices rose, farmers irrigated less, production dropped, and most households stayed locked into low-yield farming and razor-thin margins.

In 2021, a solar-powered pump and drip irrigation system replaced the diesel setup as part of a pilot project. Within one season, farmers reported that their mango production and average income from mango sales roughly doubled, as farmers could irrigate beyond the rainy season and manage their orchards more intensively. The technology change was simple—solar instead of diesel. But for farmers, it meant shifting from a fuel prone to wild price swings to an energy source they could rely on and afford.

Chamwino is not an isolated case. Across Africa and other regions, farmers, processors, and rural businesses are among the most exposed to diesel price spikes, like those happening right now. Because diesel powers irrigation pumps, generators, mills, and refrigerators, every price jump shows up as higher operating costs, thinner margins, and greater risk.

Distributed clean energy is emerging as one of the most practical ways to break that dependence.

While access to electricity has expanded significantly over the last 10 years, the reality is that diesel still powers much of rural life in places like sub-Saharan Africa. Only 33% of the rural population can access electricity. Even among those with power connections, frequent outages and poor quality have led farmers, processors, retailers, mines and telecommunications companies to rely on diesel generators for backup or primary power. An Energy for Growth Hub study estimated that 150–190 gigawatts (GW) of distributed diesel generator capacity was operating across Africa in 2024, compared with 268 GW of grid-connected capacity. Removing South Africa from the equation, Sub-Saharan Africa had nearly 1.5 times as much diesel generator capacity as grid-connected capacity. And diesel capacity exceeded grid capacity in at least 26 African countries.

The war on Iran has exposed the vulnerability created by this “shadow power system.” The average global retail diesel price exceeded $1.50 per liter in the second quarter of 2026, 20% higher than the previous three months and 32.9% higher than a year earlier. In Africa, retail diesel prices rose by 25% on average across 42 countries between mid-January and mid-June 2026.

The regional average masks sharp differences between countries. In some, subsidies, tax cuts, and administered fuel prices have cushioned consumers from rising international prices, but at a cost to government budgets, especially in fuel-importing economies with limited fiscal space. Elsewhere, consumers have faced much larger increases at the pump. Diesel prices increased by 86% in Nigeria and more than 50% in Tanzania and Ethiopia from January to June 2026.

The effects extend beyond the cost of running generators. Diesel powers agricultural machinery, irrigation pumps, mills and refrigerators. Diesel-fueled road transport connects farms with suppliers and consumer markets. The impacts of the Iran conflict are already rippling through interconnected energy, fertilizer, trade and logistics networks, raising the costs of agricultural production and food distribution across Africa and elsewhere. Fertilizer prices have increased by 30-45% in several African markets since the conflict began, increasing the risk that farmers will reduce application rates, switch to other crops or miss their planting windows.

The effects are felt most acutely at the local level. For example, members of a women’s groundnut processing cooperative in Nigeria reported that rising fuel and fertilizer costs increased the price of raw groundnuts and groundnut oil by 33%. In Myanmar, which imports more than 90% of its fuel and relies predominantly on road transport, higher diesel prices have increased the cost of moving food and agricultural inputs, and have led to rising rice prices for consumers.

We already have better alternatives. Many locations are struggling with diesel-based irrigation, cooling and backup power, but solar and other distributed renewables can provide more affordable and reliable electricity than diesel-dependent systems.

The shift is already gaining momentum. In Africa, 17 GW of solar capacity will be installed in 2026 — a 45% increase from 2025, equivalent to approximately 100,000 panels installed each day. Much of the recent growth is happening outside large power plants: Roughly three-quarters of Africa’s solar growth between 2023 and 2025 came from distributed systems, as households and businesses sought alternatives to unreliable supply and diesel generation.

The benefits are already visible for some who have made the switch.

Ethiopia’s Berbere district, or woreda, is surrounded by four rivers, yet for years farmers could not use that water for irrigation. Limited access to electricity and the high cost and unreliability of petrol and diesel made pumping water from rivers to fields impractical, keeping production closely tied to rain-fed maize and teff. In 2025, WRI and partners installed two solar-powered water pumps to lift river water to irrigated plots. In the first production season, households involved in the project earned an average $709 from onion cultivation alone, compared with around $207 annually from maize and teff before the solar-powered pumps were installed. Farmers also reported being able to harvest more than once a year, plant surplus crops such as onions and chilies to increase their incomes, and make new investments in livestock and home improvements.

Similarly, when Kenya experienced its longest nationwide power blackout in 2023, one Nairobi hospital maintained critical services thanks to its solar-plus-battery storage system. For rural clinics and county hospitals, similar systems can ensure power even when the grid fails, without tying budgets to volatile fuel prices and expensive back-up diesel generators.

There’s huge potential for distributed clean energy to further break diesel dependence and improve livelihoods in places like rural Africa and elsewhere. Energy Access Explorer, an open online geospatial platform hosted by the WRI Polsky Energy Center, lets planners examine solar potential alongside grid networks, health facilities, schools, and farming communities. Bringing these layers together can help governments and practitioners identify where clean power could cost-effectively serve livelihoods and services that currently depend on diesel.

For example, Energy Access Explorer is already informing electrification planning in Ethiopia. The Ministry of Water and Energy, working with the World Bank, has used the platform to prioritize off-grid electrification through a results-based financing program. Our latest analysis reveals that about 12.6 million people in Ethiopia live in areas with high agricultural activity and high solar potential, but little access to grid-connected electricity. These areas could be assessed for solar-powered irrigation, processing, cooling and other services that could benefit from distributed clean power.

A Uganda analysis applies the same approach to health services. The map below shows 243 health facilities and approximately 4.6 million people living in areas with limited or no connection to electricity. Yet these areas do receive abundant sunlight, making them suitable for solar power. Used alongside data on facility electricity demand, existing supply reliability, and roof or land availability, the maps can help prioritize clean power investments for rural health services.

As diesel prices continue to swing wildly with every conflict and crisis, farmers, processors, and rural businesses pay the price, alongside governments that try to keep costs low through subsidies. It’s time for energy ministers, donors and financiers to look closely at where distributed clean power can viably replace diesel and direct their investments there. The latest Tracking SDG 7 report estimates that $21 billion is needed by 2030 to provide off-grid solar to the 398 million people for whom it is the least-cost electricity option—approximately 6 times the sector’s recent investment level!

Moving from energy crisis to energy security is ultimately about knowing where clean energy truly changes livelihoods. For many of the world’s rural farmers, processors, and small businesses, that starts with swapping diesel for solar.

By Dimitris Mentiss, Lead, Energy Access Explorer

#5752. Another Surgical Treatment for Back Pain Fails in Rigorous Analysis

— Norwegian registry data show no benefit from spine fusion as part of decompression surgery

Spinal fusion added to decompression surgery in patients with spinal stenosis did not provide any added benefit versus decompression alone, Norwegian national registry data indicated.

With outcomes compared for 1,446 patients undergoing decompression alone and 806 having spinal fusion as well, no significant difference in Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) scores was seen a year later, according to James H. McAuley, PhD, of Neuroscience Research Australia in Randwick, and colleagues.

This is not the first study to question the utility of spinal fusion for patients with degenerative stenosis, the group noted in their report appearing in Annals of Internal Medicine. Earlier, prospective trials in Sweden and Norway found no improvement in disability when compared with decompression surgery alone, as did a smaller U.S.-based study (although the latter did show better quality of life with fusion). Moreover, these trials all showed a higher burden of complications such as bleeding with spinal fusion, along with prolonged operative time and increased costs.

Nevertheless, McAuley and colleagues observed, including fusion in decompression procedures is now common practice in some countries, particularly the U.S. and Australia. One analysis in 2023 found that fully 90% of U.S. surgeries for degenerative spondylolisthesis in 2019 involved spine fusion -- a 23-point increase from just 3 years previously. McAuley's group had no explanation for this explosion in popularity, while the authors of the 2023 analysis pointed to "financial incentives, lack of guidelines and/or national regulations, and delayed evidence dissemination through medical education or professional societies."

Degenerative spondylolisthesis is a common feature of spinal stenosis; it involves a forward shift in a vertebra relative to those below it. Some surgeons have viewed this as indicative of instability that should be rectified via fusion, which seems plausible on its face but, as noted above, rigorous evidence for actual benefit is weak at best.

The current study sought to extend the findings from that Norwegian trial, called NORDSTEN-DS, by examining spinal stenosis patients' outcomes as recorded in the country's national health registry. They identified a total of some 3,900 patients undergoing surgery for degenerative spondylolisthesis from 2007 to 2021. NORDSTEN-DS participants' data were included in the registry and analyzed anew in the current study, which used a "target trial emulation" approach to compare patients undergoing versus not having fusion as part of decompression surgery. After excluding patients who, for example, were very elderly or had previous surgeries in the same spinal region, the investigators had 2,252 patients for detailed analysis, including 236 who were in NORDSTEN-DS.

Mean patient age was about 65 and roughly 70% were women. ODI scores at the time of surgery averaged 38.9 for those having decompression alone and 41.4 for the group undergoing fusion (higher scores indicate worse symptoms, and the maximum is 50).

At month 12 after surgery, mean ODI scores declined to 20.0 for the fusion group and 22.3 among those undergoing decompression alone. The mean difference of 2.2 points fell short of statistical significance (95% CI -1.6 to 6.1).

McAuley and colleagues also performed some subgroup analyses to see whether patients who would be more likely to benefit from fusion could be identified from baseline characteristics, such as age, sex, body mass index, or symptom severity. This effort came up empty, as no significant differences in ODI improvement emerged. However, it did show that men with obesity (BMI ≥30) had significantly worse outcomes versus men with lower BMI values.

And, as with earlier studies, fusion led to longer operative time (mean 85 extra minutes) and longer hospital stays (mean 1.9 extra days) compared with decompression alone. Although no particular complication stood out as more common with fusion, the risk for any type of complication was doubled overall. Risk for needing additional surgery because of complications was increased even more.

"This study calls into question the highly prevalent management of pain from lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis with fusion," McAuley and colleagues wrote. "Our findings add to current evidence and should prompt reevaluation of current guidelines," which, they noted, are sparse and "offer conflicting recommendations."

Limitations to the study included the reliance on administrative records, the potential for confounding by unmeasured variables, and the 12-month window for examining outcomes, leaving open the possibility that fusion could have longer-term benefits.

#5751. Yamaha Refuses To Race In Qatar Despite MotoGP's Penalty Threats

Despite concerns that President Donald Trump will restart hostilities in the U.S. war against Iran after the midterm elections, MotoGP must go on. But Yamaha announced Sunday that it will not travel to the Lusail International Circuit for next weekend's Qatar Grand Prix. The Japanese manufacturer cited a company-wide policy currently barring travel to the Middle East. In response, MotoGP threatened Yamaha with contractual and sporting implications.

Yamaha's absence means that its two factory motorcycles and Pramac's two satellite bikes will not compete in Qatar. The company stated, "This decision reflects Yamaha's assessment of the information currently available and is independent of the measures implemented by MotoGP Group and the event organizer." While the safety of the team's employees should be paramount, Yamaha didn't have much to lose competitively. The factory team and Pramac are in the last two spots in the teams' standings. Yamaha expects to return for the next round in Portugal, but the manufacturer might not be allowed to rejoin.

MotoGP's response offered few details about the implied financial and competitive consequences, but the championship's organizers stated that every other team committed to racing in Qatar. Don't be deceived by the release, though. The riders have been far from content with the situation they have been forced into.

Riders first held a secret meeting on the matter at Phillip Island ahead of the Australian Grand Prix. It's safe to say management didn't take it well. Last week, The Race reported that MotoGP refused to even give the riders a meeting room at Sepang last weekend. Instead, they reconvened inside Yamaha hospitality. MotoGP also threatened to ban any riders who boycott Qatar from the final two rounds in Portugal and Spain. According to Motorsport.com, outgoing Pramac rider Jack Miller revealed:

"I don't want to go. Like everybody. There's 19 of us that don't want to go there. I don't think we should be racing like that. We've made our opinion very clear on that. We'll see what the decision is.

As riders, we've united and done the best we can, and threatened the best we can with what ammunition we have. Not only for us as riders, but also other people in the championship. You speak to 50% of the paddock, nobody wants to go. I don't understand why we need to. I don't understand."

Some riders are finding their own ways out of racing in Qatar without consequences. Alex Marquez elected to undergo surgery to repair his right shoulder, which he injured in May. He aims to miss only Qatar. It wouldn't be surprising if other riders with lingering injuries also withdraw.

No matter what assurances MotoGP made to all 22 riders, there's no way it could guarantee everyone's safe passage out of Qatar should things escalate in the region further. There are hundreds of people who work in the paddock across MotoGP, Moto2 and Moto3. Organizers also can't prevent the worst-case scenario of Lusail Circuit itself being the target of an Iranian drone or missile strike, and the track sits 27 miles away from Al Udeid Air Base, the largest U.S. military base in the Middle East.

#5750. The ETS Investment Engine: Scaling Europe’s Strategic E-fuel Market for Shipping & Aviation

Making the ETS a strategic investment tool for aviation and shipping

The EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) review proposal published in July 2026 is intended to make the EU’s most vital climate policy mechanism fit for its 2040 climate targets. It also carries the ambition to turn the ETS into an ‘’engine for innovation and investment”.

This policy brief looks at the investment dimension of the ETS proposal with respect to the aviation and maritime sectors. They are major contributors to the ETS revenue generation. We argue, however, that the proposed framework is not fit for purpose to adequately support clean fuel investments in these hard-to-abate sectors.

The ETS Review is an opportunity to set up a tailor-made investment tool to de-risk and boost the production and uptake of e-fuels, using the ETS funds from aviation and shipping. Early financial support is crucial for the development of a domestic e-fuels value chain, Europe’s geostrategic autonomy and the EU’s industrial position in the global competition for clean technologies. RFNBOs are the most scalable fuels needed to reach the targets under FuelEU Maritime and ReFuelEU Aviation.

#5749. Here's What The Original Tesla Roadster Cost In 2008 Vs. What It's Worth Today

The unveiling of the upcoming Tesla Roadster's new design has once again put the nameplate at the forefront of automotive discourse after the prototype stunned fans with its incredible ability to lift off the ground. So you'd imagine it's also made people take a closer look at its predecessor, the original Tesla Roadster that laid the groundwork so the current experiment could soar into the sky.

Revealed in 2006 and brought to market in 2008, the Tesla Roadster earned critical plaudits for being the first production EV to offer a usable driving range (of up to 244 miles). Performance was also noteworthy, as the Lotus Elise-based electric sports car could sprint to 60 mph in less than four seconds, thanks to its gobs of instant electric torque. With this, the Roadster not only won over buyers — a total of 2,450 during its lifetime — but also dispelled preconceived notions about electric cars being slow and impractical.

Then again, being a groundbreaker doesn't come cheap, as the 2008 Tesla Roadster's price shows. The luxury sports car went on sale for $98,000, which is equivalent to around $153,000 in 2026, and today, the amount you'll need to pay for a concours condition example will be close to the car's original MSRP. According to Hagerty, concours Roadsters carry eye-watering valuations of between $85,633 and $97,767, while examples in excellent condition start at a shade over $66,000 and top out at $79,567. Several factors contribute to the original Tesla Roadster's impressive value retention, with brand kudos, its reputation as the car that brought EVs into the mainstream, and the symbolic weight it carries as the car that launched Tesla being some of the biggest. Beyond its historical legacy, the original Roadster enjoys relative rarity, considering Tesla only made 2,450 units between the 2008 and 2012 model years. This means that used models are hard to come by, even on leading online marketplaces.

A quick glance at what's currently available on CarGurus shows a lone 19,000-mile example priced at $81,600, and it does look like prices are around this range at the moment. One recently went for $77,000 on Bring a Trailer. So, while they fetch good money for owners whenever they appear on the market, Tesla Roadsters usually sell significantly below their new price in 2008. This is not to say all Roadsters have depreciated. The limited-edition "Signature One Hundred" models, for example, have become astronomically valuable. We've already seen a Tesla Roadster with under 1,000 miles sell for $250,000, and plenty of other Roadsters like it have done well over the past few years, too, fetching well over $100,000 from buyers.

Heck, even the regular Roadsters have been pretty pricey in the past, too. According to Hagerty's data, these cars were at their high point back in 2023 when concours-perfect models fetched around $164,000, while examples in excellent condition floated around for $131,000. In good condition, Roadsters charged $95,300 then, with models in fair condition costing $61,300.

#5748. Parents' Autoimmune Disease Linked to Kids' Type 1 Diabetes Risk

— Large Swedish study highlighted shared familial susceptibility

Parental autoimmune diseases were associated with an increased risk of type 1 diabetes in offspring, according to a Swedish registry cohort study.

In an analysis of nearly 1.5 million individuals, children born to mothers with autoimmune disease during pregnancy had a 57% higher risk of developing type 1 diabetes (adjusted HR 1.57, 95% CI 1.46-1.68), according to Xingbo Mo, PhD, of Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm, and colleagues. Paternal autoimmune disease before childbirth had a comparable association (adjusted HR 1.51, 95% CI 1.37-1.67).

When parents had type 1 diabetes, the magnitude of risk was higher. Maternal type 1 diabetes was linked with a more than fourfold risk increase (HR 4.51, 95% CI 3.72-5.48), whereas paternal type 1 diabetes was associated with an even higher hazard (HR 5.79, 95% CI 4.70-7.13), they reported in JAMA Pediatrics.

"A clear gradient in type 1 diabetes risk was observed according to parental type 1 diabetes status, with the highest risk among offspring with both parents affected," the authors wrote. "The largely comparable maternal and paternal associations suggest that shared familial susceptibility may play an important role in the intergenerational transmission of type 1 diabetes risk."

While maternal and paternal estimates showed no overall difference for composite autoimmune disease, researchers identified variations across specific disease categories. Paternal associations were stronger for endocrine conditions -- most notably autoimmune thyroiditis -- whereas maternal associations were stronger for ankylosing spondylitis and gastrointestinal autoimmune disorders.

"Stronger associations for endocrine autoimmune diseases, particularly autoimmune thyroiditis, are consistent with the established clustering of endocrine autoimmune disorders and their shared immune-genetic susceptibility," the researchers noted. Yet the "disease-specific heterogeneity suggests that selected conditions may also involve parent-specific or potential intrauterine influences," they added, which "support a multifactorial model of intergenerational autoimmune transmission."

In an accompanying editorial, Mikael Knip, MD, PhD, of Biomedicum Helsinki in Finland, emphasized that an "obvious" practical takeaway is that offspring of parents with autoimmune disease warrant monitoring for type 1 diabetes.

"Consensus guidelines have been published for screening and monitoring of individuals at risk for type 1 diabetes," Knip wrote, noting that while screening efforts "may be variable based on resources available," children with a familial history "represent a definite risk group for progression to clinical type 1 diabetes."

Benjamin Nwosu, MD, chief of endocrinology at Northwell Health Cohen Children's Medical Center in New York, who was not involved with the study, underscored the necessity of early detection.

"Currently, in our practice, we screen children with type 1 diabetes for autoimmune thyroid conditions and celiac disease, because it's been published that children with type 1 diabetes have higher risk for the development of celiac and autoimmune thyroid conditions," Nwosu said in a statement.

He pointed out that the authors "did not mention that 40 to 50% of the risk for type 1 diabetes is carried on what's called the major histocompatibility complex class 2 genes or loci."

"Once you know that, you know a parent who has type 1 diabetes has some possibility of passing this condition to the offspring, not in a Mendelian autosomal dominant fashion, because type 1 is caused by what's called a polygenic aggregation of genes. But the risk is higher than in unaffected parents," he said.

The researchers evaluated 1,455,645 children born in Sweden between 2001 and 2014, with follow-up extending through 2023 (median age was 15.3 years, and 51.4% were male). Overall, 6.1% of children were exposed to maternal autoimmune diseases before delivery.

After adjusting for unmeasured shared familial factors using cousin-comparison models, the maternal association remained statistically significant (adjusted HR 1.27, 95% CI 1.08-1.50), with higher risks specifically noted for maternal endocrine autoimmune disorders and maternal type 1 diabetes.

The study team noted several limitations, including the lack of register data regarding clinical disease severity, autoantibody levels, disease activity during pregnancy, or medication use. "Such factors may modify fetal immune programming and could not be evaluated in the present study," they acknowledged.

Nwosu also cautioned that the results might not fully translate globally, noting Sweden "is located in the northern latitudes, where type 1 diabetes is almost endemic."

#5747. More of the Same Expensive Dependence on Fossil Fuels in TEP and APS 2026 Energy Plans

PHOENIX — Arizona utilities Tucson Electric Power Company (TEP) and Arizona Public Service (APS) filed their 2026 Integrated Resource Plans (IRPs) on Friday that evaluate how utilities will obtain energy for the next 15 years. While their plans include new renewable energy and storage, they continue to spend on fossil fuels, building new gas, and in the case of APS, extending coal use. Instead of facilitating a timely transition to affordable, clean energy, both utilities — and especially APS — continue an expensive dependence on fossil fuels that keep ratepayers in a dangerous cycle, paying the price for decades.

Arizonans already experience some of the highest electric bills in the country, with some of the most planned gas in the country. Yet, instead of easing energy burden and saving its customers millions of dollars, APS prolongs costly coal operations at the Four Corners coal plant, worsening climate impacts, increasing air pollution, and threatening public health.

Of all the state’s utilities, APS has the most planned fossil gas, adding over 4,000 MW of gas by 2041. APS’s gas projects include the planned Desert Sun Power Plant and the Redhawk Expansion Project, which includes constructing eight new methane gas-fired generating turbines in Maricopa County. It has also signed a coal supply contract extension to resuscitate its Four Corners Plant, abandoning APS’s previous plan to exit the plant in 2031 and instead extending coal-fired operations to 2038. In a pending case before the Arizona Corporation Commission, APS is also proposing a 14% rate hike that would increase the average residential customer’s utility bill by roughly $240 per year.

TEP’s energy plan includes coal to gas conversions of units 1 and 2 at its Springerville plant by 2031 rather than retirement of those units as TEP had previously proposed. TEP plans to exit its share of the Four Corners coal plant by 2031, but also plans to add 300 MW of new fossil gas generation. TEP had previously committed to reduce carbon emissions 80 percent by 2035 but now says in its plan that it won’t achieve that goal.

The public can submit comments on both utility energy plans. Both APS and TEP’s plans will come before the Arizona Corporation Commission to be approved or rejected.

“Arizonans across the state support a timely transition from fossil fuels to 100% clean energy by 2050, but what the utilities have presented in their energy plans further delays our move from gas and coal to solar and wind,” said Sierra Club Grand Canyon Chapter Director Sandy Bahr. “We’re seeing these utilities protect their own bottom lines, instead of making the most economical decisions for ratepayers like you and me. More than ever, we need to embrace a clean energy future to protect our health, the climate, and our wallets.”

"Everything was engulfed in flames," she said.

Palm Beach County authorities were called to the scene where it was eventually confirmed that all nine passengers on board the business jet had died. Only one individual may have sustained injuries from the crash, who was adjacent to the scene, but officials have yet to confirm that injury.

#5745. They Are Trying to Silence Us

State and federal government officials are trying to harass, intimidate, and silence NRDC and other nonprofit environmental advocates.

The Attorney General of West Virginia recently initiated an investigation of NRDC and a handful of other groups on the stated ground that we may have committed consumer fraud. The theory appears to be that it’s deceptive for NRDC to say that the burning of fossil fuels contributes to climate change, which, in turn, causes harm to the planet and its people. But that’s fact, not fraud.

To pursue his investigation, the AG served a subpoena seeking a vast trove of confidential internal and external communications relating to our advocacy around climate change for the past 10 years. The demand could cover sensitive strategy memos for policy advocacy, draft comments on regulations, exchanges with coalition partners, back-and-forth among scientists, dialogues with donors, and drafts of NRDC publications; all disclosed to a hostile adversary.

Co-counseling with Democracy Forward, we responded to the subpoena by preparing a federal lawsuit asserting infringement of our First Amendment rights to speak, associate with others, and advocate for effective solutions to the climate crisis. Those solutions include the replacement of fossil fuels with renewable sources of energy. And that is what drives the AG’s attempt to punish NRDC: pure retaliation for the content of our point of view.

At 2:13 p.m. on October 22, we advised the AG that we were going to file suit early that evening. A little more than two hours later, at 4:32 p.m., the AG withdrew the subpoena.

The AG is not alone in trying to bully NRDC. In September, the Committee on Natural Resources of the U.S. House of Representatives sent a letter of inquiry to NRDC and 18 other nonprofit environmental groups, informing us they are investigating the groups’ litigation practices. Why? According to the Committee, the targeted groups “build powerful and profitable litigation machines funded by taxpayer dollars through the exploitation of statutory fee-shifting provisions.” On this purported basis, the Committee demanded that NRDC disclose an exhaustive array of intrusive information and documents that could take months of concentrated effort to produce.

The premise of the Committee’s inquiry is that NRDC “effectively function[s] as [a] law firm[] funded by taxpayer dollars.” It calls NRDC “one of the most active litigating environmental nonprofit organizations driving the exploitation of statutory fee–shifting provisions.”

While NRDC is indeed an active litigant in federal court, it rarely receives attorney fees from the federal government. During our past five fiscal years, NRDC’s income from such fees in cases involving agencies or statutes identified in the Committee’s letter constituted 0.112 percent of our operating budget. In light of this numerical fact, contending that NRDC “build[s] a business model focused on siphoning tax dollars by weaponizing litigation awards” is unmoored from reality. With minimal effort, Committee members or staff could have discovered this from documents in the public record.

Courts have repeatedly held that the citizen-based enforcement litigation NRDC conducts, which holds government agencies accountable to the law, is a public service, and that Congress meant to encourage such suits by providing the opportunity to recover fees when a court determines an award is appropriate. This is the paradox: The Committee, which is part of Congress, accuses NRDC of stealing taxpayer money, when NRDC is doing precisely what Congress itself has empowered and encouraged NRDC to do.

It is not the only paradox. The Committee claims that its purpose is “to root out waste, fraud, and abuse of taxpayer dollars.” If so, is it investigating the nearly $4 billion in taxpayer funds the U.S. Department of the Interior has agreed to pay companies to abandon offshore wind projects that would produce economical, renewable energy? The government bought back the wind leases without any statutory authority to do so, drawing funds from the same pot of federal money that often covers attorney fee awards. The amount of taxpayer money expended on the buybacks during the past six months is more than 3,000 times the amount of attorney fees paid to NRDC over the past five years. To our knowledge, the Committee is not investigating the lease buybacks.

In response to the Committee majority’s attempt to intimidate NRDC, we sent this letter, asserting our First Amendment right to litigate to enforce the law. Thus far, the Committee has not sought to compel us to respond to its demand for documents.

The Natural Resources Committee has plenty of company within the House. The effort to harass environmental nonprofits and their funders is part of a multipronged attack that includes the House Committees on the Judiciary; Science, Space, and Technology; and Oversight and Government Reform. While NRDC is not yet a specific, named target of any of these additional House inquiries, other environmental nonprofits are.

These investigations and inquiries are designed to chill dissent, to punish those who disagree with the policies of those in power. The method of harassment is the same pernicious ploy we see repeatedly from the White House: Start with a lie (e.g., NRDC spreads deception, not facts, about climate change; NRDC feasts on federal attorney fees), then parlay the lie into a malicious attempt to deflect attention, divert resources, silence perceived enemies, and trample constitutional rights. It’s retaliation for protected speech. The West Virginia AG doesn’t want to debate the relative merits of renewable energy and fossil fuels—he wants to punish us because we disagree with him.

The recent moves by the West Virginia AG and the House Committees erode the rule of law. Not to speak out against them is to cede the narrative—to be complicit in a dangerous form of attempted repression. In the face of hostile questioning, the upright prosecutor Jack Smith recently told Congress that, while fear is contagious, so is courage. He’s right. Everyone who acquiesces in these abuses of government authority makes it easier for everyone else to do the same. Everyone who speaks out encourages others to resist.

It is not enough to survive this moment, silent and unscathed. As an organization rooted in the law, NRDC is compelled to fight for freedoms central to our democracy. The climate crisis is the existential issue of our day. But climate is not the only thing at risk.

We will persist without fear to address the ravaging effects of climate change and enforce the law against polluters. Our millions of members and supporters expect and deserve that from us. We did not succumb to intimidation, and we will not succumb to it if it comes our way again. This is the sole silver lining in the misguided attempt to bully NRDC into submission and silence: It will not work.

#5744. The Harley-Davidson Sprint 440 Is Exactly What Harley Needs

It's finally happening: Harley-Davidson is bringing a proper Harley-looking beginner bike to the United States. Not some weird half-baked attempt like the Street line, but a proper Harley-styled cruiser that just happens to be built around a smaller, beginner-friendly engine. The new bike is called the Sprint 440, it's debuting at EICMA, and I couldn't be more excited for it.

I've long said that Harley needs a proper beginner bike, a way into the brand that capitalizes on what Milwaukee does well — vintage, call it "authentic" styling — without the company's usual high prices and general skull-themed accessorizing. The Sprint 440 appears to be just that: A practical single cylinder, a Sportster-esque sloped tank, and a price that lets beginners actually cross-shop Harley with Kawasaki and Triumph. While we don't know the firm U.S. price yet, we know the bike goes for just $8,500 Canadian up north — the equivalent of just over $6,000 here.

The Sprint looks leagues better than the Nightster it displaces as Harley's cheapest bike, with styling that better hides the brake lines, wires, and radiators a modern motorcycle requires. The Sprint could be mistaken for an Iron 883 by those who don't know the ins and outs of both bikes, though it does need some indicators of its foreign coproduction — the bike is a collaboration with India's Hero MotoCorp, according to RideApart, and its chain drive demonstrates that things aren't all Harley here. Still, it's a Milwaukee bike in the ways that really matter: Despite the foreign assistance, Harley says the bike will undergo final production in Pennsylvania.

Harley hasn't yet released all the specs for the U.S. model of the Sprint, but we know the international model has a 26.4-inch seat height (though Harley specifies that's "laden") and a 412-pound weight. Horsepower is low, at just 27, though it makes a full 28 pound-feet of torque. Those numbers aren't incredibly impressive, but if you're a new rider into the looks of a classic Harley you probably won't mind — you'll just appreciate a lighter, cheaper way to get the bike you want. That kind of accessibility is what Harley has been lacking for years, and I truly hope the Sprint 440 helps the brand get some new buyers in.

#5743. The Future of Buildings in Illinois Is Electric

The Illinois Commerce Commission authorized a study of the most affordable way for the state to meet its building decarbonization goals. The report has fundamental flaws but critical insights.

Illinois’s landmark Climate and Equitable Jobs Act (CEJA) sets the goal of 100 percent clean energy across the state by 2050. For nonelectric sources of emissions and transportation—such as the 17 percent of emissions that occur when we burn gas to heat our homes and other buildings where we live, work, and play—CEJA provides little direction on how these sectors are expected to align with the state’s climate goals.

The Illinois Commerce Commission (ICC), which regulates the state’s electric and gas utilities, showed real leadership in 2023 when it found that “if the decarbonization goals of CEJA are to be met, the gas distribution system as currently operated will need to change.” To chart that change, the ICC launched a Future of Gas (FOG) open stakeholder process to identify the most efficient, cost-effective path to a gas system that fits the state’s climate goals.

As part of this FOG process, the ICC authorized a consultant to model five pathways to that CEJA-compliant system by 2050. In its recently released Gas Decarbonization Pathways Study, the consultant modeled a range of scenarios, from one where the state invests heavily in energy efficiency and helps customers replace outdated gas appliances with high-efficiency electric alternatives to others that rely on unproven biofuels with no clear evidence that they can be produced at anything close to the scale needed. For each scenario, the consultant was expected to assess technical feasibility, up-front and operating costs, impacts on the gas and electric systems, emissions reductions, and effects on environmental justice communities, all to help Illinois meet its gas decarbonization goals at the lowest cost and with the most benefits to residents.

Unfortunately, the consultant’s final report is biased by faulty (and at times, plainly unrealistic) assumptions that do not allow for accurate comparison across scenarios. Despite this, the study yields a clear finding: Gas use in Illinois’s buildings and industrial facilities must decline by at least 50 percent in order to reach the state’s climate target of net-zero emissions by 2050. Together with the state’s recently released Comprehensive Climate Action Plan, the study offers Illinois policymakers a clear agenda for initiating the transition to an affordable, equitable, and clean energy future.

The study offers some useful insights, but treating all of its findings as a road map for Illinois’s gas transition would be a mistake. Before getting into the no-regrets steps that Illinois can take now, we need to unpack the biggest problems with the report, including the flawed assumptions behind some of its conclusions.

Despite the study’s shortcomings detailed above, several key findings should influence the recommendations in the final FOG report:

The remaining technologies are incredibly early-stage, and to the extent that they are available at all over the next several decades, they are likely to be extremely expensive. The study’s assumptions around e-methane are particularly troubling. Modeling initially showed that the Continued Gas Use and Hybrid Gas cases could not meet the net-zero-by-2050 emissions requirement using only available technologies, like biomethane. As a result, in the final report, the model selected e-methane to backfill any resource gap—despite the fact that e-methane derived from green hydrogen and direct air carbon capture is still in “prototype and demonstration stage” today.

While the pathways study acknowledges that “[h]igher-gas scenarios present … greater challenges in alternative fuel procurement, technology readiness, long-term affordability, and air quality” compared to electrification-focused scenarios, this is a significant understatement. Scenarios relying on e-methane are infeasible and should not be considered on equal footing with scenarios that primarily rely on electric heat pumps, which already comprise 47 percent of air conditioner sales and have annually outsold gas furnaces since 2021.

The pathways study reinforces the need for Illinois to proactively plan for a future where gas demand declines, which occurs under all five scenarios despite flawed assumptions that heavily favor continued gas use scenarios. The state can and must act now to achieve the state’s climate goals in an affordable and equitable way. Illinois does not need to solve every aspect of the transition in the next few years. However, it can begin taking the following no-regrets steps now to prepare for a changing energy landscape.

Despite its numerous flaws, the study underscores the transformative role that clean, electric heat pumps will play in Illinois’s energy future and the need to plan for a smaller gas system. The ICC and the state legislature can and must begin advancing no-regrets building electrification policies today to ensure tomorrow’s energy system is healthy, clean, and affordable for all of the state’s residents.

By Madeline Semanisin, Policy Director, Illinois, Climate & Energy, NRDC; and Kiki Velez, Equitable Gas Transition Lead, Climate & Energy, NRDC

#5741. CTE in NFL Players: What a New Study Tells Us -- And What It Doesn't

— Does the new research mean 3 in 4 football players are at risk?

A statistical model that extrapolated data from deceased National Football League (NFL) brain donors to include all former NFL players who died from 2008 through 2023 estimated that nearly three in four had chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).

Yorghos Tripodis, PhD, of the Boston University School of Public Health, and colleagues developed the model by quantifying cognitive symptoms of NFL brain donors who had CTE assessments. CTE can be identified only through autopsy.

After adjusting for bias associated with brain donation, the model estimated the prevalence of CTE at death was 74.5% (95% CI 69.6-78.3) for all former NFL players who died from 2008 through 2023, Tripodis and colleagues reported in JAMA Network Open.

The analysis incorporated a selection ratio to estimate the prevalence of CTE. The ratio assumed that brain donation was driven primarily by family members observing cognitive symptoms in former NFL players.

"This is an interesting attempt to statistically account for the problem of selective donation into a brain bank so that they can estimate the prevalence of CTE among all NFL players who died during the time interval they were looking at when they only could analyze a subset of them," observed Marc Weisskopf, PhD, ScD, of the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health in Boston, who wasn't involved with the study.

The numbers don't necessarily apply to all NFL players, he pointed out. "The deaths they are working with are about 10% of all that could have occurred in that period, and there are reasons to suspect CTE would be less common among the still-living players when they eventually die," Weisskopf told MedPage Today.

"The statistical approach is sound, although it's important to realize that it is very dependent on some assumptions -- notably that brain donation is entirely driven by cognitive symptoms and that those are captured by dementia on the death certificate and their adjustment for additional mild cognitive impairment," he said.

CTE has four distinct stages, with higher CTE stages correlating with more severe cognitive symptoms. "Even if we were able to determine an unbiased estimate of the proportion of living and deceased players with CTE, we still don't have information on their probable CTE stage, which has the most meaning for their everyday lives and health," noted Rachel Grashow, PhD, MS, also of Harvard, who also wasn't involved with the study.

The study findings do not apply to other groups, observed Julie Stamm, PhD, of the University of Wisconsin-Madison, who wasn't part of the study. "It does not provide an estimate of CTE among athletes in other sports or at lower levels of play," Stamm told MedPage Today.

"Greater lifetime repetitive head impact exposure has been linked to an increased risk of developing CTE, so it is likely that the prevalence would be higher among NFL players than those who played at lower levels," she added. "However, we cannot estimate the prevalence among players at lower levels at this time."

Tripodis and colleagues used UNITE brain bank data and national death index records to evaluate former NFL players who died from 2008 through 2023. The mean duration of play was 5.1 years and 41.1% of deceased players were ages 80 or older when they died.

Of 2,362 deceased former NFL players, 396 were brain donors and 1,966 were nondonors. Of 387 donors, 362 (93.5%) had CTE at autopsy. The estimated prevalence of all-cause dementia was 27.2% (95% CI 22.6-31.6).

The median selection ratio was 4.97 (95% CI 4.72-5.26), meaning that former players with cognitive symptoms were five times more likely to have their brains donated by their family than those without these symptoms.

"The findings of this cross-sectional study suggest that selection bias materially inflates donor-based prevalence estimates but is unlikely to fully explain the high burden of CTE neuropathology among this population," Tripodis and co-authors stated.

Studies like this can refocus attention to the "20,000 living former NFL players, some of whom are suffering with cognitive symptoms or have been diagnosed with dementia," Grashow told MedPage Today. The Football Players Health Study at Harvard has more than 5,000 former players in its cohort, she noted.

"In our conversations with and ongoing study of these NFL players, we've found that head injury increases risk for treatable conditions that -- if left untreated -- increases risk for cognitive issues and dementia. These include sleep apnea, high blood pressure, low testosterone, depression, anxiety, tinnitus, and more," she added.

"So, if we are thinking about how these recent findings relate to the many thousands of former living players, the story shifts to one of surveilling and treating former players for treatable conditions so we can reduce their dementia and heart disease risk," Grashow said. "This, we believe, is one of the best ways we can tackle the potential symptoms, risks, and challenges of CTE right now -- before we turn to estimating prevalence, which is at the end of life."

#5739. Congress Is Cutting Off Transportation Investments that Help Families Save Money

The loss of guaranteed federal funding could stall projects that make it easier and cheaper for Americans to get where they need to go.

UPDATE: On October 27, 2026, an update to the Senate Commerce Committee’s Chopping Block report provided a state-by-state assessment of the harm to transportation systems if Congress fails to renew the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law’s $36.8 billion in advance appropriations funding. Led by Ranking Member Cantwell, the report demonstrates that these cuts will only drive increased costs for families and business across the country.

At a time when Americans are struggling to pay staggering prices at the fuel pump and the Trump administration sows uncertainty for states and communities by clawing back committed transportation infrastructure funds, Congress is moving to scale back more critical federal funding for affordable and clean transportation.

The need for consistent funding is clear: Transportation costs are the second-largest household expense in the United States, and our roads and transit infrastructure remain structurally inadequate. Nevertheless, state transportation and transit authorities are facing a significant funding cliff due to the expiration of the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law (BIL) on September 30, 2026. Over the past five years, the infrastructure law has provided a guaranteed pot of funding worth $36.8 billion for transportation projects. These “advanced appropriations” cover a wide breadth of programs and include large amounts of funding for clean transportation, such as electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure projects, transit, and rail investments. This funding has helped state transit and transportation authorities plan for longer-term projects and has been critical to the infrastructure law’s support of almost 70,000 unique transportation projects across the country.

But transportation funding from the infrastructure law ran out on September 30, 2026, and while Congress passed a short-term extension until December 11, 2026, it does not include these guaranteed dollars. This means that, for the three-month duration of the extension, states will lack the continuity and certainty they need to plan for both large- and small-scale infrastructure projects.

To add insult to injury, Congress also seems to be contemplating leaving this guaranteed funding out of the next transportation bill altogether. The House BUILD America 250 Act proposal, released in May, proposes cutting all advanced appropriations funding. The proposal, in fact, slashes transportation funding from current infrastructure law levels by almost 50 percent, leaving Americans without access to travel options that help defray rising costs.

Historically, transportation bills have included authorizations of two types of funding: (1) contract authority, which is supported by revenues that flow into the Highway Trust Fund and (2) general funds, which Congress has to “appropriate” and assign annually. The current infrastructure law includes another category—advanced appropriations—which makes money available in the future for certain programs without the need for any congressional action in future years, guaranteeing states and communities secure funding over the five-year bill period. This certainty allows for states to plan in advance for future projects and grant opportunities.

Any cut to this pot of money takes a sledgehammer to clean transportation programs that reduce household costs and improve the health of our communities. Particular programs at risk include the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure program, which helps states build a national network of EV chargers; the Capital Investment Grants, a transit-related discretionary grant program; and the Reconnecting Communities Pilot, which aims to address harms caused by past transportation decisions. Also of concern are the BUILD and MEGA grants, which help support the build-out of transit, bicycle, and pedestrian infrastructure.

Congress is unlikely to agree on a new bill before the current extension comes to an end in December 2026, meaning that there is an opportunity to include advanced appropriations in any future extension of the current infrastructure law and the next transportation bill so that states and local governments can avoid having to grapple with temporary or potentially even permanent funding interruptions. This guaranteed funding is even more important now as transportation decision-makers contend with the Trump administration interfering with implementation and funding guidance. Additional funding clawbacks will only serve to stall progress. The sustained funding will also allow states and local governments to continue to build on the progress that the current infrastructure law made on clean transportation investments.

Even more important, American households are currently struggling to afford their basic daily necessities, and soaring gas prices have left many searching for ways to save on their transportation costs. In 2024, when gas prices averaged below $3.50 a gallon (a far cry from the current average price of $4.35 a gallon), transportation was the second-largest cost for American households, averaging 17 percent of household budgets. Cutting advanced appropriations funding for transit, EV charging, and rail will only serve to penalize the very households struggling the most, at a time when those investments would give Americans access to a wide range of affordable, reliable, and safe transportation options.

By Shruti Vaidyanathan, Director, Transportation Advocacy, Climate & Energy, NRDC

In the leadup to his election in 2024, Donald Trump asked about 20 oil executives at Mar-a-Lago to raise $1 billion for his campaign, promising to reverse dozens of Biden-era regulations if elected. The policies put in place by the Republican party, who has had control of congress and the White House since the last election, have been very pro oil & gas, whether they were anti-EV, anti-solar, anti-energy efficiency, anti-fuel efficiency, anti-wind, or just flat out subsidies to oil and gas.

They ended many of the Biden Administration’s clean energy policies. They ended the Solar For All Program (or tried to). They ended residential and commercial solar tax credits. They signed Executive Order 14315 to terminate wind and solar production and investment tax credits and impose additional restrictions. They made solar development on Federal lands more difficult. On his first day in office, Trump signed a memo withdrawing federal offshore areas from new and renewed wind leasing – but the rule didn’t apply to oil and gas. They ended wind tax credits. They kneecapped the federal standards for vehicle fuel efficiency. They tried to eliminate Energy Star, a program that costs the government $32 million a year and saves Americans $14 billion a year. If this isn’t quid pro quo, I guess I don’t understand what quid pro quo is. But the Iran War took it to a whole new level.

Since it began on February 28, as Americans have spent about $150 billion more on gasoline and diesel, U.S. oil and gas companies earned more than $130 billion in profit from April through September, nearly triple what they earned a year earlier, according to the New York Times.

Wars fought for oil are nothing new. But there are things about this conflict that are new.

CleanTechnica’s analysis argues that global oil demand is on track to fall by 2–3 million barrels a day this year, the first drop not caused by a recession or pandemic, as high prices push consumers away from fuel. Every driver, trucker, and country that electrifies becomes less exposed to the next oil shock. The question for the U.S. is how fast it joins in. And this election will go a long way toward answering that question.

#5736. EV Owners Need To Lend Out Their Cars If They Want Regular People To Go Electric

Electric vehicles will probably never fully replace the internal combustion sports car, but mainstream daily drivers are living on borrowed time. It's not like anyone with no idea which wheels are powered or how many cylinders their car has cares about a missing exhaust note. But while EVs are taking off in the rest of the world, the U.S. lags behind, thanks in large part to pro-oil propaganda. People believe all sorts of myths about EVs, and I'm sorry, but short test drives won't fix it. Which means EV owners need to start acting like they have an obligation to lend friends and family their cars.

A few days in an EV won't change anyone's mind if their lifestyle doesn't match what EVs currently offer, and that's fine. But if they've been tricked by a bunch of pro-oil myths, you may find that a few days with your car is all it takes to convince them that EVs are the best thing ever. Because even an hour-long test drive doesn't show you the benefits of living with a gas station in your garage. It's the kind of thing that probably requires a three-day loan at a minimum, because they have to see how it fits into their regular lives.

Ideally, the automakers would take the lead here, but that's probably not happening anytime soon. I've discussed this idea with employees at several automakers, and so far, I don't think anyone wants to take on the cost and complexity of dealing with dealerships to make longer-term test drives happen. So without the automakers, it falls on the EV owners who want to see EVs become more popular. We need to be the ones pushing our cars on people like they're the supposed free samples that Deputy D. Diggity Dawg Dawson insisted drug dealers would force me to take.

At least anecdotally, I don't know of anything more powerful for changing minds about EVs than time spent with your butt in the seat. Most recently, a friend had to replace their beloved Mazda CX-5 after someone hit them; they asked me about EVs, and almost before I knew it, they were the proud new owners of a Hyundai Ioniq 5. So they were already open to a car that would save them money on gas, but even they quickly realized the things they were worried about weren't actually a big deal.

According to the friend, who I will call Bill, "driving them is super f—ing fun," and he did not think he "would enjoy trying to max out the mi/kWh using the regenerative braking... But [he does]." After only a few days of driving an EV, someone experiencing their first EV was already realizing how strong the oil propaganda is and how much better EVs are at things beyond saving money on gas.

An example of a borrowing experience changing minds is my brother — he borrowed my Fiat for a week while he was in the process of replacing his company truck. With three (soon to be four!) kids, he was never going to buy a two-door hatchback, but he loved being able to charge at home so much that he went out and bought a non-Fiat EV. All it took was a little time living with an electric car that he didn't even have any interest in owning, and it changed his mind about EV ownership before he'd even driven a competitive one.

I know it's scary letting other people borrow your car, and I certainly wouldn't want you handing the keys to someone you know is irresponsible. But without automaker or federal support, we're going to have to do this on our own, and the best way to get people to change their minds about EVs is to get some real time with the cars. And what better way to make that happen is there than trading cars with someone for a few days? Friends and family help each other out, after all.

If you lend your car to someone who decides they probably shouldn't buy an EV, that's fine. No harm, no foul. But just think how happy you'll be if a few days if your car convinces someone they've been wrong about EVs and should actually get one. It's pretty nice, I'm not going to lie, and definitely worth the risk of letting someone you know drive your car. They quite literally sell themselves.

#5735. Kennedy's HHS relaxes enforcement on 6 popular wellness peptides

Kennedy's HHS relaxes enforcement on 6 popular wellness peptides" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Stopping short of a formal declaration allowing their use, Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has cleared the way for the compounding of six popular wellness peptides.

The move, which comes after the same peptides won favor at an FDA advisory committee meeting this summer, is being hailed by some in the industry as offering a more accountable alternative to the gray market many peptide-seekers currently use, while others have charged that it undermines institutional FDA pushback on the drugs, which have become increasingly popular among fitness influencer circles and the MAHA crowd.

Under Kennedy’s “enforcement discretion policy” issued Wednesday, HHS will not take enforcement action against pharmacies, physicians and federal facilities compounding six specific peptides, assuming those parties meet certain specific qualifications.

The specific compounds included (PDF) in the list are BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, semax and TB-500, all of which were discussed in a meeting of the FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) in July, with the panel ultimately voting to recommend including the treatments onto the 503A Bulk Drug Substances list.

Advisory committee votes are recommendations, not binding decisions, and the peptides still haven’t been added to the drug substances list in an official capacity.

Kennedy cited that meeting in his enforcement decision, alongside data on utilization of peptides, noting that HHS believes there is “significant interest in the use of these peptides in compounding given the lack of availability of approved products.”

The letter clarifies the agency may revisit the interim policy if it leads to new safety signals or product quality issues.

The new policy comes with several other caveats that compounders must satisfy too, including sourcing their bulk drug substance from an FDA-registered facility and ensuring that the ingredients are properly characterized and identified. The original manufacturer of the bulk drug substance must also be registered with the FDA, according to HHS’ document.

In another change from typical compounding practice, compounders will be required to report quality issues and serious adverse events associated with the newly unrestricted peptides that are associated with their use, whether the drug itself is considered related or not, HHS clarified.

Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved. Traditionally, the compounding practice has focused on the mixing or altering of ingredients of a drug to create a custom medication for a patient.

The practice can also come into play in order to fill drug shortages, which led to the pop-up of a GLP-1 compounding cottage industry for obesity that branded drugmakers Novo and Eli Lilly have continued to grapple with, even after supply shortfalls of their licensed medicines were declared formally ended in the United States.

In a statement Wednesday, Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding (APC) CEO Scott Brunner said he welcomed the decision, noting that it isn’t a question of whether patients are already using these six peptides, but of “where they’re getting them.”

“Right now, far too many patients are obtaining peptides from illicit suppliers with little assurance about what's actually in the vial,” he said. “That's an existing public health threat, and one that isn't going away simply because compounding of the substances is prohibited.”

While noting that the policy now offers a “more accountable alternative” to that murky peptide supply chain, Brunner emphasized the importance of the limits the enforcement action puts in place as well, while also highlighting questions that remain, including when the policy actually takes effect, how API testing and analysis will be validated and how product utilization reporting will work.

“That last point is especially important,” Brunner said. “A credible federal policy with meaningful patient safety safeguards gives states a sound basis for their own oversight and helps discourage a patchwork of state rules and restrictions that could undermine the access HHS is trying to provide.”

Others, including consumer advocacy nonprofit Public Citizen, adopted a decidedly more antagonist tone toward the new enforcement policy. In a statement issued this week, the group noted the peptides included in the new list are “popular but unproven and unapproved,” flagging Kennedy’s own personal support of the compounds.

Questions around conflicts of interest among panelists on the PCAC panel were also raised this summer, with the FDA quickly slotting in eight temporary voting members ahead of the confab in a bid to appease some of the criticism.

With the move, Kennedy “has acted recklessly and unilaterally to put Americans in danger,” Robert Steinbrook, M.D., Public Citizen’s health research group director, said in a statement, contending that the HHS secretary ought to “support, not sabotage, needed FDA enforcement actions to protect consumers.”

#5734. Washington State Resident Dies From Bird Flu Following Exposure to Infected Cattle

— Two other U.S. deaths have been tied to bird flu since 2024

A person in Washington state has died from complications of the bird flu, the first such U.S. death in a year.

The Yakima County resident, who had previous health conditions, was exposed to avian influenza at a dairy with infected cattle and had been hospitalized. The person died Sunday, county health officials said.

Two other U.S. deaths have been tied to bird flu since it became a national public health concern in 2024. The first, announced in January 2025, was an elderly person in Louisiana who had a version of bird flu known as H5N1. The other, in Washington state, died in November 2025 from a rarer version called H5N5.

Yakima County officials did not release any additional details about the person who recently died. The CDC said the person was infected with H5N1.

County officials have reported that 33 dairy herds recently have tested positive for H5N1.

They say three human infections have been linked to exposure at a dairy, and that the Yakima Health District is working with the state health department to find people who were in close contact with those people and monitor them for symptoms.

The H5N1 bird flu has been spreading widely among wild birds, poultry, cows, and other animals for several years. Health concerns escalated in early 2024 when infections spread among U.S. livestock. Its presence in the environment increases the chances that people will be exposed, and potentially catch it, officials have said.

More than 70 human infections have been reported in the U.S. since the beginning of 2024, according to the CDC. But there is no known person-to-person spread and the risk to the general public is low, the agency says.

The agency analyzed the genetic sequence of the virus from the person who died in Washington and found no changes that would make the virus spread more easily or cause more severe illness, a CDC spokesperson said Monday.

Officials continue to urge people who have contact with sick or dead birds to take precautions, including wearing respiratory and eye protection and gloves when handling poultry. People who work on farms are considered to be at higher risk.
