Building on its massive adoption with clinicians, the company is now pushing deeper into health systems.

The agreement with NYU Langone builds on OpenEvidence's broader reach in New York. The company already has an enterprise rollout across NewYork-Presbyterian's 10 hospitals and nearly 350 care sites, a health-system-wide deployment at Mount Sinai, and a specialized precision oncology partnership with Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. It also has partnerships with leading New York City medical schools around clinical training and research.

A recent large-scale study examined OpenEvidence’s rapid adoption and how clinicians are using AI in the clinic. Nearly 1 million U.S. clinicians submitted 271 million AI-enabled clinical queries through OpenEvidence's platform from January 2024 to June 2026, according to a paper published in JAMA. More than half of the users in the sample (556,200) were physicians, according to researchers from Harvard Medical School and Brigham and Women’s Hospital. These physicians submitted an average of 37 queries per month of use. Early-career physicians and those in oncology, hematology, internal medicine and family medicine submitted a higher-than-average share of queries, according to the study.

The study found that most of the queries were related to clinical decision-making (51.9%), particularly treatment and management. Diagnosis accounted for 13.9% of queries.

“Two key takeaways are that an enormous number of physicians are using AI for clinical care and that they are often using it in areas where they don’t have specific expertise,” said corresponding author Anupam Jena, the Joseph P. Newhouse Professor of Health Care Policy in the Blavatnik Institute at HMS and HMS professor of medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital.

“Everyone appreciates the huge potential for AI to change how medicine is practiced, but right now, we have limited information on how many doctors are using it, what they are using it for, and how it’s impacting patients,” Jena said. The JAMA study tackles the first two of those questions, the researchers noted.

The study also found that monthly active OpenEvidence users increased from 355 in January 2024 to 703,265 in June 2026. Queries per active user increased substantially, from 18 per month to 39.5, and month-to-month retention reached roughly 90% in 2026. By June, 92.5% of active users were returning users rather than brief adopters, according to the study.

#5731. Labor Department finalizes PBM transparency rule

Labor Department finalizes PBM transparency rule" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration has locked in a regulation that will require pharmacy benefit managers to disclose fees and compensation to self-funded employers.

The rule, finalized by the Department of Labor's Employee Benefits Security Administration, aims to ensure that employers can see what drug manufacturers, pharmacies and other entities are paying their PBMs and any affiliated brokers and consultants.

The department said in an announcement that this data will support employers in negotiating contracts and pushing to lower drug costs for their workers and their dependents.

“This is a win for every American worker who has ever paid too much at the pharmacy counter,” said Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling in the announcement. “For years, PBMs have operated in the shadows, pocketing hidden fees while workers and employers were left in the dark."

Under the rule, PBMs must disclose several key sources of compensation, including manufacturer rebates, any compensation when the price for a drug paid by the plan exceeds reimbursement to the pharmacy, and any payments recouped from pharmacies for dispensed drugs.

The rule was first proposed in late January, and while it enjoys support with employer groups, pharmacy benefit managers have pushed back on the changes.

The Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, the leading lobbying organization for PBMs, in March called for the agency to rescind the proposed rule, as after it was unveiled, lawmakers passed industry reforms as part of a bipartisan health funding package.

Those congressional PBM reforms include multiple provisions around transparency, and PCMA argued that the DOL rule would create duplicative reporting and disclosure requirements for these companies to navigate.

In a statement Thursday, PCMA President David Marin said that the organization is "extremely concerned that it will lead to higher patient costs and less competition, the opposite of the Department’s stated intent."

"The Department has made modest efforts to harmonize the rule with the recently enacted federal law, but we are concerned it may have exceeded Congress’s intent and its own authority," Marin said. "Patients, employers and unions will have no new meaningful transparency from this action, but prescription drug benefits will now be more expensive."

"This could also lead to greater concentration in our industry as smaller PBMs face excessive reporting demands," Marin added.

DOL said in the announcement that the final rule "implements the bipartisan transparency reforms Congress enacted earlier this year." One of the key goals, the agency said, is to better support employers and plan sponsors in meeting their fiduciary duties under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA).

As they face additional pressure on their ERISA compliance, employers cheered the DOL rule and PBM reform more broadly. The ERISA Industry Committee (ERIC) said in a statement that the rule will offer "a clearer view of what their health plans actually pay."

"We applaud the administration for advancing much-needed transparency related to PBMs and affiliated entities," said James Gelfand, CEO of ERIC, in the release. "Large employers pay for their workers’ prescriptions, but many can’t see how much of that money their PBM and any affiliated entity keeps."

"This rule will fill a critical gap in the legislation Congress passed earlier this year, for the first time giving employers a real view into so-called 'spread pricing' arrangements and helping plan sponsors to improve the affordability of prescription drugs for working families," Gelfand said.

#5730. Late-Stage Sickle Cell Disease Study Splits on Main Goals

— Mitapivat improved hemoglobin response, but no significant benefit for pain crises

The thalassemia drug mitapivat (Aqvesme) significantly improved hemoglobin response in patients with sickle cell disease but failed to top placebo when it came to reducing pain crises in a phase III trial that aims to support an expanded approval.

In the RISE UP trial, 41% of patients assigned to the oral pyruvate kinase activator had a hemoglobin response, as compared with 3% of placebo recipients (P<0.0001). But that didn't translate into a reduction in the annualized rate of sickle cell pain crises (2.6 for mitapivat vs 3.1 for placebo, P=0.1213), reported researchers led by Biree Andemariam, MD, of the New England Sickle Cell Institute at University of Connecticut Health in Farmington.

Beyond those two primary endpoints, treatment with mitapivat was associated with improved markers of hemolysis, reduced transfusion burden, and additional clinical benefits in the subset of patients with a hemoglobin response, but not with improvements in patient-reported fatigue, the study authors wrote in The Lancet.

These mitapivat data, which are currently under review with the FDA, arrive amid turbulence in the drug market for sickle cell disease. Crizanlizumab (Adakveo), approved in 2019, lost its marketing authorization in Europe after randomized trial data showed the drug failed to top placebo when it came to vaso-occlusive crises, though it's still available in the U.S.

And voxelotor (Oxbryta), which was granted accelerated approval, also in 2019, was pulled from global markets after trial data turned up an imbalance in deaths and acute vaso-occlusive crises for patients on the hemoglobin S polymerization inhibitor.

Mitapivat is currently approved as a disease-modifying treatment for anemia in adults with alpha- or beta-thalassemia, and an approval decision in sickle cell disease is expected by February of next year.

Labeling for mitapivat includes a boxed warning due to the risk of liver injury, which also warranted a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS) program. The FDA has requested an analysis on whether a REMS would be needed in sickle cell disease, but drugmaker Agios Pharmaceuticals said the data so far have shown no cases of liver injury that follow the pattern or severity seen in the thalassemia trials.

The RISE UP trial was conducted across 69 sites in 15 countries and randomized 207 patients older than 16 years with anemia and recurrent sickle cell pain crises in a 2:1 ratio to twice-daily mitapivat (100 mg) or placebo.

At baseline, participants had a median age of 25 years, 57.5% were female, mean hemoglobin was about 8.5 g/dL, and they averaged 3.4 sickle cell pain crises per year.

The primary endpoint of hemoglobin response was defined as a 1 g/dL or greater increase in average hemoglobin concentration from week 24 to week 52 compared with the baseline.

In a commentary accompanying the study, Jennifer Knight-Madden, MBBS, PhD, and Zachary Ramsay, MBBS, both of the University of the West Indies in Kingston, Jamaica, noted that despite the mixed results on the primary endpoints, "there could be clinical benefit" among the mitapivat responders.

The findings should be interpreted with caution, they noted, but post-hoc analyses suggested the mitapivat-treated participants "who achieved a hemoglobin response experienced lower annualized rates of sickle cell pain crises, fewer related hospitalizations and emergency department visits, longer times to first and second sickle cell pain crises, and lower fatigue scores compared with non-responders."

"The findings provide evidence that a clinically meaningful benefit can exist within a subset of patients," they wrote. "As acknowledged by the authors, this study was not designed to identify patients likely to achieve a hemoglobin response, and differences in hemoglobin response could be due to genetic and epigenetic modifiers, red cell metabolic differences, and co-inherited red cell variants."

As for safety data, mitapivat was associated with lower rates of grade ≥3 adverse events (AEs), at 33% versus 41% with placebo, and lower rates of serious AEs (20% vs 29%), Andemariam and colleagues reported. One of the serious AEs in a mitapivat-treated patient was considered treatment-related, however.

Overall, AEs leading to treatment discontinuation occurred in 4% of patients in the mitapivat group and in 3% of the placebo group. Despite no signal of liver injury in the study, some hepatic-related AEs did lead to mitapivat discontinuation, including one patient with increases in aspartate aminotransferase (grade 3) and bilirubin (grade 2), another patient with hepatic enzyme increases (grade 4) deemed unrelated to treatment, a patient with hepatic cytolysis (grade 2) and other AEs, and one patient with transaminase increases (grade 2) considered secondary to an infection.

Deaths occurred in 2% of the mitapivat arm and 3% of the placebo arm, with none deemed treatment-related.

#5729. New Florida ‘Agrihood’ Development Bets on Organic Farming to Lure Homebuyers

A new masterplanned community in Northeast Florida will offer multiple organic farms to attract buyers who are more interested in fresh vegetables than the state's famed beaches.

Saratoga Springs, a new development from Freehold Communities, will eventually have about 4,500 homes within multiple communities on 2,400 acres of land.

Located in Green Cove Springs, outside of Jacksonville, the "agrihood" will contain numerous working farms, bringing sustainable agriculture, farm-to-table dining, farmers' markets, and all things farm-related to the community.

Agrihoods, which mix subdivision developments with agriculture, most often appear in communities with large, undeveloped tracts of land or existing agricultural zoning.

This combination of agricultural land and neighborhood must then be developed to include housing while still incorporating an agricultural component of the community, according to Freehold Communities.

The first phase of the Saratoga Springs agrihood—a 55-plus community called Sagebrooke—began sales in August 2026.

The gated senior community is built by Ryan Homes, with eight single-family home designs ranging from 1,488 to 2,729 square feet.

The active adult community will contain the usual amenities—such as a resort-style pool and pickleball, tennis, bocce courts and a putting green—but also boasts a private working farm and vineyard, a farm share from harvested crops, and a farm store.

Here, the signature crop will be a muscadine vineyard featuring Florida’s native grape, which thrives in the heat and humidity.

Home prices in the development range from $349,990 to $556,990. A spokesperson for Freehold wouldn't reveal the number of sales thus far but says that "it's exciting to see the level of demand."

Carmen Eldridge, 40, cofounder with her husband, Tripp, of Convivial Foodscapes, is heading up the farm aspect of Saratoga Springs. The couple led farm planning on two other Freehold agrihoods—Arden, in Palm Beach County; and Carnes Crossroads in Goose Creek, SC.

The pair navigate the process for creating functional agrihoods—everything from vetting land purchases, to business planning and budgets, to irrigation needs, to farm design and infrastructure construction, as well as distribution models for getting the produce into the wider community.

"It's a movement that is catching on," she says of agrihoods.

According to an Urban Land Institute study, agrihoods are a growing trend, available in at least 27 states. Key agrihood features include conservation space, protected farmland, farm stands and markets, and edible landscaping.

"People are drawn to the idea of living closer to where their food comes from," says Eldridge. "They like the wide open green spaces, and are into healthy eating and longevity."

"It's more appealing to live near an organic farm than a golf course," she adds, noting that a lot of parents want their children to know that "a carrot comes out of the ground, not from a bag in the grocery store."

The Saratoga Springs farms will be cultivated by professional farmers—not the residents. But residents will be able to pick or bring home farm produce round the clock, a perk included in the HOA fees. (They will not have private plots or gardens.)

Eldridge tells Realtor.com that her agrihood consultancy has been in brisk demand as sustainable farms become the latest trend in the masterplanned community world. But she asserts that farms go far beyond typical amenities such a pool, fitness center, or pickleball courts.

"A farm is social infrastructure, it's not just an amenity," she says. "It creates repeated, meaningful touch points between neighbors. A farm actively builds a community identity in a way that other amenities can’t replicate. That’s why it’s catching more attention now."

She counts Freehold as among the leaders in the agrihood trend.

"Some developers want to put in a community garden to check the box, like, got the dog park, got the pool, got the community garden, check," she says. "But they go all-in and do it really well."

Eldridge says farming is in her blood, as her maternal immigrant grandparents had been farmers in Spain.

"At the time, everyone was a farmer," she says. "There were no grocery stores. You farmed or you died."

She grew up with plenty of fresh produce from her family's backyard gardens.

"I didn't think much of it at the time," she says. "I was just told to go out back and pick some green beans for dinner."

When she informed her grandparents that she was going to study organic crop production in college, they weren't too pleased.

"They said, 'We moved here so you didn't have to be a farmer!'"

After graduating from the University of Florida with a degree in Political Science, focusing on Agriculture Policy and Organic and Sustainable Crop Production, Eldridge served as a Sustainable Agriculture Peace Corps volunteer in Panama, then founded a teaching farm at the University of North Florida.

Eventually, she and husband, Tripp, worked to set up the farms at Freehold's Arden agrihood, where they served as farm directors for five years; then they designed and built the farm at Carnes Crossroads.

The pair, who jokingly refer to themselves as "landless farmers," formed Convivial Foodscapes in 2020, and soon afterward came aboard the Saratoga Springs project.

Agrihoods, and the employment of local farmers to work the land, have been somewhat of an unexpected and steady income source for those in the notoriously difficult farming industry.

Farmers from the vicinity are also invited into the private community to sell produce and goods, offering a larger customer base for those who work the land on tight margins.

"Our farmer population is aging," she says, noting that agrihoods offer "a job for farmers with a living wage and health benefits."

Eldridge, who uses only organic farming techniques, takes great joy in people's reactions to fresh produce.

"I love when people's faces light up when they learn what a real tomato actually tastes like," she says. "I live for those moments."

But what most excites Eldrige about the concept of agrihoods and their growing popularity is the social aspects.

Farms offer diverse ways for communities to connect through food—picking produce, volunteering, helping to farm, attending workshops, hosting farm-to-table meals, or mingling at special events tied to fresh food or signature crops.

Eldridge, who often attends model home showings at Saratoga Springs, says that the buyer pool is very broad—everyone from young families to downsizing retirees—but they often have one thing in common: they are foodies at heart.

"There is something universally appealing about food," she says. "We all like to eat and we all have a food story."

Court rejects CMS' definition of 'medical frailty' under Medicaid work requirements" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

A Massachusetts judge has sided with a coalition of states in an ongoing lawsuit over the rollout of Medicaid work requirements, and rejected the Trump administration's definition of "medical frailty" for critical exemptions.

Judge Richard Stearns ruled Thursday that a regulation issued over the summer that aimed to offer guardrails to the implementation of the work requirements unlawfully limited the group of people who would qualify as "medically frail" and would thus be exempted.

In the rule, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said that the frailty exemption would apply when a "physical, mental, or other behavioral health condition significantly impairs the individual’s ability to comply with the community engagement requirement."

This runs afoul of existing law, as there are individuals in five frailty categories established by Congress who may not qualify for the exemption under CMS' definition, Stearns said.

"Because enforcement of an unlawful definition of 'medically frail' may lead to the disenrollment of otherwise eligible vulnerable individuals relying on Medicaid coverage for continuity of care, the States (and public) face potential for great hardship in the absence of an injunction," Stearns wrote. "The court accordingly will issue the permanent injunction requested by the States."

Stearns' ruling isn't a complete win for the state plaintiffs, as he allowed other challenged provisions to stand. Under the order, he determined that CMS should offer states a six-month stay of enforcement on frailty determinations given the short timeline ahead of the work requirements' rollout.

States are down to the wire in implementing the requirements, which were established as part of the massive H.R. 1 legislation in the summer of 2025. The eligibility determinations must be in place nationally on Jan. 1, and experts have warned that the added administrative burden is likely to lead millions to fall out of the Medicaid coverage rolls.

A federal judge has rejected a request from 26 states for a preliminary injunction in the Trump administration's rollout of work requirements in Medicaid.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services finalized implementation guidelines for states in June, with the eligibility requirements set to take effect on Jan. 1. States have until Aug. 31 to communicate with enrollees about the impacts of the changes.

In the lawsuit, the states argued that they do not have the resources necessary to meet the timelines that CMS established in June. They also pushed back on multiple provisions of the final rule, including regulators ultimate definition of medical frailty, which will have a significant impact on who qualifies for exemptions to the requirements.

In an order issued Wednesday, Massachusetts District Judge Richard Stearns wrote that the states did not prove that establishing the systems necessary to make the eligibility determinations would cause them irreparable harm, as CMS said it would reimburse them for 90% of the costs for setting up those mechanisms.

However, he said that the order does not reflect the court's opinion on the merits of the broader litigation, which challenge provisions of the rule under the Administrative Procedure Act. Making a determination on that, as it questions whether officials hewed closely to Congressional intent in regulating the rollout of the requirements, requires a more complete picture.

"These are determinations that, in the view of the court, should be made on a developed record of the kind that informs a court’s decision at the summary judgment stage of a case," wrote Stearns.

A coalition of 26 states is suing the Trump administration over its rollout of Medicaid work requirements.

In the lawsuit—jointly led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta, Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell, and New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport—the states seek to challenge provisions in the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services' recently-finalized rule establishing guardrails for the work requirements implementation.

A key pillar of that rule is the agency's definition of who would be considered "medically frail," and thus qualify for an exemption to the requirements. The states argue that the newly established definition will make it far harder for people who may need an exemption to obtain one.

In addition, under the rule, states are now asked to notify Medicaid enrollees of the incoming work requirements by Aug. 31, though the requirements will not be in place until Jan. 1. The suing states argue that this new window leaves them with insufficient time to reach out to members.

The lawsuit is asking the courts to block or strike down these parts of the rule, as they have already made strides toward implementing the work requirements based on previous CMS guidance and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which established the national mandate for the eligibility requirements.

If states fail to comply with the final rule, they face significant potential fines, the suing states said.

In a press release from Massachusetts Attorney General Campbell's office, the state notes that officials raised concerns with CMS about the impact of sudden changes to the timeline, which could lead to disruptions in implementation.

In addition, the states argue that the work requirements violate the Administrative Procedure Act, as there is "substantial" evidence that the administrative barriers can lead people who are eligible to lose coverage given the burden in keeping up with the requirements.

“The Trump Administration’s attempt to impose new, burdensome requirements on Medicaid recipients threatens access to healthcare for our most vulnerable residents and families,” said Campbell in a press release. “Congress made clear that people with serious medical conditions should not lose coverage. We are asking the court to block these unlawful provisions to protect Medicaid recipients and prevent needless strain on Massachusetts’ healthcare system.”

Beyond California, Massachusetts and New Jersey, other states signed on to the lawsuit include Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Kentucky, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington and Wisconsin.

#5727. Study Strengthens Case for Stent-Free PCI in De Novo Coronary Lesions

— Magic Touch drug-coated balloon was noninferior to drug-eluting stent

For de novo coronary lesions, drug-coated balloons (DCBs) were just as effective as standard drug-eluting stents, the TRANSFORM II trial showed.

Among patients with native coronary lesions undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), the incidence of target lesion failure at 12 months -- including cardiac death, target vessel myocardial infarction (MI), and ischemia-driven target lesion revascularization -- was 2.1% with the Magic Touch sirolimus DCB and 2.4% with standard everolimus drug-eluting stents (DES; HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.47-1.59).

The DCB thus met prespecified criteria for noninferiority (P=0.004), reported Bernardo Cortese, MD, MSc, of Fondazione Ricerca e Innovazione Cardiovascolare in Milan, at the Transcatheter Cardiovascular Therapeutics annual conference hosted by the Cardiovascular Research Foundation.

"All of this put into the context of the available literature and the SELUTION De Novo clinical trial, I can conclude that the DCB approach is a safe and effective alternative to stents in a selected population of de novo lesions, but bear in mind that there is no class effect for drug-coated balloons," Cortese said.

The Magic Touch is a DCB designed to release sirolimus and have it stay in the arterial wall for 8 to 12 weeks. The appeal of a DCB is that, unlike DES, the standard of care for native coronary artery disease, no permanent metal is left behind during PCI.

DCBs are already established as a treatment for coronary in-stent restenosis, an indication for which paclitaxel- (the Agent DCB) and sirolimus-eluting DCB models (the Selution SLR) are available on the market. The evidence is more shaky for DCBs in native coronary artery disease, especially following the negative REC-CAGEFREE I trial, though in last year's SELUTION De Novo trial, the Selution DCB was shown to be noninferior to DES for rates of target lesion failure.

Of note, though rates of clinically driven target lesion revascularization were comparable between groups in TRANSFORM II, rates of any target lesion revascularization were higher in the DCB group (2.5% vs 1.1%, HR 2.31, 95% CI 1.10-4.85).

One theory, noted Cortese, is that physicians in this open-label trial may have tended to re-treat patients if they had subpar angiographic results after DCB therapy, whereas they may have been more conservative if they saw stents in the picture. "But the numbers were very low, so this is very, very speculative," he cautioned.

Besides the concern for target lesion revascularization, there is also the question of costs.

Session co-chair Ajay Kirtane, MD, of NewYork-Presbyterian/Columbia University Irving Medical Center in New York City, questioned if cath labs will be willing to switch to DCBs if the listing prices are about $6,000, compared with the $300 to $400 for DES.

"Financial reimbursements are still a big issue for centers, and I think it will continue to be, and particularly as we get farther along, and all the Medicare mandates end. So I think we'll have to wait and see," said panelist Jennifer Tremmel, MD, of Stanford University Medical Center in Palo Alto, California. "We're going to have to decide who gets DCB, who gets DES, when do they get it, and the financials are going to make a difference. So I'm curious to see how things go over the long term, and ultimately which patients we decide to use this in first."

TRANSFORM II was an open-label multicenter trial conducted in Europe, Asia, and Brazil. Participants had to have native coronary lesions with reference vessel diameters measuring 2.0 to 3.5 mm and lesion lengths no greater than 50 mm.

Following successful vessel preparation, patients were randomized 1:1 to the Magic Touch sirolimus DCB or the everolimus DES. Out of 2,699 people screened, 2,223 met criteria for entry, and 1,842 had successful lesion preparation and were ultimately randomized.

Mean age was about 63 years, and most patients were men. Initial presentation was roughly split between acute coronary syndrome and chronic coronary syndrome. Over 35% had diabetes, and about one in three had a prior MI. Approximately 30% had a high bleeding risk.

Lesions were type B2/C in about two in three cases. Bailout stenting was required in 7.6% of the DCB group.

Cortese reported that the minimum lumen diameter at baseline was about 0.92 mm, and in-device acute lumen gain averaged 0.76 mm with DCB and 1.30 mm with DES. On quantitative coronary angiography, the percent diameter stenosis at baseline was about 59%, and this dropped to 31% after lesion preparation. After PCI, the in-device percent diameter stenosis was 26.8% with DCB and 12.3% with DES. The proportion of patients with in-device residual stenosis <30% was 61.2% with DCB and 97.9% with DES.

Regarding the primary endpoint, intention-to-treat results were consistent with the per-protocol analysis, according to Cortese. Individual components of target lesion failure were also generally favorable with DCB:

A secondary endpoint, net adverse clinical events (all-cause mortality, any MI, ischemic stroke, or major bleeding), was not significantly different between the DCB and DES arms (4.1% vs 5.3%, HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.50-1.17).

Cortese stressed that these results do not apply to lesions with unsuccessful lesion preparation and excluded groups (patients with severe calcification, highly tortuous vessels, and left main or vein graft lesions; ST-segment elevation MI within 48 hours; previous PCI in the target vessel; complex bifurcation lesions; and ejection fractions below 30%, among others).

Among other study limitations, event rates were much lower than expected, and the results may have limited generalizability given that the operators were all from experienced DCB centers.

As for the question of whether DCBs might eventually reach superiority over DES for native coronary lesions, Cortese said this will require long-term data, and his group does plan to continue patient follow-up out to 5 years.

"We are expecting to see fewer events starting from year 3, like we have seen with paclitaxel-coated balloons in a patient-level meta-analysis," he said.

#5726. BCBSMA, Medzown team up to match members with clinical trials

BCBSMA, Medzown team up to match members with clinical trials" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts is teaming up with precision medicine company Medzown to make it easier for members with complex conditions to participate in clinical trials.

In the partnership, Medzown's tech stack will identify the members that are most likely to benefit from a novel therapy for their condition, and then match them with potential clinical trials. The company will then deploy a team of scientists, clinical trial experts and care navigators to work alongside the patient and their care team through the process.

Jennifer Levin Carter, M.D., the CEO of Medzown, told Fierce Healthcare that there's no shortage of new drugs and therapies coming through the pipeline for complex diseases like cancer, but access is a significant challenge.

"The next frontier for precision medicine is making sure that the right patient can actually get access," Carter said.

BCBSMA will notify members of their eligibility for the program, and participation is voluntary. The program is offered at no additional cost for members.

Karl Laskowski, M.D., vice president for clinical programs and strategy at BCBSMA, said in an interview that complex diseases like cancer are often scary and difficult for patients to navigate, and clinical trials offer access to therapies or care they "wouldn’t have otherwise at their disposal."

"It is not always clear what to do, and there’s a lot coming at you," he said. "We want to show up as a trusted ally, making sure that we are filling a need there for people to get advice, taking advantage of whatever may be the most appropriate."

The insurer said that the partnership with Medzown builds on its existing work to manage complex diseases. For example, in June, BCBSMA entered a value-based care contract with Thyme Care, offering its services as an extension of the patient's current care team.

It's BCBSMA's first specialty-specific value-based care relationship, the insurer said.

Laskowski said that it's early days for the partnership with Medzown, but the team is gathering feedback on what's working and what's not to continue improving and building on this foundation.

Carter echoed the sentiment, saying that while there's likely "tremendous opportunity" to grow from here, the focus is on making sure the current program is functioning at the highest level for the members it serves.

She added that the Medzown team believes that a precision medicine data layer will be critical to healthcare more broadly as the treatment for complex disease becomes more and more personal.

"Treatment of cancer has totally changed for many cancer types," she said. "It has turned into a disease that can be managed on a long-term and chronic basis."

"We need to be able to integrate that ... so that these great and fabulous new esoteric therapies get into the continuum of care," Carter said.

For the quarter, executives generally described rising hospital activity and continued expense reductions that outpaced industry-wide weak surgical volumes and payer mix challenges.

Specifically, same-hospital admissions rose 2.8% year over year, adjusted admissions rose 3.2% and hospital surgeries dipped 1.1%. Net hospital revenues rose 6.1% year over year while revenue per adjusted admission rose a narrower 0.2%, as “continued pricing strength” and volumes outpaced 18% declines in exchange admissions and revenues, executives said.

Adjusted EBITDA for the hospitals business grew from last year’s $607 million to $818 million (including the $147 million one-time items). The segment also recognized $32 million more in favorable pre-tax impact tied to supplemental Medicaid payments compared to the prior year, or $356 million in total.

In Tenet’s high-margin ambulatory segment, same-facility net patient service revenues rose 4.5% year over year despite a 1.5% drop in same-facility cases. Same-facility net revenue per case rose 6.1%, which executives said reflects the company’s ongoing strategic push to capture high-acuity patients. Adjusted EBITDA rose 9.1% year over year to $537 million.

On surgical numbers, which have been a sore spot for systems over the last few months, Sutaria said the company was pleased that both sides of the business were performing “generally consistent or better than we’re seeing in the general industry. … I would not say this is a gangbusters surgical environment right now.”

The ambulatory surgery market in particular has been heating up as health systems look to flesh out their networks and meet the calls for care in lower-cost settings. Sutaria, in response to an analyst question, acknowledged this week’s news that Bon Secours Mercy Health would be acquiring Surgery Partners in a $5.7 billion deal. Taken alongside the summer’s $3.9 billion AmSurg close by Ascension, he said that Tenet’s platform remains the standout for differentiated earnings growth. What’s more, the “attractive valuation of our equity, relative to what are some reasonable valuations of … ASC-hospital combination platforms” gives the company additional reason to repurchase its shares, he said.

“Look, in terms of the two recent ASC acquisitions, you know, I personally extended my congratulations to both new owners,” he said. This is an important part of the market and we have a lot of work to do together from an advocacy perspective in order to support and build the growing interest in ambulatory surgery, maintain high quality and safety, and also ensure that regulators understand the benefits that this portion of the surgical sector is providing to the cost of healthcare going forward. And so I look forward to those collaborations with those leaders.”

On concerns of dealmaking competition, Sutaria noted that the company was “very successful” in new ASC acquisitions during the quarter and that “the vast majority of which were not competitive processes, but came exclusively to [us] in those processes.”

As for next year, executives said Tenet is expected to grow its overall EBITDA. That’s after excluding the impacts of the CommonSpirit contract termination, and taking into account “the current known regulatory frameworks” such as those outlining Medicaid work requirements and supplemental payments.

Tenet’s stock was trading about 1% below the day’s open as of early afternoon. Its report comes after other large for-profits like HCA Healthcare and Universal Health Services outlined persistent payer mix and surgery concerns as well as tepid early guidance for 2027.

#5724. Novel Therapy Lands Speedy Approval for Wart-Like Airway Disease

— Plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy reduced surgery need in recurrent respiratory papillomatosis

The FDA granted accelerated approval to doruxapapogene ralaplasmid and lalikinogene sifuplasmid (Voceryq) to reduce the frequency of surgical papilloma excisions in adults with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP), the agency announced late on Friday.

As the first FDA-approved recombinant plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy, doruxapapogene ralaplasmid-lalikinogene sifuplasmid targets the wart-like growths that characterize RRP. The growths are caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) and develop in the airways, particularly around the larynx. Severe cases of the rare disease can spread into the respiratory tract and make breathing difficult. There is no cure, but repeated surgeries can remove growths if they return.

FDA based its decision on efficacy data from RRP-001, a phase I/II clinical trial. The open-label trial included 32 patients who'd undergone at least two surgeries in the prior year to remove RRP growths. Among 26 patients who had at least three surgeries in the 12 months before treatment, 27% had a complete response to the plasmid therapy, defined as requiring no surgical excisions during 12 months of follow-up.

"The approval of Voceryq is an important step in improving the quality of life for RRP patients as every surgery carries the risk of laryngeal injury," said investigator Simon Best, MD, of Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, in a statement from manufacturer Inovio Pharmaceuticals. "I believe it is in the best interest of RRP patients that the standard of care quickly transition away from surgical interventions to immunotherapy after RRP is diagnosed."

Doruxapapogene ralaplasmid-lalikinogene sifuplasmid includes two plasmids that contain genetic coding for HPV proteins and interleukin 12. Patients' own healthy cells transcribe that coding to stimulate immune system attacks against cells infected with the HPV types 6 and 11 that cause RRP.

The therapy's treatment regimen begins with surgical debulking of visible papilloma, followed by an intramuscular dose of the plasmid therapy every 3 weeks for a total of four doses. Label warnings include potential adverse events (AEs) such as muscle contractions, transient bleeding, and vasovagal reactions. The most common AEs in trials included injection site reactions, headache, fatigue, hypertension, nausea, and dizziness.

The new treatment was approved in combination with a proprietary DNA medicine delivery device (CELLECTRA 5PSP). Postmarketing trials will be required to verify and describe the therapy's clinical benefit.

The FDA approved the immunotherapy zopapogene imadenovec (Papzimeos) for RRP in 2025, the first approved medical therapy for the condition.

#5722. Community Health Systems logs $86M net loss in Q3, hopes for return of 'pent-up' electives in 2027

Community Health Systems logs $86M net loss in Q3, hopes for return of 'pent-up' electives in 2027" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

A “challenging macro environment” serving up more uninsured patients and fewer commercial elective procedures dragged Community Health Systems below internal and analyst operating forecasts for the third quarter.

The 59-hospital system reported $2.76 billion in third-quarter net operating revenue, down about 10.7% year over year due to several divestments but up 3.8% on a same-store basis. Net loss was $86 million, -$0.63 per diluted share or -$0.48 after adjustment, compared to the prior year’s $1.27 per share net income.

The consensus estimates for revenue and earnings were $2.78 billion and -$0.22 per diluted share, per Zach’s Investment Research. The company’s shares were trading over 10% below the open late Thursday afternoon.

“While overall financial results fell below our internal forecast, due to the same factors that many peers are experiencing—namely elevated uninsured volumes and temporary softness in commercial elective procedures—we delivered sequential volume gains and solid cash flow performance,” CEO Kevin Hammons summarized Thursday morning on the company’s earnings call. “Importantly, our leading indicators clearly demonstrate that care is being deferred rather than lost to competitors.”

CHS has reduced its 2026 guidance ranges for net operating revenues, adjusted EBITDA and cash ranges.

Same-store admissions rose 2.2% while adjusted admissions increased 3.6% year over year. However, about half of the adjusted admissions growth was among uninsured patients, Chief Financial Officer Jason Johnson explained, and a 2% overall increase in same-store surgeries masked low numbers for commercial electives. These factors held same-store net revenue per adjusted admission to just 0.2% year-over-year growth.

Executives, in response to analyst questions, noted that the 2% increase is a clear improvement from recent quarters’ declines.

“We saw more cardiac procedures and more GI procedures this quarter,” Hammons explained. “The cardiac procedures, though, … are low margin because of the high cost of the devices. What we were short on were the elective orthopedic and elective general surgery-type procedures that are higher-margin business, and those are more elective type procedures. […] Again, kind of fits back into the story of we believe this is a patient decision around care, and being influenced by financial decisions.”

In the meantime, Hammons said the company is “proactively managing our cost structure,” yielding more than $100 million in projected annual savings so far “without compromising our clinical capacity or operational readiness for tomorrow” when those electives return.

Looking to the tea leaves in 2027, executives suggested there would be a “modest” headwind from Medicaid work requirements. While more than half of the company’s Medicaid volumes are in expansion states, “we think it’s likely that the very large majority will qualify for continued coverage under the various exemptions like age, caregiver status or medical frailty, but we really just don’t know exactly what the impact will be until the data starts coming in,” Johnson said during the call.

Exchange volume reductions due to coverage drop-offs could see “some potential future degradation” based on how open enrollment goes, he said, although “we think there will be a modest headwind there.” Provider tax cuts will also likely bring another “modest” hit, while medical specialty fees expected to grow “well above inflation” are “the big question mark on cost,” Johnson added.

On the other hand, executives counted payment rate updates, investments in outpatient and ambulatory locations, expense management and $25 million to $30 million in year-one funds from the Rural Health Transformation Program as positive factors for 2027 earnings.

Further, they suggested that this year’s “uncharacteristic” dearth in elective procedures could come to an end as cost-conscious patients—who are still captured in CHS’ care networks—eventually book their deferred care.

“There’s pent-up demand,” Hammons said. “Ultimately, we think that it comes back into the system because when you need a joint replacement, it’s not going to heal on its own.”

“Our initial expectations [were that when] we got into the back half of this year, we would see that seasonality growth. We did not see as much of that in the third quarter as we had previously expected,” he explained. “As you get to October, if people have not met their co-pay and deductible, it’s likely they could push that off until next year, get their procedures in the first half of the year and have a longer period of time to have other medical procedures done without having to pay a co-pay and deductible again. So we’ve adjusted our guidance accordingly to reflect our outlook on that.”

CHS is hardly alone in navigating surgery and payer mix challenges. Fellow for-profits HCA Healthcare, Universal Health Services and Tenet Healthcare each described varying levels of impact during earnings calls held this week. Each held off from detailing concrete estimates for the coming year, noting a need to monitor year-end trends and the exchanges’ open enrollment period, but acknowledged that Medicaid coverage will likely continue to be a sore spot.

#5721. A Pristine 1950s John Lautner ‘Time Capsule’ Just Listed for $2.1M—and It’s Had Only One Owner

Referred to as the Rosemary and Joseph Baldwin Residence, a John Lautner-designed home seeks a new steward in the trendy Los Angeles neighborhood of Silver Lake.

But what’s even more rare is that this three-bedroom, two-bath property spanning 1,679 square feet has had just one owner. With very few updates, it’s a veritable time capsule.

Tucked into a wooded, hillside setting, Lautner balanced the home on posts anchored by shear walls. This creates a floating effect, made even more dramatic with floor-to-ceiling glass and a wraparound deck. That the home is seamlessly integrated into nature, including redwood-plank siding and skylights that coax in nature light, are two other marvels.

“The house is completely original, minus a tree that was growing through the teak deck in the backyard and that needed to be removed,” says Louis Magnano of Modern California House, who is handling the $2,099,999 listing. “It’s about as original as you can get in 2026.”

This includes the entire kitchen as well as lighting fixtures, mahogany paneling, and terrazzo and parquet flooring. As well, the fireplace is original, and all of the windows, too. Each bedroom’s built-ins are also intact. The living room’s inverted-pyramid ceiling and triangular clerestory windows are also striking.

“It’s completely original, which is very rare for these types of homes in L.A.,” says Magnano.

“They get traded (and) things are done to them when they shouldn’t be. This house doesn’t have that. Whoever is going to purchase this home and be the next steward will need to restore and bring it up to today’s standards but while maintaining the original quality of the home. The sellers want to see it restored.”

This could mean updating the systems, for starters.

How often does a Lautner-designed home hop onto the market, though?

“They have been coming up quite frequently for sale in the last few years,” says Magnano, “but there’s so few and far between, maybe it’s just a special time in the marketplace.”

In 1955, Lautner—a Taliesin Fellow under Frank Lloyd Wright during the 1930s—was commissioned by commercial artist James Baldwin and his wife Rosemary to create their family home, utilizing a 7,491-square-foot lot. Rosemary’s sister introduced them to Lautner.

Lautner’s residence (Silvertop) is on the same street as the Baldwin home.

“Silver Lake is really known for a lot of its architectural history, not only by John Lautner, but Richard Neutra, Rudolph Schinder, to name a few starchitects,” says Magnano.

Lautner would later design three other Southern California homes that put him on the map: The Chemosphere (1960), The Sheats-Goldstein Residence (1961-1963) and The Elrod Residence (1968).

“The Baldwin Residence marks a pivotal moment in that career: its siting, spatial progression, and detail recall Wright, even as they reveal Lautner's own emerging voice,” reads the listing, adding that this is “an authentic piece of Los Angeles architectural history and a rare stewardship opportunity that may not come again.”

In addition to the striking interior design, another wow-worthy feature are views of the Hollywood Hills and San Gabriel Mountains.

What will also likely attract buyers is the location. As a haven for artists, it’s similar to the type of community that drew the Baldwins there back in the 1950s.

“Silver Lake has a very rich artist community and it’s vibrant, with young people, and there’s new cafes and a lot of nightlife happening in the area,” says Magnano. “There’s a lot of development happening in Silver Lake and a big restoration project taking place in the reservoir that the city of Los Angeles is getting ready to break ground on soon, to beautify the area.”

The ideal buyer, he says, is “somebody who understands the significance of these historical properties, who wants to restore them and honor them and keep them in the original glory that they all are. It was a family home for the Baldwins. They had three children. It could be a family home (again) but it could be somebody’s second home or ‘home away from home.’”

Based in Milwaukee, Kristine Hansen writes for TravelandLeisure.com, ArchitecturalDigest.com, Vogue.com, and other outlets. She’s also the author of “Frank Lloyd Wright’s Wisconsin: How America’s Most Famous Architect Found Inspiration in His Home State.” She lives in a 1924 bungalow.

#5720. Teladoc Health beats Q3 expectations as BetterHelp insurance growth accelerates

Teladoc Health beats Q3 expectations as BetterHelp insurance growth accelerates" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Teladoc Health raised its 2026 outlook after better-than-expected third-quarter results, as BetterHelp’s insurance pivot gained traction and Integrated Care profitability improved.

The virtual care company posted declining revenue but still beat Wall Street on both revenue and profit. Teladoc Health's Q3 beat drove shares up nearly 27% Thursday after the company reported Q3 earnings Wednesday after market close.

Teladoc Health faces near-term pressure as it transitions its virtual mental health business, BetterHelp, from a cash pay model to an in-network, insurance-covered model.

The company's consolidated revenue was $605.1 million, down 3.4% year-over-year but towards the high end of management's guidance range, as solid performance in the integrated care business and strong BetterHelp insurance growth was partially offset by ongoing headwinds in BetterHelp’s cash pay revenue, Chief Financial Officer Michael Grasher, who joined the company in August, told investors and analysts on the company's Q3 earnings call Wednesday. Teladoc's Q3 revenue exceeded the $588.4 million analyst consensus.

The company reported third-quarter adjusted EBITDA of $79.4 million, up roughly 14% year-over-year and compared to the $67.7 million consensus target. Teladoc reported a net loss of $26.9 million, or a loss per share of 15 cents, versus Street expectations for a loss of 22 cents per share.

The company generated $79 million in free cash flow in the third quarter, and it ended the quarter with $850 million in cash and cash equivalents.

Teladoc Health raised its full-year 2026 revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance. The company now expects 2026 revenue of $2.39 billion to $2.44 billion, raising the midpoint of its full-year 2026 revenue outlook by $13 million, “driven largely by the updated BetterHelp outlook,” Grasher said.

The company expects adjusted EBITDA of $277 million to $303 million, up $3 million at the midpoint versus the prior range.

Teladoc Health is focused on expanding access to its direct-to-consumer virtual mental health services, BetterHelp, through insurance coverage while also growing its integrated care enterprise business.

"As we consider the market more broadly as a company, we continue to see opportunities for virtual care to play an increasing role in addressing key challenges in healthcare," Teladoc Health CEO Chuck Divita said during the call.

As a scaled virtual care company, Teladoc's technology and services help address rising healthcare costs, expand access, improve chronic disease and mental health care and ease pressure on providers and the broader healthcare system, Divita said.

The BetterHelp segment brought in $207 million in revenue, down 13% year-over-year. BetterHelp commercial insurance revenue exceeded expectations, coming in at $32.1 million, up from $3.7 million a year ago and beating management's forecast of $25 million to $31 million. BetterHelp cash-pay revenue declined 25% to $174 million in Q3, as fewer users paid out of pocket. But cash pay performance for BetterHelp was "better than anticipated," Divita said. The company continues to reduce advertising spend for the BetterHelp business while also "adapting its advertising and marketing approach to reflect insurance priorities," he noted.

BetterHelp's pivot to an in-network insurance model is gaining momentum with 27,000 covered sessions per week in Q3, an annualized run rate above $140 million and more than 11,000 credentialed therapists, Divita told analysts and investors. That compares to the $110 million annualized run rate from weekly sessions referenced in Teladoc's second-quarter earnings call.

In Q3, 36% of acquired U.S. users came from insurance, up about 8 percentage points from the second quarter, according to executives. The company added more than 3,000 therapists to the network during the quarter.

"We believe expanding insurance access can help create a more durable position for BetterHelp over time," Divita said.

The company expects continued growth in 2027 as it expands provider capacity, improves therapist engagement and grows utilization of BetterHelp’s services, Grasher said.

Teladoc is targeting a $200 million annualized BetterHelp insurance run rate by the end of 2027.

“While there is more work ahead, this was a solid quarter driven by execution, and continued progress across our key strategic priorities,” Grasher said.

Teladoc Health continues to invest in its core business, integrated care, which brought in $399 million in Q3 revenue, up 2% year-over-year, and adjusted EBITDA of $74.9 million, up 13% year-over-year. Adjusted EBITDA margin reached 18.8%, and Grasher noted on the call that the Q3 margin expansion occurred despite the ongoing mix shift toward visit-based arrangements.

The virtual company is focused on moving health plan and employer clients away from fragmented point solutions to its broader Teladoc One model. Teladoc One, unveiled in July, is designed to offer a more coordinated, personalized approach for members, while tying payment to clinical and financial outcomes, executives said. As part of the model, Teladoc Health care teams deliver and coordinate care across virtual settings and in partnership with a member's local providers.

The company has moved forward with initial launch partners for Teladoc One, and the platform will be more broadly available in 2027, executives said.

"We are encouraged by the level of client engagement and member feedback on Teladoc One at this point, reinforcing our view that clients are looking for solutions that can deliver a more connected experience, address more care needs, and demonstrate greater accountability for outcomes and impact," Divita said.

Outside the U.S. market, Teladoc Health developed a "hybrid care" model that combines its technology with virtual clinical services delivered into physical healthcare settings. The company sees opportunities to build out that model with U.S. hospitals and health systems. To support that strategy, Teladoc Health acquired Teledigm Health, a company that provides virtual clinical services to U.S. hospitals and health systems. Teledigm partners with hospitals and clinics to deliver remote acute, outpatient and specialty care.

Financial details of the Teledigm Health deal were not disclosed.

"We believe the market dynamics supporting the adoption of our hybrid care models in other countries are also increasingly prevalent with hospitals and health systems in the U.S., including healthcare workforce and capacity challenges, financial pressures and the need to improve access for underserved and rural communities. As a result, we see an opportunity to leverage our experience in hybrid care within the U.S. to support future growth," Divita said during the call.

"This is a company that we've worked with for a long time that's used our technology and really commercialized the services part of the equation using our technology. The tracks have been laid in terms of using our technology and support and use cases to those health systems. We think bringing that expertise we have in non-U.S. markets, which is considerable and has been a nice source of growth for us, bringing that expertise combined with our technology and telehealth services together, we can really go after that market opportunity in 2027," he told investors and analysts during a Q&A on the earnings call.

Teladoc also continues to invest in product innovation to support its integrated care business. The company expanded its Solo enterprise platform with two AI tools designed to add clinical capabilities without forcing hospitals to adopt more standalone technology. The two new capabilities—dubbed SoloVitals and SoloScribe—bring contact-free vital sign measurement and ambient clinical documentation directly into clinical workflows.

Wall Street analysts saw positive signs of progress in the turnaround of Teladoc's BetterHelp business in the latest quarter.

Ryan Daniels, group head of healthcare technology and services at William Blair, wrote that Teladoc's third-quarter results provided a positive update on the company’s ability to convert strong insurance demand into revenue.

"We continue to view BetterHelp’s transition toward greater in-network coverage as the key driver of business stabilization, particularly as insurance growth increasingly offsets cash-pay declines and added capacity of credentialed therapists enables the company to capture strong underlying demand," Daniels wrote in an analyst note.

"We are also encouraged by the company’s continued 2026 product introductions and launches across virtual care, including implementing Teladoc One with early launch partners and expanding hybrid care and AI-enabled solutions set to support continued growth in the Integrated Care segment," Daniels wrote.

However, ongoing weakness in BetterHelp’s cash-pay business "is likely to weigh on overall segment performance and temper the pace of the company’s broader turnaround," Daniels noted.

Teladoc remains in a transitional phase, Daniels noted, "navigating slower growth and a challenging end-market, with increased emphasis on profitability, product enhancements and capital deployment into new growth avenues."

#5719. Industry Voices—The other AI divide is already opening in healthcare

Industry Voices—The other AI divide is already opening in healthcare" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The debate over AI and inequality has largely focused on people—who will have access to the technology, who will benefit from it and who risks being left behind. But inside healthcare, another AI divide is already taking shape. This one is between the hospitals that have the money, talent and infrastructure to put AI to work and those that don't.

The numbers are striking. According to federal data on hospital AI adoption, 71% of U.S. hospitals used predictive AI integrated with their electronic health records in 2024. But adoption reached 96% among large hospitals compared with just 59% among small hospitals. Among hospitals belonging to multi-hospital systems, 86% used predictive AI. Among independent hospitals, it was only 37%.

That gap matters because AI is quickly becoming part of how hospitals survive, not simply an innovation project. The same federal data show some of the fastest-growing hospital AI applications are decidedly practical, including billing and scheduling. These are exactly the kinds of labor-intensive functions where financially stressed hospitals need to find efficiencies.

Yet those hospitals may be the least equipped to make the investment.

Hospitals remain extraordinarily dependent on people to operate. According to the American Hospital Association, workforce spending accounted for about 60% of hospital expenses in 2025, exceeding $1 trillion. Total hospital expenses grew 7.5% that year, more than twice the growth in hospital prices.

This creates a dangerous catch-22. The hospitals with the greatest need to use technology to redesign labor-intensive operations frequently have the least capacity to invest in doing so.

A large health system can afford an AI pilot that fails. It can hire an innovation team, absorb a lengthy implementation, build governance and compliance infrastructure, and try again if the economics don't work. A safety-net, community or independent hospital often has far less room for error. A multi-year software contract that might eventually produce savings still requires money today.

And buying the technology is only the beginning.

Successful AI deployment requires workflow redesign, change management, integration, measurement and governance. Even among hospitals already using predictive AI, the federal data show meaningful variation in how comprehensively models are evaluated for accuracy, bias and performance after implementation. Smaller, rural and independent hospitals also continue to lag their larger counterparts in adoption.

If we leave the market to work this out one hospital at a time, we should expect that divide to compound. Systems that successfully automate expensive workflows can reinvest those savings into their next technology investment. They build institutional knowledge. Their employees get better at implementation. They become more attractive partners to technology companies looking for sophisticated customers and proving grounds.

The hospitals that wait don't simply remain where they are. They lose ground. The answer cannot be telling every hospital to develop a better AI strategy. We need to change the ownership and financing model for healthcare AI.

Hospitals already know how to collaborate when acting collectively creates an advantage. Group purchasing organizations allow them to aggregate purchasing power rather than negotiate for every product independently. Clinical research networks allow institutions to pool patients, expertise and infrastructure to answer questions no single organization could address as effectively alone.

We should apply the same instinct to AI. Instead of requiring every health system to independently buy, implement and govern variations of the same technology, health systems should increasingly pool their purchasing power, operational expertise and capital to build common AI capabilities. And smaller, independent and safety-net organizations need a path into those collaborations rather than simply another vendor contract.

The venture community has a responsibility here as well. We need financing structures that acknowledge the economic reality of the organizations that really need to adopt technologies. That could mean performance-based models where payment is tied to verified savings rather than large upfront commitments. It could mean consortium models in which multiple health systems share implementation resources and governance.

And increasingly, it should mean giving health systems ownership in the companies and infrastructure they help create. Ownership matters because the economics of AI are changing quickly. As the technology itself becomes increasingly commoditized, enduring value will come from distribution, proprietary workflows, real-world implementation knowledge and access to the environments where healthcare actually happens. Health systems contribute enormously to each of those things. Under the traditional vendor model, however, they can provide the workflows, clinical expertise and proving ground and then pay someone else an annual fee for the resulting product.

That bargain deserves to be reconsidered. Collective ownership can help address the trust problem, too. AI adoption isn't only a technology decision. It requires decisions about validation, monitoring, clinical safety and who is accountable when something goes wrong. Federal researchers found that hospitals increasingly rely on multiple parties to evaluate AI, with 74% reporting more than one entity accountable for evaluation. Smaller hospitals should not each have to recreate that infrastructure from scratch.

Shared infrastructure could include common validation standards, clinical oversight, monitoring and implementation expertise. That would give more hospitals access not only to AI, but to the capabilities required to deploy it responsibly.

None of this means every hospital needs to own every AI company, or that traditional vendors disappear. It means we should stop assuming that the only scalable model for healthcare innovation is one technology company selling essentially the same capability to thousands of hospitals one contract at a time.

The AI divide between hospitals is already here. If adoption continues to depend primarily on the size of an organization's balance sheet, the institutions best positioned today will keep accumulating advantages while those with the least room for error fall further behind.

AI gives hospitals a real opportunity to break their dependence on increasingly expensive, labor-intensive ways of operating. But the organizations that need that opportunity most cannot be the last ones able to afford it. Preventing that outcome will require more than making AI cheaper. It will require giving more health systems the ability to build, govern and share in the technology's value, transforming them.

AI should become something hospitals build together, not another advantage reserved for those that could already afford to move first.

Amanda DeMano is SVP of venture creation at Abundant Venture Partners.

Editor's Note: Abundant Venture Partners is a strategic investor in the makers of certain AI technologies, including SpendRule and Playback Health.

Alignment Healthcare lowers 2026 outlook as it navigates cost headwinds" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Alignment Healthcare is lowering its guidance for the year as it faces significant headwinds to finish out 2026.

The company said in an earnings report released late Thursday that it now expects to bring in $100 million in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or EBITDA, as well as $5.2 billion in revenue. Total membership is set to be at least 305,000, according to the report.

Alignment reported an $8 million loss in the third quarter, compared to a $3.8 million profit one year ago. Profits were $39.9 million through three quarters, up from $10.3 million across the first nine months of 2025.

Revenue in the third quarter was $1.4 billion, compared to $663.7 million in the prior-year quarter. Revenues through the first nine months of 2026 were $3.9 billion, up from $2.9 billion through three quarters in 2025.

CEO John Kao told investors on the company's earnings call Friday morning that some headwinds Alignment is facing include cost spikes in certain service lines, like catastrophic care and skilled nursing, as well as volatility in claims processing.

Last year, Alignment kicked off an effort to migrate to a comprehensive claims system with the goal of accelerating payment speed, growing automated adjudication rates and enhancing payment integrity. Through that process, once the dust settled on the shift, Alignment found "a notable increase in aggressive provider appeal and disputes in our paid claims data" that also drove up costs, Kao said.

Kao said that the insurer has spent the last several months building out its payment integrity capabilities, as well as deploying additional resources to support clinical best practices to mitigate the variation in outcomes for members.

He said that these investments have driven improvements, particularly in September and into October, but the company is still taking a cautious approach to the end of the year.

"Despite our progress, we are taking a prudent approach to the increased trend seen in Q3 and assume that higher costs in the third quarter will continue to weigh on our results for the remainder of the year," Kao said. "I want to emphasize that the guidance we have provided today is a guidance that we are confident in delivering."

Kao also addressed Alignment's performance in the latest round of star ratings scores. Based on federal data, 25% of its members are in plans with at least four stars in 2027, down from 100% in 2026. That four-star threshold is the key to securing quality bonus payments in Medicare Advantage.

He said that six of the company's seven contracts were above four stars, but a 3.5 score on the remaining plan, a core HMO offering in California, dragged down its overall performance.

Kao said that the team is "focused on really getting to the root issues in Stars." Alignment has also sued the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services over the 2027 calculations.

"That's something that we're going to be underscoring yet again," he said. "This is something that everybody in the company has to focus on ... and we'll get this fixed."

#5717. Scientists discover a hidden immune weapon against deadly lung cancer

Scientists have identified a previously overlooked type of immune cell that can detect and destroy small cell lung cancer, the most aggressive form of lung cancer worldwide.

The discovery, reported in the journal Cancer Cell by researchers at WEHI, revealed that patients with greater numbers of these specialized immune cells tended to survive longer. The findings point to a previously unrecognized immune defense that could provide a new way to attack tumors that are notoriously difficult to treat.

The research team also demonstrated that medications already in use could enhance the ability of these immune cells to kill cancer. This approach could eventually improve existing treatments and increase the number of patients who benefit from immunotherapy.

Why Small Cell Lung Cancer Is So Difficult to Treat

Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is among the deadliest cancers, with fewer than 7% of patients surviving for five years after diagnosis.

Immunotherapy has dramatically improved treatment for several types of cancer, but its success against SCLC has been much more limited. Only a small proportion of patients experience lasting benefits.

A major challenge is the cancer's ability to escape immune surveillance. SCLC tumors frequently avoid detection by the conventional immune cells that many immunotherapy treatments depend on, allowing the disease to persist despite the body's natural defenses.

The findings published in Cancer Cell suggest there may be another way for the immune system to recognize and attack these tumors. By identifying a previously overlooked immune pathway, researchers have uncovered a potential strategy for overcoming the cancer's ability to remain hidden.

Professor Kate Sutherland, the study's senior author and a laboratory head at WEHI, said the discovery could help address a longstanding challenge in lung cancer research: finding ways to make immunotherapy effective for more patients.

"For decades, we've known that small cell lung cancer is exceptionally good at hiding from the immune system," Prof Sutherland said.

"We've found an immune cell that appears to be able to see through that disguise.

"Strikingly, patients whose tumors contained more of these specialized immune cells often had better treatment outcomes.

"This is the strongest evidence yet that gamma delta T cells are present in small cell lung cancers and appear capable of fighting the disease.

"It suggests these cells may offer an alternative immune attack route for tumors that are able to evade conventional cancer-fighting immune cells, opening up new possibilities for treating a cancer that has seen few advances over the past decades."

Miniature Tumors Reveal a Powerful Immune Response

To investigate whether gamma delta T cells could directly attack lung cancer, the scientists developed miniature tumors in the laboratory using tissue samples donated by patients. The samples were obtained through the Victorian Cancer Biobank in partnership with the Royal Melbourne Hospital.

These miniature tumors, often called "mini tumors," provide one of the most realistic laboratory models of SCLC created so far, allowing researchers to study how cancer behaves and responds to potential treatments.

The team then introduced gamma delta T cells collected from the same patients' blood into the tumor models. The results showed that these immune cells were highly effective at identifying and destroying SCLC cells.

The scientists went a step further by testing whether two medications already approved for other uses could make this immune response even stronger. The drugs were tarlatamab (a cancer treatment approved for SCLC) and zoledronate (approved for osteoporosis and cancer-related bone disease).

Each medication contributed in a different way. Zoledronate increased the number of available gamma delta T cells and improved their ability to identify the lung cancer tumors. Tarlatamab helped bring the immune cells and cancer cells together, effectively directing the immune attack toward the tumors.

When used together, the drugs substantially increased the ability of gamma delta T cells to kill cancer cells in laboratory experiments. The findings suggest that combining existing treatments could provide a new strategy for strengthening the immune system's response to SCLC.

Could Existing Drugs Lead to New Lung Cancer Therapies?

Dr. Jin Ng, the study's first author, said the discovery could also support a treatment approach known as adoptive cell transfer. This involves collecting immune cells, multiplying them outside the body, and then delivering large numbers of those cells back into a patient to help fight cancer.

Because methods for expanding and reinfusing gamma delta T cells have already been developed, the researchers believe their findings could help accelerate the development of new treatments.

"For patients with lower gamma delta T cell levels, therapies such as zoledronate may offer a way to boost their cancer-fighting immune cells and responsiveness to treatments," Dr. Ng said.

"As therapies that expand and reinfuse gamma delta T cells already exist, our findings raise the exciting possibility of rapidly translating this discovery into new treatment strategies.

"This could open an entirely new avenue for personalized treatment approaches in small cell lung cancer and other solid cancers that are often missed by conventional immune cells."

Clues From Major Lung Cancer Immunotherapy Trials

The investigation began with an examination of data from two influential clinical trials, IMpower133 and CASPIAN. Both studies helped establish immunotherapy as a standard treatment option for patients with small cell lung cancer.

Researchers noticed evidence pointing toward an important role for gamma delta T cells and used sophisticated genomic and computational techniques to investigate further.

Analyses conducted by WEHI's genomics and bioinformatics teams revealed that patients with stronger gamma delta T cell signatures were among those who benefited most from immunotherapy.

Together with the laboratory findings, these results strengthen the evidence that gamma delta T cells play an important role in the immune response to SCLC and could become useful targets for future therapies.

The WEHI team is now working with scientists at the Doherty Institute to build on the discovery, with the goal of translating the findings into a new class of immunotherapy drugs for small cell lung cancer.

The research received support from Cancer Council Victoria, the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC), The CASS Foundation, and The International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer.
