#5704. Fierce Healthcare Policy Brief: HHS launches breast cancer screening initiative; RHTP funds flow to 6 states

Fierce Healthcare Policy Brief: HHS launches breast cancer screening initiative; RHTP funds flow to 6 states" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Stay up to date on the latest across Washington, D.C. with this weekly brief. Read below for news from Oct. 26 to Oct. 30.

HHS’ Office on Women’s Health (OWH) announced Tuesday a coordinated initiative with the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) and DenseBreast-info.org (DBI) to improve breast cancer screening and early detection efforts nationwide.

The OWH–AHRQ Breast Cancer Screening and Diagnostic Follow-up Initiative will analyze national screening and follow-up patterns, with more than 40 health systems poised to expand evidence-based practices and address delays in care.

“Women deserve clear information about breast cancer screening options beyond mammography, particularly if they have dense breasts or other risk factors,” said Tammy Huizenga, AHRQ senior advisor for nutrition and women’s health, in a statement. “Understanding their individual risk and available options helps women and their healthcare providers make informed decisions that support earlier detection.”

OWH and DBI will also collaborate through a memorandum of understanding to expand access to evidence-based educational resources aimed at supporting informed discussions between women and providers, promote understanding of screenings and diagnostic follow-up options, and improve breast density awareness.

HHS' health information technology arm finalized a rule that streamlines the health IT certification program, projecting to save billions in compliance costs.

The rule, called Health Data, Technology and Interoperability: ONC Deregulatory Actions to Unleash Prosperity (HTI-5), is projected to save more than $1.5 billion in regulatory costs, according to the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC). Full story.

The Trump administration awarded $233 million in Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) funding to improve healthcare access across California. This investment will help rural providers deliver and coordinate care locally through regional care networks, telehealth, workforce development and upgraded healthcare technology. California has committed its full fiscal year 2026 funding to improve healthcare in rural communities across the state.

The state plans to use the investment to expand rural primary, maternal, specialty and behavioral healthcare; grow the healthcare workforce; expand telehealth and regional care networks; modernize technology and infrastructure; and support new care delivery and payment models, according to a CMS announcement. Regional care networks and telehealth will connect patients with providers and help coordinate care, while partnerships with midwives, doulas and community health workers will support maternal and primary care. Investments will also support education and training pathways to grow the rural healthcare workforce, improve technology and modernize infrastructure.

It is the full amount of funding the state will receive for fiscal year 2026.

CMS doled out $193.7M in RHTP funding to 45 organizations across Florida to expand healthcare access in rural communities, with a particular focus on bringing care closer to patients.

Florida will use the substantial investment to build out telehealth, remote monitoring, mobile and community-based services; increase access to preventive and specialty care; strengthen rural providers and the healthcare workforce; and support new care delivery and payment models.

The state's approach uses telemedicine, remote patient monitoring, pharmacy-based services, diagnostic kiosks and community paramedicine to give patients more ways to access needed care. Partnerships are a defining feature of Florida’s approach, with more than 500 partnerships across the 45 awardees bringing hospitals, clinics, local governments and community organizations together to support statewide rural healthcare transformation, according to CMS in an Oct. 23 announcement.

Florida will receive $209,938,195 in total RHTP funding in fiscal year 2026.

CMS awarded $186 million in funding to improve healthcare access across rural Idaho. This investment will help rural providers deliver and coordinate care locally through modern technology, new care models, an expanded healthcare workforce and improvements to healthcare facilities, the agency announced.

The investment supports five initiatives designed to strengthen healthcare delivery and modernize rural Idaho’s healthcare system. Funding for telehealth, cybersecurity and electronic health record modernization will help rural providers deliver and coordinate care better locally. Investments in community health workers and emergency medical services professionals will help bring services into homes and communities, while training, recruitment and retention efforts will grow Idaho’s rural healthcare workforce. The funding will also support programs addressing chronic disease, behavioral health, maternal and child health as well as improvements to rural healthcare facilities and equipment.

It is the full amount of funding the state will receive for fiscal year 2026.

The Trump administration locked in a regulation that will require pharmacy benefit managers to disclose fees and compensation to self-funded employers.

The rule, finalized by the Department of Labor's Employee Benefits Security Administration, aims to ensure that employers can see what drug manufacturers, pharmacies and other entities are paying their PBMs and any affiliated brokers and consultants.

The department said in an announcement that this data will support employers in negotiating contracts and pushing to lower drug costs for their workers and their dependents. Full story

CMS awarded $87 million in RHTP funding to 129 rural healthcare providers through Rural Texas Strong to strengthen healthcare across rural communities. The investment will help improve health outcomes for rural Texans, build a strong healthcare workforce and modernize facilities and equipment across rural Texas, according to an agency announcement.

The funding will help rural providers prevent and manage chronic conditions, including diabetes, cardiovascular disease and chronic respiratory disease; recruit and retain physicians, emergency medical personnel and other healthcare professionals; replace aging medical equipment; and improve existing facilities. Together, these investments will help rural providers maintain essential services and bring quality healthcare closer to home for rural Texans.

Key initiatives the overall RHTP funding will focus on include:

Texas is slated to receive $281,319,361 in total RHTP funding in fiscal year 2026.

A Massachusetts judge has sided with a coalition of states in an ongoing lawsuit over the rollout of Medicaid work requirements, and rejected the Trump administration's definition of "medical frailty" for critical exemptions.

Judge Richard Stearns ruled Thursday that a regulation issued over the summer that aimed to offer guardrails to the implementation of the work requirements unlawfully limited the group of people who would qualify as "medically frail" and would thus be exempted.

In the rule, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said that the frailty exemption would apply when a "physical, mental, or other behavioral health condition significantly impairs the individual’s ability to comply with the community engagement requirement."

This runs afoul of existing law, as there are individuals in five frailty categories established by Congress who may not qualify for the exemption under CMS' definition, Stearns said. Full story

Missouri will receive nearly $40 million in RHTP funding to modernize rural healthcare services and expand access to care across the state. The investment will support 26 rural healthcare providers as they renovate, reconfigure, equip or repurpose existing facilities and expand maternal health, behavioral health, diagnostic, outpatient and chronic disease management services across Missouri, according to an announcement.

The funding will support new labor, delivery and private triage rooms; expanded behavioral health services for older adults and people with substance use disorders; and upgraded diagnostic equipment, including MRI, mammography and ultrasound services. The funding will also expand primary care and increase the capacity of rural health clinics, helping rural providers update existing facilities and capabilities to better match the healthcare needs of the communities they serve, CMS said.

In total, Mississippi will receive $216,276,818 during fiscal year 2026.

The Trump Administration announced more than $19 million in RHTP funding through 11 awards to strengthen and modernize healthcare delivery throughout rural West Virginia. The state plans to invest in virtual and specialty care, mobile health services and chronic disease management, growing the rural healthcare workforce and modernizing technology and health data systems.

The investment will support new tools and services across the state, including mobile health units and drone delivery for time-critical medical supplies; remote eye care and patient monitoring technology; nursing education and apprenticeship programs; and secure systems that allow healthcare providers to better share information. Investments will also support mental health and substance use disorder recovery services and tools that reduce administrative burden for healthcare professionals, CMS announced.

West Virginia will receive a total of $199,476,099 in RHTP funding in fiscal year 2026.

#5703. Scientists discover a hidden messaging system deep inside the brain

Deep within the brainstem is a tiny group of nerve cells that plays an outsized role in how the brain functions. This region, called the locus coeruleus (LC), gets its name from the Latin words for "blue place." Although it contains only a small fraction of the brain's neurons, it produces norepinephrine (NE), a chemical messenger that helps regulate attention, learning, heart rate, and the body's reactions to stress and excitement.

Scientists have long assumed that the LC operates like a loudspeaker, sending essentially the same norepinephrine signal across the brain. However, a new study published in Nature challenges that understanding. Using brain imaging, recordings of neural activity, genetic techniques, and behavioral experiments in mice, researchers at the Allen Institute discovered that the LC communicates through several distinct pathways. Rather than broadcasting one general message, it delivers signals to specific destinations, with different groups of neurons responding to different experiences.

A Hidden Brain Network That Sends Precise Messages

By tracing the connections of LC neurons, researchers found that different groups of cells communicate with specific regions of the nervous system. These pathways determine where signals trigger the release of norepinephrine, creating a much more organized communication network than previously recognized.

Neurons in the upper (dorsal) portion of the LC primarily connect to the cerebral cortex and forebrain. Meanwhile, cells in the lower (ventral) portion send their signals mainly to the brainstem and spinal cord. This arrangement allows different parts of the LC to influence separate brain functions.

"The findings suggest the brain's norepinephrine system is far more like a targeted postal network than a foghorn," said Karel Svoboda, director of Neural Dynamics at the Allen Institute and study co-author.

Why the Discovery Could Matter for Brain Disorders

Understanding how this signaling network is organized could eventually change how certain neurological and mental health conditions are treated.

Norepinephrine plays a central role in regulating attention and mood, making it an important target for medications used to treat depression, anxiety, and ADHD. Neurons in the LC are also among the earliest brain cells to deteriorate in Alzheimer's disease, suggesting that the new findings could have implications for understanding and treating these conditions.

Current treatments that influence norepinephrine can affect multiple brain circuits at once, sometimes producing beneficial effects in one region while causing unwanted effects elsewhere. A clearer map of the LC's specialized pathways could help scientists develop therapies that act more selectively on the circuits involved in particular symptoms.

The research received support from the National Institutes of Health's Brain Research Through Advancing Innovative Neurotechnologies® Initiative, also known as The BRAIN Initiative®.

Scientists Identify Brain Cells Involved in Learning

The researchers also uncovered an important distinction between the functions of different LC neurons.

Cells in the dorsal LC that connect to the cortex were particularly active during learning. When mice performed decision-making tasks and adjusted their choices after an unfavorable result, these neurons increased their activity.

Neurons in the ventral LC behaved differently. Their activity rose shortly before mice ignored signals indicating that a reward might be available. This suggests that these cells help regulate whether animals respond to opportunities in their surroundings.

"What emerged was a clear map: neurons in the dorsal LC that send signals upward to the cortex are involved in learning, whereas neurons in the ventral region projecting downward to the brainstem and spinal cord govern whether animals engage with their environment at all," said Svoboda. "We also showed that these anatomical differences are mirrored by distinct gene expression patterns."

These findings indicate that the differences between the two groups extend beyond their locations and connections. They also have distinct patterns of gene activity that reflect their specialized roles.

Researchers Discover a Record-Breaking Neuron

The study involved an extensive examination of the mouse brain. Scientists used whole-brain imaging to study nearly 35,000 neurons, analyzed the genetic profiles of almost 400,000 cells, and reconstructed the complete structures of several exceptionally complex nerve cells.

During this work, they encountered another remarkable finding: LC neurons possess extraordinarily long axons. These projections carry signals from nerve cells to other cells, allowing information to travel across the nervous system.

The researchers found that LC axons measured approximately 35 centimeters long on average. One particularly extraordinary axon had a total reconstructed length of 70.32 centimeters, making it part of the longest single neuron ever measured in a mouse.

"This neuron, like many others that we studied, supplies NE to a very large volume of the cerebral cortex. For the brain, this is highly unusual. Most neurons are more specific in their targets," said Jeremiah Cohen, scientist at the Allen Institute and study co-author. "But this neuron doesn't release NE everywhere. It ignores the cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal cord."

Despite its remarkable length and extensive reach, the neuron does not distribute norepinephrine throughout the entire brain. Instead, its connections remain selective, reinforcing the discovery that the LC operates through carefully organized signaling pathways.

A New Understanding of How the Brain Learns

The researchers also identified intriguing similarities between the norepinephrine system and the brain's dopamine signaling system.

Dopamine is another major chemical messenger that sends signals to the basal ganglia, a brain region involved in forming habits. Scientists suspect that dopamine and norepinephrine work together to support learning, potentially allowing the brain to acquire several complex and abstract concepts at the same time.

By revealing the intricate connections, specialized functions, and unusual physical structure of neurons in the locus coeruleus, the research provides a more detailed picture of how the animal brain communicates and learns.

Although the findings come from experiments in mice, they could eventually help scientists better understand human brain function and design treatments that target specific neural circuits rather than affecting entire signaling systems.

Materials provided by Allen Institute. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

And so, another working week will soon draw to a close. Not a moment too soon, yes? This is, you may recall, our treasured signal to daydream about weekend plans. AstraZeneca has launched a three-year cost-cutting program that aims to slice off $1.5 billion a year, with the savings reinvested in R&D, Pharmaphorum writes. There’s no word yet on the job implications from the initiative, which the company estimates will carry a one-time charge of around $2 billion and is expected to be completed by the end of 2029. The drug maker is already facing headwinds from the loss of patent protection for some products, including diabetes blockbuster Farxiga, with a string of other big brands due to lose exclusivity between now and the mid-2030’s, including three cancer drugs.

Indian regulators ordered Sun Pharmaceutical to stop manufacturing, selling and distributing ophthalmic products made at its Assam facility after finding failure in ​its quality management system, Reuters reported. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organization and the office of Drugs Controller Assam ordered the shutdown on ‌Aug. 20 after a joint federal-state inspection identified lapses in the system meant to ensure product quality and safety, following Sun Pharma’s move in July to voluntarily recall about 11 eye-care brands. Sun Pharma had previously said the site was expected to become one of its largest manufacturing ⁠hubs for sterile products in a business identified as a key global growth driver.

#5701. In Midterm Toss-Up States of Ohio, Iowa, Texas, and Maine, Housing Affordability Is Top of Mind

As the country heads into the final days before the 2026 midterm elections, housing affordability weighs heavily on many voters’ minds.

A recent Pew Research Center poll found that 66% of Americans are “very concerned” about housing costs. And this past July, CNBC’s All-America Economic Survey found that housing affordability is the top concern for Gen Z voters and men aged 18 to 44.

That’s likely because Americans are spending more money—and more of their incomes—on housing than they have in recent memory.

A 2024 study from Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies found that nearly half of all Americans—49%—spend more than the recommended 30% of their income on housing.

Yet lawmakers and voters remain divided on how to ease the economic burden so many Americans now face. Is it an issue of building more housing or backing more programs to subsidize rents and mortgages? Will raising wages solve the problem, or will creating more tenant protections offer relief? Or is the answer some combination of all of the above?

That's why, ahead of the 2026 midterms, Realtor.com® examined the housing issues animating voters in the four states that Decision Desk HQ has deemed Senate race toss-ups, with no clear leader in the polls: Maine, Iowa, Ohio, and Texas.

The goal was to understand better how housing issues are animating voters and what residents hope lawmakers will do once elected.

Despite radically different local environments, several common themes emerged: People feel that owning a home has become increasingly out of reach. They worry about people on the lowest end of the economic spectrum. They are also skeptical that an election will really change much.

Read on to learn what housing advocates and average citizens across Iowa, Ohio, Texas, and Maine want lawmakers to focus on after the electionn.

In the race for Maine's Senate seat, Democrat Troy Jackson is narrowly favored to defeat longtime incumbent Susan Collins, a Republican. Both agree that private equity investment in residential properties was a major problem in the state, though they don’t necessarily agree on how to solve it.

Jackson criticized Collins for voting against an amendment from Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-NH) that would support building 7 million new homes and expanding affordable housing opportunities. Collins has criticized Jackson for claiming two homes as primary residences for tax benefits.

Dan Martin, 41, and his family moved to Freeport, ME, from New Jersey five years ago, trading proximity to New York City for more space and a better quality of life.

He’s one of more than 126,000 people who have moved to Maine since 2020, and he says he was struck by the disparity in housing access in the state.

“Landowners here own a lot of land, and they’re often unwilling to give it up,” he says. “And that’s fine, but it does create a disparity in what’s available.

“We have a wide breadth of wealthy generational Mainers alongside Somalian refugees," he continues. "And we don’t have enough housing—low-income housing for those folks."

The National Low Income Housing Coalition estimates that Maine has a shortage of 20,000 rental homes for extremely low-income residents.

Wages in the state also haven’t kept up with housing costs. At the state minimum wage of $15.10 an hour, a worker must put in 67 hours a week to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment at a fair market price of $1,323 a month, according to NLIHC.

On Tuesday, Republican incumbent John Husted faces Democrat challenger Sherrod Brown in the Ohio race for U.S. Senate. Brown, a former Senator, narrowly leads in the polls, according to Decision Desk.

Husted’s campaign has stressed increasing the housing supply, cutting federal regulations, and enabling private investment rather than direct government funding. Brown favors lowering housing costs, expanding inventory, and protecting affordable housing.

Sonya Fix is a professor at Columbus College of Art and Design in Columbus, OH, and has lived in the city on and off for most of her life. She purchased her home in 2018, but says that many of her fellow 40-something friends are struggling to do so now.

"I’ve seen friends who are even in better positions than me not be able to buy a house. All of a sudden, during the [COVID-19] pandemic, everyone wanted to buy a house, and rates started going up. So I consider myself pretty lucky to have bought what I did."

Some of those friends "might have owned a house at one point but got divorced and have been renting. You know, it's just, it's really hard to reenter the market as a buyer now because houses are so expensive."Some of her friends who are renting are also feeling the squeeze.

"I am just absolutely shocked. I have no clue how working-class, lower-income, or even lower-middle-class families who have to rent are doing it," she says. Apartments that once rented for $500 to $600 a month now cost twice as much.

Fix would like to see stronger tenant protections, especially since two-bedroom rents in Ohio increased 28% between January 2020 and January 2025, according to the Coalition on Homelessness and Housing in Ohio.

"Especially in Columbus and the surrounding areas, where there's a lot of big tech coming in,” she says. "There has to be rental protections to allow people to stay in their homes as opposed to getting shoved out so that the landlord can get someone with more money."

Marcus Roth, communications director of the Coalition on Homelessness and Housing in Ohio, sees the housing crisis in the state as a multipronged problem, one that’s no longer just an issue for low-income Americans.

"The housing crisis is really reaching higher into the middle class," Roth says. "Elected officials themselves now have their, like, 20- and 30-year-old children living with them. They're seeing it  up close where [their children] can't afford to buy a place and are struggling to find a new place to rent. And so I think that has really helped to raise awareness."

But he says the greatest struggles still exist for the lowest-wage workers in the state—and it's the difference between being “inconvenienced” and being "in crisis."

Around 1.3 million Ohioans—around 9% of the state’s population—spend over half their income on housing and are considered severely housing cost-burdened.

The state also faces a severe affordable housing shortage. According to COHHIO, there are 37 units of affordable housing for every 100 extremely low-income renter households.

"Leaders and candidates are generally more interested in homeownership and trying to help the middle class because, essentially, middle-class voters are more likely to vote and they have more political power," Roth says. "But the folks at the bottom of the scale are the ones who are really facing the crisis. It is a real shame when somebody can't afford to buy a home anymore, but folks who are working those lower-wage jobs can't afford their apartment, and they're at constant risk of eviction and homelessness. That's the real crisis."

More and more, low-income people in Ohio are finding themselves completely locked out of the rental market. The child of one of Fix’s friends has been living in an extended-stay hotel—at $2,000 a month—because they don’t have the credit or work history to qualify for a lease.

"In Ohio, our challenge is to make sure that the people that need the help the most get that help, and that they're not just passed over as public resources go more toward the people who are dealing with inconvenience," Roth says.

This election cycle, voters in the Iowa Senate race are choosing between Republican Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek, both running to replace retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst. Hinson holds a slight lead over Turek ahead of Tuesday’s election.

Hinson’s housing platform focuses on expanding homeownership tax incentives and restricting large institutional investors. Turek supports banning private equity from buying single-family homes, increasing support for first-time homebuyers, and simplifying federal and local permitting for new construction projects.

Unlike several other toss-up states, Iowa doesn’t face the huge housing deficits that other states do. It faces a shortage of around 8,000 homes but is expected to close it by 2028.

Matt Kruegar, 33, began buying investment properties in and around Des Moines in 2015. He now owns 12 single-family homes and says his tenants stay an average of six years.

"We enjoy being in Des Moines. It's a great place to invest. It's always been. Things have changed over the last three, four years for sure, but it's always been easier to invest here in my opinion," he says.

As a homebuyer, Kruegar says it’s not simply home prices that have gone up—it’s also property taxes and insurance costs.

Many of the older homes he purchased are not as well insulated as newer construction, so utility costs are also an issue.

"My electric bill throughout the summer is, you know, over $300 a month," he says.

He would like to see the state government work on getting property taxes down, Kruegar says.

"I'm a statistics guy. Iowa was ranked 12th nationally for affordability versus earnings, which is great. But property taxes accounted for 18.4% of the monthly housing cost. So, you know, almost 20% of what you're paying each month is just in property taxes alone. So I think if we can figure out a way to mitigate some of those property taxes, it will become a lot more affordable for people to buy a house—even if the price of that house is increased from what it used to be."

In Iowa, the typical 20% down payment now requires 42% more income than the average household earns, according to the Common Sense Institute Iowa. However, Iowa remains ahead of the national average, where the gap is 47%.

Even so, Iowa is the ninth most affordable housing market when factoring in property taxes, the think tank found.

In Texas, Decision Desk puts Democrat James Talarico slightly ahead of Republican Ken Paxton in a hotly contested race for the Senate seat currently occupied by Republican John Cornyn.

Talarico has run on support for modular and factory-built homes and favors increased restrictions on institutional investors in single-family homes, as well as zoning reform and stronger corporate landlord regulation.

Paxton supports increased first- and second-homebuyer deductions, corporate restrictions on single-family home purchases, and cutting the red tape around new builds.

Betsy Seltzer, an educational instructional designer, is in her 40s and lives with her teacher husband and two children in Cady, TX. They purchased their home in 2014 for $230,000 and have been looking to move, but high prices and elevated interest rates have kept them tethered to their current home.

In a place where temperatures regularly climb above 100 degrees Fahrenheit in the summer months, Seltzer would like to move to a home with a pool, especially because her son with autism responds well to being in the water.

"He responds very well to being in the water,” she says. “It gives him some sensory feedback that helps regulate him."

But prices in her area have nearly doubled in the past decade while her family’s wages have not.

Compounding their problems, the family’s current home was built in the 1980s, and because of the extreme weather and heat in Cady, they’ve had to spend a lot on repairs—including replacing the water heater three times in 12 years.

They still hope to move soon, but for now, she says they "feel stuck."

That sense of feeling "stuck" is common, says Favianna Orriols, statewide advocacy director for Texas Housers, a low-income housing information service that primarily works with renter populations in the state.

"We’re of the position that if you look at the affordable housing bills passed in the last legislative session, there was a push by the governor and the lieutenant governor to address housing affordability," she says. "And they did so in a way that was almost exclusively through land use deregulation."

But she notes that the “barriers that are facing the hardest-hit renters are much more complex than land use regulation. It includes insurance, property taxes, operating costs, incomes. ... The prices of homes have greatly outpaced incomes.”

In the Rio Grande Valley, where Orriols is from, the population is overwhelmingly Hispanic, and "there is this culture down there of, you know, homeownership equals the American dream,” she says.

Heading into the next legislative session in January, Orriols hopes lawmakers will focus on expanding the state housing trust fund, which offers Texans around $5 million per year through two initiatives: one is a “bootstrap fund” that provides dollars for prospective homeowners who want to build their homes. The other offers resources for people with disabilities who need to retrofit their homes to make them accessible.

“What we are advocating for is to put more money into that bucket and create some different programs to make them more accessible to people,” she says.

Kathryn Saar, who is the regional vice president for Texas at Ulysses Development Group and the president of the Texas Affiliation of Affordable Housing Providers, agrees that prospective homeowner support is part of the solution. But she also wants to see reform to state-level housing tax credit initiatives.

Saar's group works primarily on affordable housing units. Texas is short around 864,000 affordable housing units and nearly half of all renters in the state are considered cost-burdened, spending more than 30% of their income on housing.

Under current state regulations, a builder can receive up to $2 million in tax credits per approved project. In 2017, she built 115 units of housing with that $2 million credit.

"The deals that I'm looking at today, I might be able to do 65 to 70 units at most with the $2 million in credits."

Further, the value of that $2 million in credits is less these days.

In 2017, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act passed, which decreased the corporate tax rate and had the knock-on effect of making housing credits less valuable to banks. Saar says she now typically gets 80 cents on the dollar from banks, whereas she used to get $1 for every tax credit dollar.

That’s partly due to rising construction costs. Tariffs have increased the cost of materials, but general panic around increased ICE raids has made immigrant construction laborers fearful of going to job sites.

“There's fewer people available to actually do the building,” Saar says.

Because of rising housing costs and the general overall sense that the cost of living is unaffordable, Saar believes voters are going to be more motivated by "kitchen-table issues" this time around.

"We have, you know, a person who is talking about the things that the voters are concerned with. And then we have another ideological candidate on the Republican side," she says.

"I think there's probably a lot of disillusionment with the voting population because we, you know, send people to Congress, and then nothing changes," she continues. "Unfortunately, that's just kind of where we're at. This election next week, it will be interesting to see where things land. I don't have a crystal ball, but I really can't wait till next week, if only so that my inbox will stop being flooded by requests for donations."

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5700. Scientists discover a surprising double benefit of exercise for Parkinson’s

People with Parkinson's disease who are more physically active may experience slower declines in memory, thinking, and movement, according to a new study published October 7, 2026, in Neurology, the official medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology.

The findings suggest that staying active could offer two important advantages for people living with Parkinson's. However, researchers emphasize that the study identified a connection between physical activity and slower symptom progression. It does not establish that exercise directly causes the disease to progress more slowly.

"Parkinson's disease is a brain disorder that causes movement and cognitive problems that gradually worsen leading to disability and a loss of independence," said study author Dong-Woo Ryu, MD, PhD, of the University of Cincinnati in Ohio. "Previous research has shown associations between physical activity and movement symptoms. Our study found physical activity may have dual benefits, with associations with slower declines in movement and cognition."

Tracking Exercise and Parkinson's Symptoms Over Seven Years

The research involved 294 adults with mild to moderate Parkinson's disease. Participants were 66 years old on average, and researchers monitored their health for up to seven years.

To understand their activity habits, participants completed questionnaires estimating how many hours each week they spent being physically active. The questions covered activities performed at work, around the home, and during hobbies or recreation.

Researchers classified activities by their intensity. Moderate activities included brisk walking, doubles tennis, leisurely swimming, and household tasks such as cleaning windows, vacuuming, or mowing the lawn. More demanding activities included running, cycling at higher speeds, participating in team sports, playing singles tennis, shoveling, and carrying heavy objects.

The team examined physical activity in three ways. First, they calculated the total time participants spent doing moderate or vigorous activities. Second, they estimated overall activity volume by combining duration with intensity, giving greater weight to strenuous exercise. Third, they separately measured the amount of time spent doing vigorous activities.

Based on total weekly activity time, participants were placed into three categories. Those in the least active group reported up to four hours per week, the moderately active group reported four to eight hours, and the most active group reported more than eight hours.

Each year, participants also completed assessments designed to track changes in thinking and memory, along with tests evaluating the severity of their Parkinson's symptoms.

More Activity Linked to Slower Memory Decline

One of the most striking differences emerged in cognitive performance. Researchers used a 30-point test of thinking and memory, with lower scores reflecting poorer cognitive function.

Among participants in the least active group, scores fell by an estimated average of 0.478 points each year. The moderately active group experienced a much smaller annual decline of 0.090 points.

For the most active participants, the estimated average yearly decrease was only 0.007 points, indicating that their cognitive scores remained nearly unchanged over time.

The researchers also examined changes in Parkinson's movement symptoms using an assessment scored from zero to 132. Higher numbers represented more severe symptoms, and participants began the study with an average score of 23.

In the least active group, symptom scores increased by an estimated 0.143 points annually, indicating a slight worsening. By contrast, scores decreased by 0.225 points per year in the moderately active group and by 0.783 points in the most active group.

Even after accounting for participants' age, sex, and how long they had been living with Parkinson's, the researchers found that the most active group experienced slower cognitive decline and less worsening of movement symptoms than the least active group.

The connection was not limited to one measure of exercise. Higher total activity time, greater overall activity volume, and more time spent exercising vigorously were each associated with slower deterioration in both thinking abilities and movement symptoms.

Why Consistent Physical Activity May Matter

The results suggest that remaining physically active over time could be especially important for people with Parkinson's disease. Researchers noted that even relatively small differences in the rate of decline might become more significant when they accumulate over several years.

"The possible benefits of physical activity for people with Parkinson's disease may depend on how long they stay active and whether they continue exercising over time," said Ryu. "While our study found small differences between activity levels, these differences may become more meaningful over time. Since participants generally had good thinking and memory skills at the start of the study, our results should be interpreted with caution and further studies are needed."

The researchers also identified an important limitation. Physical activity levels were based on participants' own reports rather than direct measurements, meaning some estimates may have been inaccurate.

Although the findings strengthen the evidence connecting physical activity with better long-term outcomes in Parkinson's disease, additional research will be needed to determine whether exercise itself can slow the progression of symptoms.

Funding for the study came from a grant provided by the Gardner Family Foundation and the Precision Medicine in Neurodegenerative Diseases Fund.

#5698. Who’s responsible when clinical AI goes wrong? AMA weighs in

Who’s responsible when clinical AI goes wrong? AMA weighs in" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Building on its recent guidance for organizations’ use and governance of clinical AI, the American Medical Association on Thursday gave a deeper breakdown of how it believes different parties should be responsible for decisions, actions and failures involving the technology.

The latest framework from AMA’s Center for Digital Health and AI addresses liability issues the group said are currently unanswered by existing liability frameworks. Those structures, it said, could leave physicians facing "liability for risks they cannot reasonably prevent, while patients may struggle to seek remedies when AI causes harm."

Other key issues with the status quo liability frameworks, AMA said, are ambiguity around when product liability applies to AI; how contract terms and disclaimers from developers can distance responsibility from risk control; and whether deploying healthcare organizations hold various responsibilities specific to AI, such as local testing or outcomes monitoring.

AMA said the clinical AI liability framework it’s advancing "recognizes that multiple parties may bear liability for the use of AI when something goes wrong," and then aligns that accountability based on a party’s ability to prevent harm. Responsibility is spread out in areas where control is shared, but it does not become interchangeable, and no party’s obligations disappear because another party also bears some,” AMA wrote in a brief outlining its thinking.

As for the physicians AMA represents, the liability framework calls for doctors to "be responsible for the clinical judgment they can meaningfully exercise, based on the system’s intended use, known limitations and the information available at the point of care."

The group also said that oversight from a physician "cannot substitute for adequate evidence, appropriate system design or the conditions necessary to make clinical review meaningful." Physicians should also retain the authority to decline an unproven AI system, or those "whose clinical validation, usefulness or place in the standard of care remains uncertain," without penalty from their organization, AMA said.

"Patients must have meaningful avenues for recourse when clinical AI causes harm, and physicians must be able to use these technologies with confidence that responsibility reflects what they can reasonably know and control," AMA President Willie Underwood III, M.D., president of the AMA, said in a release on the liability framework. "As AI assumes more clinical functions, developers, healthcare organizations and physicians each have important responsibilities. We need clear expectations that protect patients, support sound clinical judgment, and ensure accountability remains with those best positioned to prevent harm."

The liability framework breaks down in detail one aspect of a broader clinical AI governance framework unveiled by AMA and its Center earlier this month. Those principles and focus areas will guide how AMA works with providers and stakeholders as it tackles issues like licensure and regulation for the fast-moving technology.

"We cannot afford to wait for these questions to be answered through trial and error in patient care," AMA CEO John Whyte, M.D., told Fierce Healthcare of the efforts earlier this month. "The AMA's new framework sets out our ambitious agenda to address these questions. … It will guide our work with physicians, patients, technology developers and policymakers to ensure clinical authority is earned through evidence, how oversight must evolve with risk, and how accountability is maintained."

#5697. Breakthrough PTSD treatment achieves 68% remission rate in clinical trial

A new approach to treating post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) has received FDA clearance, offering a personalized alternative for people who have not found sufficient relief through existing treatments. Developed by California-based Wave Neuroscience in collaboration with researchers at the Texas A&M Health Institute of Biosciences and Technology, the technology uses brain activity measurements to guide targeted magnetic stimulation.

Early clinical trial findings have been encouraging. According to Wave Neuroscience, patients experienced a 52% reduction in PTSD symptoms, while 68% achieved remission. The full findings are still being prepared for public release, but researchers believe the technology could significantly expand treatment options for millions of people.

The need for more effective PTSD care is substantial. In the United States, approximately 17.5 veterans die by suicide each day, and about 7% of veterans receive a PTSD diagnosis annually.

PTSD can develop after traumatic experiences such as military combat, serious accidents, natural disasters, or violence. An estimated 6% of Americans will experience PTSD during their lifetime, with higher rates among women and veterans.

Why Current PTSD Treatments Are Not Enough

Since PTSD was formally recognized as a diagnosis in 1980, treatment has largely centered on psychotherapy and medications known as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), including sertraline and fluoxetine.

Although these approaches can help, many patients continue to experience symptoms despite receiving treatment.

A 2020 review of PTSD medications found that patients reported improvements ranging from 6.8 to 10.1 points on symptom assessments. However, remission rates reached only 10.9% at most.

Wave Neuroscience reported substantially stronger preliminary outcomes in its clinical trial. Erik Won, DO, the company's chief medical officer, described the results as a major advance over previously reported medication outcomes.

“In comparison to that study, our FDA trial reported a 52% reduction in symptoms, so more than a four-fold increase in efficacy,” Won said. “And more importantly, we saw 68% remission in our clinical trial. So, it’s really a quantum change, an inflection point in what we can offer to patients. From a clinical care perspective, that’s really meaningful.”

These findings are promising, although the results come from different studies and should not be interpreted as a direct comparison of treatment effectiveness.

The newly cleared system uses Magnetic e-Resonance Therapy (MeRT), a technology that combines measurements of brain activity with targeted magnetic stimulation.

First, an electroencephalogram (EEG) records the brain's electrical signals. This information helps guide a personalized treatment plan using transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS.

During TMS, a coil positioned against the scalp delivers magnetic pulses that stimulate brain activity. The technique has already been used for other psychiatric conditions, including treatment-resistant depression.

What distinguishes MeRT is its use of an AI-assisted algorithm to customize stimulation protocols based on each patient's brain activity rather than relying on a standardized approach.

“Transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS, was previously FDA cleared for treatment-resistant depression,” Won said. “By adding an augmented AI derived multivariate algorithm, we were able to personalize protocols that received FDA clearance for post-traumatic stress disorder, which should open up market access to about 13 million people who may be struggling with PTSD.”

Dr. Kenneth S. Ramos, a physician-scientist at Texas A&M Health with extensive experience in precision medicine, helped guide the research.

His work focuses on adapting medical care to the characteristics of individual patients instead of assuming that everyone will respond to the same treatment.

“Most clinical interventions for the treatment of PTSD do not work very well,” Ramos said. “So, this is a huge area where identifying interventions that could hopefully add quality of life to the people impacted by this disorder would be tremendously impactful.”

Wave Neuroscience CEO Fred Walke said Ramos was a natural fit for the project because of his expertise in personalized medicine.

Conventional TMS generally follows treatment protocols that are less individualized. MeRT builds on the same underlying technology but adjusts treatment according to the patient's specific brain activity.

Ramos emphasized that even small biological differences between people can have major implications for medical care. Humans are approximately 99.9% genetically alike, yet the remaining 0.1% contributes to differences that can influence how individuals respond to treatment.

By accounting for these differences and tailoring stimulation to each person's brain, researchers observed substantial reductions in PTSD symptom severity.

Ramos illustrated the distinction with an analogy involving a leaking roof.

He likened conventional TMS to covering a leak with a tarp to manage its effects. MeRT, in contrast, aims to provide a more targeted solution, comparable to identifying and replacing the damaged shingles responsible for the problem.

The broader goal is to move beyond treating patients with standardized protocols and toward interventions guided by measurable biological information.

From Breakthrough Designation to FDA Clearance

The regulatory process reached an important milestone in 2024, when MeRT received an FDA Breakthrough Device designation.

Dr. Rick Silva, executive director of clinical trials at the Texas A&M Health Institute of Biosciences and Technology, explained that the designation helps promising technologies move through regulatory review more efficiently.

It does not eliminate scientific or medical requirements. Instead, it can streamline communication and reduce administrative delays while preserving the standards needed for FDA clearance.

Silva said the progress was particularly meaningful because the project began during the COVID-19 pandemic and advanced through the regulatory process unusually quickly.

According to Silva, medical device development and clinical evaluation can often take around 10 years before clearance is obtained. This project completed the relevant process in just over two years.

He credited the experience and dedication of the Wave Neuroscience team with helping make that accelerated progress possible.

“I’ve been involved in probably close to 1,000 projects in academic medical centers over the years at varying degrees of depth and detail,” Silva said. “Patients are why I do what I do. It’s hard, and the failure rate is high, and it’s a lot of work. But when you get to a point where something is going to benefit patients, it’s very professionally gratifying and personally gratifying in many ways as well.”

Dr. Israel Liberzon, distinguished professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at the Texas A&M Naresh K. Vashisht College of Medicine, served as the study's lead psychiatrist and PTSD specialist.

He believes the clearance represents an important expansion of the available treatments for PTSD.

According to Liberzon, MeRT will become the only FDA-cleared nonmedication treatment specifically for PTSD once it reaches patients.

“Right now, the FDA has approved only two medications for PTSD,” Liberzon said. “It doesn’t mean that only two of them are used, but both are SSRIs. This is the first time that in addition to the medication, we have a non-medication option. There is psychotherapy that people use for PTSD, but psychotherapies require a lot of effort. People must participate actively, and many drop out because it’s too anxiety provoking. So now we have a unique alternative.”

In the clinical trial, participants received five treatment sessions each week over a period of five to six weeks.

Researchers reported that the improvements appeared to persist after the treatment sessions ended, suggesting the benefits may extend beyond the active therapy period.

For patients who struggle with medication side effects or find psychotherapy difficult to complete, a treatment based on personalized brain stimulation could provide another option.

“People living with PTSD have been left with trial-and-error treatment, medications and their side effects, and limited outcomes—even when treated by the most dedicated and experienced physicians,” Won said. “Wave’s FDA clearance signals a fundamentally different future: one in which PTSD can be objectively evaluated, precisely treated and meaningfully healed.”

Won also believes the technology could eventually be adapted to other psychiatric conditions, including depression and anxiety.

Could Personalized Brain Therapy Transform Mental Healthcare?

Dr. Leslie S. Prichep, chief scientific officer at Wave Neuroscience, sees the FDA clearance as an important step toward treatment decisions guided by objective measurements of brain function.

“The FDA clearance of the MeRT System reflects decades of scientific research using electrophysiological biomarkers in identifying abnormal brain activity profiles and guiding personalized intervention strategies,” Prichep said. “We believe this represents an important advancement toward a more objective, data-informed model of mental healthcare.”

Walke believes that giving patients clearer information about their brain activity could also help change public attitudes toward mental illness.

He compared the idea to treating a broken bone with a cast. By making mental health conditions easier to understand through measurable physical information, the company hopes to reduce stigma and help patients better understand their experiences.

“One of the goals of the company is to create a platform for mental healthcare that uses objective imagery to help patients understand why they’re experiencing life the way that they are,” Walke said. “That insight, compounded with proven technologies, promises incredibly high efficacy when personalized.”

An important next step will be ensuring that patients can actually obtain the treatment. Wave Neuroscience and Texas A&M Health are working with other stakeholders to expand availability and make the therapy more affordable through insurance coverage.

“Our hope is that this research and technology can be a catalyst for more widespread development and innovation of more effective, personalized and precision-guided treatments,” Won said. “This is proof positive that population-scale personalized medicine is not just an aspirational goal but is an achievable reality today.”

The project combines years of work across medicine, neuroscience, clinical research, and technology, all directed toward improving the lives of people affected by PTSD.

For Ramos, the opportunity to help veterans carries particular significance because of Texas A&M's longstanding involvement in military and veteran initiatives.

“Texas A&M has a very rich history of military and veteran priorities,” Ramos said. “It’s a no-brainer that Texas A&M faculty would be interested in and supportive of an initiative that hopefully would bring positive solutions to a big problem. And anything we could do to help alleviate that problem is going to go a long way towards making a difference in the individual’s life as well as the people who are close to them. I feel very fortunate that we at Texas A&M were meaningfully involved in this project.”

#5696. How Election Day can affect your heart

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Liz covers cardiovascular and metabolic disease, asking why we’re not doing better or even losing ground against the world’s leading killer. Send tips on Signal at LizC.22.

The reminders to vote in Tuesday’s midterms are ubiquitous. Some health scholars have another reminder: that elections, especially divisive ones, can stress the heart.

Studies have found a significantly higher chance of arrhythmias in the weeks just before and after elections, and an increased rate of hospitalizations for heart attacks right after voting day.

“Your political party doesn’t matter to your heart; stress does,” Lindsey Rosman, assistant professor of medicine in the division of cardiology at Northwestern University, told STAT on Thursday. “Your emotional health and your heart health are connected.”

Take the last two presidential elections. Compared with other timeframes, researchers noted distinct changes in early November that aligned with heightened anxiety. Even if transient, higher blood pressure or abnormal heart rhythms can turn serious for people diagnosed with cardiovascular disease, or for those unaware of a condition that might make them more vulnerable.

To see how elections may stress the heart, Rosman studied people who already had a heart rhythm disorder, taking advantage of data provided by their implanted cardiac devices. Her team found a 77% higher rate of irregular heartbeats during the six weeks around the 2016 election, compared with a control period.

The arrhythmia pattern was similar across age, sex, race, and other health conditions; Democrats and Republicans had similar risk. The retrospective observational study was carried out in North Carolina, when Rosman was at the University of North Carolina. Because it was a swing state in 2016, residents saw an especially heavy volume of political ads and campaign events.

After the 2020 presidential election, Matthew Mefford, a cardiovascular disease epidemiologist and research scientist at Kaiser Permanente Southern California, asked whether hospitalizations for acute cardiovascular disease went up immediately after Election Day, akin to admissions after natural disasters. The answer was yes, with the rate of heart attacks significantly higher compared with the same five-day period two weeks before. The retrospective cohort study looked at people with and without a history of heart disease.

“Stress comes in many forms, including both positive and negative, and the stress impact associated with elections is just one situation that can result in adverse heart outcomes,” Mefford told STAT on Thursday. “Being aware of how stress, generally, can impact your body is important especially for those with pre-existing heart disease.”

While stress responses in the body follow the same mechanisms, they’re not the same in all cases. “Not everyone responds to stress in the same way or to the same magnitude that triggers a heart event,” he said.

Other caveats: The two studies can’t establish cause and effect, just an association between health events and exposure to political campaigns.

Ten years after Rosman’s study, today’s exposure may be magnified beyond political ads, thanks to the saturation of social media. Whatever the source, the deluge of news can cause acute stress and anger, triggering a fight-or-flight response. Adrenaline rises, the sympathetic nervous system ramps up, and the calming influence of the vagus nerve drops.

These changes can alter the heart’s electrical activity, making abnormal rhythms more likely in someone already prone to them, Rosman said. Inflammation and stress hormones like cortisol may also play a role, as can stress-related behaviors, such as sleeping poorly, skipping medications, eating more foods high in fat or salt, or drinking more alcohol or caffeine.

Her findings apply most directly to people at higher cardiac risk, she said, but she pointed out that nearly half of U.S. adults have some type of cardiovascular disease, including high blood pressure.

“People with existing heart disease are more vulnerable to arrhythmias triggered by emotion, but these events can also happen in people without known heart disease,” she said, citing reports of more heart attacks and cardiac events after 9/11, earthquakes, and World Cup matches. “Chronic stress is also an established risk factor for heart disease over time.”

Next up for Rosman is using wearables to study acute stress events. She hopes a larger, nationwide follow-up study looking at the 2020 and 2024 elections will offer some answers before the next U.S. presidential election.

In general, acute stress raises heart rates and blood pressure readings in the short term. But for people with uncontrolled hypertension or coronary disease, spiking stress adds strain.

Rosman suggests setting limits on news and social media, especially before bedtime. Focus on sleep and physical activity. Take your medications. Both Rosman and Mefford recommend meditation or yoga, taking a walk, hiking in nature, or engaging in exercise.

#5695. The Efficacy of Broad Match + Audiences Strategy in Real Estate

When considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry. The key objective remains the same - reaching the target audience with an impactful, compelling message that can inspire action. An increasingly popular approach adopted by real estate agents is the broad match + audiences strategy. This approach leverages the power of Google AdWords' broad match feature and combines it with audience targeting to attain superior marketing results.

The real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers. Recognizing this immense diversity and matching it with the correct buyer is a daunting challenge that real estate agents constantly grapple with. This is where the broad match + audiences strategy steps in, optimizing the process by expanding reach while ensuring relevance.

The broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase. It can include searches that are misspellings, synonyms, related searches, and other relevant variations.

With the broad match feature, you're casting a wide net over an extensive range of search queries. It brings with it the advantage of gaining visibility across a wider spectrum of potential buyers who might not use the exact keywords that you've selected for your campaign.

In the real estate industry, property attributes can be incredibly diverse, ranging from "3-bedroom apartments in New York City" to "colonial-style houses with large gardens in Austin". By leveraging the broad match feature, agents can reach potential clients who use various search terms that directly or indirectly relate to their listing.

Audience targeting is a method used in digital marketing to segment audiences based on specific criteria like demographics, interests, buying behavior, etc. Google AdWords allows you to target your ads to specific audiences, ensuring they are seen by those who are most likely to be interested in your offerings.

In the context of real estate, audience targeting can be a game-changer. For instance, if an agent specializes in selling luxury homes, they can target audiences with high-income levels and a demonstrated interest in luxury living. Alternatively, if an agent focuses on properties suitable for first-time buyers, they can target younger audiences who have recently started searching for homes.

The marriage of broad match keywords with audience targeting may seem counter-intuitive at first, considering one aims at breadth and the other at specificity. However, the combination forms a robust strategy that takes the best of both worlds - wide reach and precise targeting.

The broad match feature ensures a wide reach, allowing real estate agents to surface their listings to a large number of prospective clients. But, broad match alone can lead to high impression counts with low conversion rates as the ads may be presented to irrelevant audiences. This is where audience targeting steps in to bring precision.

When used in conjunction, the broad match feature ensures that your ads reach a wide array of searchers, while audience targeting ensures these ads are shown to a specific subset of this wide audience who are most likely to be interested in your property listings.

This synergistic approach allows real estate agents to achieve two key objectives:

In the dynamic and competitive world of real estate, digital marketing strategies need to be both comprehensive and precise. The broad match + audiences strategy does precisely that - it maximizes the reach of property listings while maintaining relevance to the audience. As such, it is not surprising that this strategy is being widely adopted by savvy real estate agents seeking to gain a competitive edge in the digital realm. The power of a wide-reaching yet finely tuned marketing strategy should not be underestimated in a market as diverse and competitive as real estate.

#5693. Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist

A new optical sensor costing just $10 could bring laboratory-level precision to wearable health monitors, potentially allowing people to track blood glucose without needles. The technology could also transform food testing, industrial quality control, and environmental monitoring.

Researchers at the University of Cambridge and GlitterinTech (a start-up founded by the same research group) have developed a new type of optical spectrometer that combines exceptional accuracy with a remarkably small size and low cost. Measuring just centimeters across, the device could be incorporated into portable electronics and wearable health technology. Its potential applications range from monitoring important health markers in real time to identifying materials and detecting changes in chemical composition.

Optical spectrometers work by analyzing light to reveal information about the substances it interacts with. They are essential tools in medicine, manufacturing, chemical testing, and environmental research. However, making these instruments smaller has traditionally meant compromising their performance. Compact spectrometers often have limited measurement ranges, reduced resolution, or lower accuracy, making them better suited to identifying substances than performing precise measurements.

The researchers believe their new design could overcome these limitations. Known as a convolutional spectrometer, it uses a mathematical principle called the convolution theorem to analyze light in a fundamentally different way. According to the team, this approach delivers performance that surpasses existing types of spectrometers in several key areas, including designs based on light dispersion, Fourier transforms, and computational reconstruction.

A New Way to Analyze Light With Extraordinary Precision

Traditional spectrometers generally separate incoming light into its component wavelengths or use complex calculations to reconstruct its spectrum. The new device takes another approach by performing a mathematical operation called convolution directly on the incoming light.

To accomplish this, the researchers arranged optical components with repeating spectral responses in a sequence. These components can include unbalanced Mach-Zehnder interferometers or micro-ring resonators. By adjusting them in proportion to one another, the system can shift its response to different wavelengths in a controlled, linear fashion. Fast Fourier transforms are then used to accurately recover the light spectrum.

"The key insight was to go back to the mathematics and ask whether there was a fundamentally cleaner way to retrieve spectra," said Dr. Chunhui Yao, a lead author of the study. "By using the convolution theorem directly in the optical domain, we avoid many of the limitations that have held miniaturized spectrometers back. This gives us high precision, strong noise tolerance, and very low computational overhead, all in a compact and low-cost system."

The researchers built the spectrometer using a silicon nitride photonic platform and integrated it with onboard electronics. It operates across a broad range of near-infrared wavelengths (1200-1700 nm) and can collect and process measurements in less than a second.

Another important advantage is its ability to expand its measurement capabilities without major hardware changes. Because the system uses repeating optical patterns, its spectral bandwidth can theoretically be extended almost without limit. Adding more optical components in sequence can also increase its resolution exponentially.

A $10 Sensor That Could Transform Food Testing and Healthcare

To evaluate the device outside purely theoretical measurements, the researchers tested it on a variety of materials and substances. The results demonstrated its potential for applications that normally depend on larger, more expensive laboratory instruments.

When used to identify plastics, pharmaceuticals, coffee, flour, and tea, the spectrometer achieved a 100% classification success rate in the reported tests. It also measured concentrations in water-based and organic solutions with accuracies of approximately 0.01%, exceeding the performance of commercial benchtop spectrometers in those experiments.

The healthcare demonstrations were particularly promising. Under conditions designed to reflect real physiological environments, the device accurately measured several human biomarkers, including skin moisture, blood alcohol, blood lactate, and blood glucose.

The researchers also demonstrated noninvasive glucose tracking over an extended period in one participant. Although further testing would be needed before the technology could become a practical medical product, the finding suggests a possible route toward monitoring blood sugar without repeatedly piercing the skin.

"These biomedical demonstrations are particularly exciting," said Prof. Qixiang Cheng, who led the project. "What makes this work stand out is not just performance in the lab, but technical readiness. Dr. Chunhui Yao's contribution was crucial in translating a mathematical concept into a fully packaged, robust system that operates reliably across temperature extremes and real-world conditions. That combination is what opens the door to practical deployment."

The sensor also demonstrated impressive resistance to temperature changes. It continued operating reliably between -20°C and 80°C, an unusually wide temperature range for a miniature spectrometer. This durability could be especially valuable for wearable devices, factory equipment, and sensors operating outdoors.

Why a Simpler Design Could Be a Major Breakthrough

The new spectrometer's advantages extend beyond its accuracy, size, and price. Its internal design also reduces the amount of computing power needed to analyze incoming light.

Many existing miniature spectrometers depend on complicated calibration procedures and demanding algorithms to reconstruct spectral information. These methods can become unreliable when measurements contain noise, and they often require substantial processing resources.

The Cambridge team's convolution-based approach avoids much of this complexity. Because the measurements follow a linear mathematical relationship, the system can recover spectra rapidly and consistently while using relatively little computational power.

"This is a beautiful example of how elegant engineering can unlock real impact," said Prof. Richard Penty, who contributed to the photonic system design and integration. "The architecture is simple, scalable, and manufacturable, yet it delivers precision that rivals or exceeds much larger instruments. Dr. Chunhui Yao played a central role in bringing together the photonic design, system integration, and experimental validation that made this possible."

Its relatively simple construction could also make the technology easier to manufacture on a large scale, potentially bringing sophisticated optical measurements to devices where conventional spectrometers would be too bulky or expensive.

Bringing Laboratory-Grade Measurements to Everyday Devices

The researchers envision a future in which accurate optical sensing becomes a routine feature of everyday technology rather than something largely confined to specialized laboratories.

In industrial settings, inexpensive spectrometers could be installed throughout manufacturing facilities to continuously check material composition and product quality. Similar sensors could monitor food freshness, identify substances, and analyze environmental conditions on a much larger scale than is currently practical.

Healthcare could see equally significant changes. Compact sensors might eventually enable wearables to measure hydration levels, detect signs of alcohol intoxication, track biomarkers related to physical fitness, or continuously monitor glucose levels for people managing diabetes.

"Our vision is to make spectrometry as ubiquitous as temperature or motion sensing," added Prof. Qixiang Cheng. "This work shows that high-quality spectral information doesn't have to be confined to the laboratory -- it can be embedded directly into the technologies people use every day."

As photonic technology becomes smaller and more advanced, the convolutional spectrometer provides a promising example of how mathematical insights and practical engineering can make sophisticated scientific instruments simpler, cheaper, and more accessible. By combining high precision with a device that costs around $10, the researchers have opened a potential path toward a new generation of smart sensors capable of measuring the hidden chemistry of our bodies and surroundings.
