#5679. Opinion: The economics of the U.S. health care system are broken

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Markovich is president and CEO of Ascendiun, the nonprofit parent company of Blue Shield of California, Blue Shield Promise Health Plan, Altais, and Stellarus.

On my recent travels, I met a healthy, active man in his early 60s who runs a small business.  This year, his family’s monthly premium reached nearly $5,000 — more than a quarter of his pre‑tax income. He made the difficult choice to keep coverage only for his wife and two children, hoping to stay healthy until he is eligible for Medicare.

No family should have to make that choice, but this story is not unusual. More than 27 million Americans lacked health insurance in 2024, and millions more have coverage they cannot afford to use because their deductibles are so high. The average employer‑sponsored family premium is nearly $27,000 a year.

So why not just have the federal government pay more? Increasing federal subsidies is helpful in the short term, but it is not a sustainable long-term solution. In August, the federal debt exceeded $40 trillion. This sum is larger than the entire American economy and is nearly enough to purchase every single-family home in the country. Meanwhile, nearly 70% of federal, non-interest spending is on health care and income support like Social Security. Therefore, the only way to make health care affordable for everyone is to get costs under control.

The core problem is that the economics of the U.S. health care system are broken: There is no mechanism to keep total spending within any reasonable bounds. Every other major industry faces market checks when prices rise, from groceries to the family car. Health care does not.

One clear way to break this cycle is to put American health care on a budget, one that applies to all participants in the system. Everyone must be tasked with holding health care cost inflation at or below the rate of inflation, and must be held responsible for meeting the same target.

One way to do this is to create a national office of health care affordability responsible for ensuring that health care costs become sustainable. This new body would require reporting and analysis of how prices are set to drive greater transparency in health care costs. It would set thresholds for year-to-year cost increases, holding health care cost hikes at or below the rate of inflation.

When targets are not met, the office would work with the organization on corrective actions and, as a final step, could levy progressive financial penalties on organizations that did not fall within these thresholds. Finally, the office would establish mechanisms to ensure these savings resulted in lower premiums and out-of-pocket costs for families, employers, and taxpayers.

California is showing what this could look like. Its Office of Health Care Affordability sets enforceable cost‑growth targets for the whole sector and for individual organizations, with fines beginning in 2028 and a goal of holding growth near 3%, in line with wages. This is not the first time a state has tried such an idea. Eight states have set cost-growth targets over the past decade. But California is the first state to combine transparency of cost increases with financial enforcement that holds entities accountable to a target.

California’s approach was supported by a coalition of unlikely allies, including health plans like mine, labor unions like the Service Employees International Union (SEIU), large businesses including the Purchasers Business Group on Health (PBGH), and consumer groups led by Health Access California. Today, California’s Office of Health Care Affordability continues to seek feedback on its work from an advisory committee and workgroups comprised of stakeholders to ensure it has the benefit of a breadth of experience and expertise, including California consumers, insurers, labor unions, hospitals, and physician organizations.

As my colleagues and I at Blue Shield of California have said publicly, we support this approach because it is rooted not in the costs of one industry segment, but in a complete transformation of the entire health care system in the state. For example, a big part of OHCA’s work is focused on encouraging value-based payment models and ensuring investments in primary care.

But even with that support, California’s approach is drawing fire. The state’s hospital association has gone to court to block the targets, arguing they don’t reflect the real cost pressures providers face. Those concerns deserve a serious answer. But they also reinforce the need for a federal version of this model since these issues are national forces.

Without enforceable cost targets, every breakthrough, from GLP‑1s to gene therapies to artificial intelligence, risks becoming another layer of cost rather than a source of savings. Because the entire system is rewarded by doing more, investments in prevention are financially irrational. Without accountability, payment reform stays incremental. And without cost certainty, policymakers cannot responsibly expand access to coverage.

Health care has put Americans and America in a massive financial bind, and no one is coming to bail us out. The only way fix this is to make our wasteful health care system a lot more efficient and effective, which is only going to happen when we demand that the health care industry do what most American families have to do every year: manage to a budget.

Paul Markovich is president and CEO of Ascendiun, the nonprofit parent company of Blue Shield of California, Blue Shield Promise Health Plan, Altais, and Stellarus.

#5678. Housing Week Ahead: Monthly Trends Data, Mortgage Rates, and Jobs Report

With all eyes on Election Day, this marks a relatively light week for new Realtor.com economics research reports and housing market indicators.

On Wednesday, I'll be issuing our October monthly housing trends report, taking a look at whether elevated mortgage rates caused buyers or sellers to pull back more, as well as what happened to inventory, asking prices, and contract signings.

The September snapshot showed a housing market softening under the weight of rising mortgage rates. Median list prices fell, while inventory and price cuts rose. I expect more of the same from the October data, after mortgage rates hit their highest levels since 2023.

On Thursday, senior economist Joel Berner will issue our Realtor.com weekly listing data update. As well, senior economist Hannah Jones will have commentary on Freddie Mac's latest mortgage rate reading on Thursday.

It’s too early to call the direction of rates this week. But I’ll be watching the bond market, especially the 10-year Treasury yield, for any reaction to the midterms, new developments in the Middle East, and any Fed signals about a December hike.

Rates matter locally, too. For buyers in Phoenix; Tucson, AZ; Raleigh, NC; Charlotte, NC; and Louisville, KY, Nov. 1–7 is your best time to buy. If rates ease for a third week in a row, buyers there and elsewhere could have more purchasing power than a month ago, more homes to choose from than a year ago, and fewer buyers to compete with. That’s a winning combination heading into the slow season.

One final indicator: I’ll be up bright and early on Friday morning to track the latest labor market data, which covers October unemployment and job growth.

September's jobs report was disappointing but not a disaster, adding just 29,000 jobs while unemployment rose to 4.2%. We expect the low-hire, low-fire labor market to continue, which keeps the Federal Reserve focused on inflation ahead of its December meeting.

Jake Krimmel is a senior economist at Realtor.com.

#5677. Could lowering high blood pressure be as simple as stimulating your ear?

A small device that delivers gentle electrical pulses through the ear could offer a new approach to treating stubborn high blood pressure. In a clinical trial led by researchers at Queen Mary University of London, the technology proved safe, well tolerated, and practical for patients to use at home.

Although the treatment did not significantly lower blood pressure compared with a placebo device across all participants, researchers observed encouraging results in patients with more severe hypertension. The findings suggest that stimulating nerves in the ear could eventually help certain people whose blood pressure remains elevated despite taking medication.

The results come from the SCRATCH-HTN trial, published in Hypertension, a journal of the American Heart Association. Researchers emphasize that larger studies are needed to determine whether the approach can provide meaningful benefits and which patients might respond best.

How Ear Nerve Stimulation Could Lower Blood Pressure

The experimental treatment uses a technique called transcutaneous autonomic neuromodulation (tAN), which aims to influence the autonomic nervous system. This network of nerves automatically controls essential bodily functions, including heart rate, digestion, and blood pressure.

By delivering mild electrical signals to nerves in the ear, researchers hope to influence the body's natural mechanisms for regulating blood pressure without requiring an invasive procedure.

The handheld device, developed by Afferent Medical Solutions, uses two small clips positioned on the tragus, the small flap of cartilage located just in front of the ear canal. These clips deliver gentle electrical stimulation, allowing patients to administer the treatment themselves without visiting a clinic.

Clinical Trial Tests the Device in 63 Patients

The clinical trial, funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), enrolled 63 people with uncontrolled hypertension. All participants were already taking at least one medication to lower their blood pressure, but their readings remained above recommended levels.

Researchers randomly divided the participants into two groups. One received active nerve stimulation, while the other used a sham device designed to serve as a comparison. This approach helped investigators assess whether the electrical stimulation produced benefits beyond those associated with using the device itself.

Participants used their assigned devices for 30 minutes daily during the first two weeks. For the following 10 weeks, they reduced their sessions to once per week.

The results showed that the treatment was safe and generally comfortable for participants. Most also followed the prescribed schedule, suggesting that the technology could be practical for regular use at home.

However, when researchers compared blood pressure changes across the entire study population, they found no statistically significant difference between patients receiving active stimulation and those using the sham device.

Promising Results in Patients With Severe Hypertension

Despite the lack of a significant overall benefit, the researchers identified a potentially important finding among participants who entered the trial with more severe hypertension.

A prespecified subgroup analysis, meaning the researchers had planned this comparison before examining the results, revealed a greater reduction in blood pressure among these patients when they received active nerve stimulation rather than the sham treatment.

This finding raises the possibility that the technique may work better for people with particularly difficult-to-control blood pressure. However, the trial was relatively small, and the subgroup results require confirmation in larger studies before any conclusions can be drawn about its effectiveness.

Dr. Ajay Gupta, Chief Investigator, Clinical Reader at Queen Mary University of London and Consultant Physician at Barts Health NHS Trust, said:

"This is an exciting, highly patient-acceptable technology that could ultimately provide a cheap, scalable solution for millions. Although the trial did not achieve significance across the broad unselected group, those with more severe hypertension exhibited a clear blood pressure reduction in the active group compared to sham.

"As the first and most thorough study of its kind, this points towards important new research directions that could help us understand whether non-invasive neuromodulation can benefit particular groups of patients with uncontrolled hypertension."

A Potential New Option for Hard-to-Control Blood Pressure

High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, is a major contributor to cardiovascular disease and increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes. It places additional strain on blood vessels and the heart, potentially causing serious damage over time.

Although medications help many patients manage their condition, a substantial number continue to have blood pressure readings above recommended targets even while receiving treatment.

This ongoing challenge has encouraged scientists to explore additional approaches that could complement existing therapies.

Ear nerve stimulation is one such possibility. Because the device is small, does not require surgery, and can be used at home, it could offer a convenient option if future research establishes that it reliably lowers blood pressure in certain patients.

For now, the findings represent an early step rather than proof of an effective new treatment. The researchers say larger clinical trials will be essential to confirm the encouraging results in patients with severe hypertension and identify which groups, if any, could benefit most from this approach.

#5676. Opinion: Cancer patients are often pressured to end a pregnancy early. They shouldn’t be

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Cardonick is a maternal fetal medicine physician and founder of the Cancer and Pregnancy Registry.

Early in my career as a maternal fetal medicine specialist, I met two pregnant women who had ovarian cancer. One of them was expecting twins. They were introduced to be each other’s support network during and after the pregnancy, often meeting for coffee with their newborns and comparing wigs after hair loss from the chemotherapy they received.

The mother of twins is still alive today. The other didn’t survive beyond her child’s second birthday. When I spoke with the one who is still alive, she was distraught that her new friend died of her disease. “Why did she die and I am still alive?” she asked.

I didn’t know how to answer her out loud, but in my head, I thought: “Your doctor went to the library and researched managing ovarian cancer during pregnancy, and her doctor didn’t.”

The woman who lived was treated as if she were not pregnant. Without delay, she underwent a CT scan and workup of her ovarian cyst, and even received chemotherapy while pregnant. Her twins are now 28 years old, and all are thriving.

For the woman who died, treatment was electively delayed until her third trimester.

I do not know if removing her mass or giving chemotherapy earlier in pregnancy would have made a difference in her case, but I can’t help wondering.

Patients diagnosed with cancer are often advised to terminate their pregnancies without discussing the very real option of treating cancer during pregnancy. Other women diagnosed in their second or early third trimesters, after the fetal organs have developed, are advised to have an elective preterm birth.

But much of the time, chemotherapy can be safely administered during pregnancy and the infant delivered at term.

Compounding the problem, cancer is diagnosed significantly later in pregnant women. This is partly due to common symptoms between certain types of cancer and pregnancy, but also because physicians (and patients) are reluctant to perform imaging during pregnancy, which delays biopsies and management.

Why are doctors not offering cancer treatment to their pregnant patients? Is it fear of litigation, as obstetrics is one of the most litigated of all medical specialties? Lack of medical investigation? Or just paternalistic advice?

I recall a patient diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma in pregnancy. When I discussed starting chemotherapy in the second trimester, another physician told me: “She already had two kids. She should terminate.”

People often assume that ending a pregnancy, whether through termination or early delivery, improves the mother’s outcome. But that is not the case. When compared with non-pregnant women with the same cancer, pregnant women have similar survival rates. No study has shown an improvement in a woman’s survival if she terminates her pregnancy compared to if she continues.

When I observed during my fellowship that oncologists and obstetricians very infrequently faced a pregnant woman with cancer, I realized the medical community needed a way to pool all of the scattered cases into a central database to track these pregnancies and follow the outcomes for women and their babies. Six hundred and fifty cases later, I am still asking the same questions I asked when I encountered that very first pregnant cancer patient:

Understandably, giving chemotherapy to a woman during pregnancy sounds dangerous, but the longitudinal research closely examining children exposed to chemotherapy backs up this approach. Children exposed to chemotherapy perform as well on standardized tests for development as unexposed children. This has been repeated at ages 18 months to 3 years, 6 years, 9 years, and 12-15 years of age. We did find that children exposed to chemotherapy are three times more likely to need eyeglasses.

And guess which children didn’t do as well? The ones electively delivered preterm to avoid maternal cancer treatment.

No options in such cases are without risk: an elective preterm birth to avoid cancer treatment, delaying cancer treatment until after delivery, or starting chemotherapy during pregnancy so the fetus can develop longer in utero and reach term. As any treatment in medicine, it is a balance between risks and benefits.

I understand many physicians are afraid to do something wrong when it comes to a pregnant woman. But denying cancer therapy by withholding or underdosing chemotherapy doesn’t serve her well, either. You can do everything to protect the fetus during the remainder of the pregnancy and forget that if their mother dies too young, due to delayed diagnosis or treatment, the child will still be affected. What is best for the mother/baby unit as a whole is a healthy mother.

I’ve worked with the Society of Maternal Fetal Medicine and the American Society of Clinical Oncology to publish guidelines to help other physicians handle this medical dilemma.

These guidelines address avoiding delays in pregnant women and discuss the safety to perform MRIs without contrast and CT scans with contrast. They also discuss performing necessary surgeries at any gestational age in pregnancy when this would be the clinical solution if the patient were not pregnant.

And they lay out how to give chemotherapy during the second and third trimesters and time treatment for safe delivery for mother and child.

I am honored to have participated in the development of these guidelines to increase the chances that when cancer and pregnancy collide, saving both lives will be considered.

Elyce Cardonick is a maternal fetal medicine physician and founder of the Cancer and Pregnancy Registry. She has spent nearly three decades caring for women diagnosed with cancer during pregnancy and advocating for mothers and their babies.

#5675. Midstream Health nabs $20M series A to help hospitals recover lost margin

Midstream Health nabs $20M series A to help hospitals recover lost margin" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Health systems are losing margins they’ve already earned, according to Sumit Kadakia, CEO and co-founder of Midstream Health. The startup bets that artificial intelligence can improve hospital margins by finding money that is already embedded in contracts and transactions.

Midstream Health, an autonomous financial operations platform for health systems, picked up $20 million in series A funding to expand its AI financial platform. The company is expanding across a customer network representing more than $100 billion in annual operating expenses and over 250 hospitals nationwide.

Valtruis led the financing round with continued participation from Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), Foundry and CommonSpirit Ventures, bringing Midstream’s total funding to $29.2 million. Fairview Health Services and Keck Medicine of USC are among the newest health systems to join the platform, alongside CommonSpirit Health, Mount Sinai Health System and Houston Methodist.

Midstream says its AI financial platform helps health systems find and recover margin across revenue and cost, strengthening the financial capacity needed to keep investing in care and serving their communities.

"We bring all of a health system’s data together, across pharmacy, supply chain, managed care, revenue and cost, into a single source of truth, and then put AI agents on top of it to find and recover money the system is owed. We call it the 'second financial brain' for a health system," Kadakia said in an interview.

He added, "That’s a lot of technical talk for a pretty shocking problem: hospitals are multibillion-dollar enterprises, and most of them don’t have any form of managerial finance."

With that data foundation in place, Midstream Health's domain-trained agents proactively flag and prioritize cost-saving and margin opportunities such as missed rebates, pricing errors, payer underpayments and policy-driven denials.

Kadakia describes the platform as "an army of agents that runs alongside a health system’s finance and supply chain teams, never sleeps, and is constantly finding and recovering margin."

The company plans to use the fresh funding to expand its product and engineering capabilities, particularly as it moves into new verticals. It also plans to continue formalizing its sales and marketing functions and building a dedicated research function that owns its underlying data connections, Kadakia said.

Health systems are facing a financial sustainability crisis, fighting to protect razor-thin margins. More than 110 rural hospitals have closed over the past 20 years, and another 720—representing roughly a third of all rural hospitals—are at risk of closure. Much of what’s slipping away is money health systems have already earned, buried in their own contracts and spend.

According to Kadakia, one system can have thousands of contracts across supply chain, pharmacy and managed care, each with its own pricing tiers, rebate triggers and amendments. "Nobody has time to check every one against what the system actually buys and pays, so a six-figure rebate can disappear because one form was missed. Meanwhile, most healthcare AI money has gone into the claims fight between hospitals and insurers. Every dollar one side wins, the other side loses, and the total cost of care goes up. Deflationary AI will make care cheaper to deliver, and the most direct way to do that is making sure [that] health systems collect what their contracts already say they’re owed. Margin that stays buried in a contract never reaches patients," he said.

Kadakia says he has a personal perspective on the issue—his father practiced at two rural West Virginia hospitals that have since closed.

"In today's challenging healthcare environment, we have to be thoughtful about how we manage our resources and continually look for opportunities to operate more efficiently," said James Hereford, CEO of Fairview Health Services, in a statement. "By leveraging AI-driven financial operations, we can improve financial performance, allowing us to focus more resources on delivering care to our patients and communities."

CommonSpirit Health, one of the largest nonprofit health systems in the U.S., was an initial investor in Midstream and became one of the first healthcare partners chosen to implement and validate the platform through integration with supply chain operations. After implementation, Midstream's AI agents provided "measurable gains within days, surfacing opportunities like missed rebates and underpayments," according to Daniel Barchi, CommonSpirit Health's chief information officer.

"It is a closed-loop AI system that transforms financial intelligence into real-time action, delivering a data foundation, visibility and execution capability," Barchi said in a statement.

Across its customer base, Midstream claims it has identified more than 1,500 financial recovery opportunities this year, from six-figure rebates buried by a single missed form to systemic payer underpayments. Early Midstream partners are projecting more than 5x ROI this year. The platform is on pace to reach $100 million in client savings by the end of 2026, the company claims.

In the near term, Midstream is on pace to reach $100 million in client savings by the end of 2026.

"The longer-term piece is what I’m most excited about, because I think this enables a renaissance in value-based care. Value-based care was built on an unstable foundation. To take on risk, a hospital needs a clear view of what care is actually costing it and why, and the systems to give hospitals that view were never built. If we give them that foundation, they can take on more risk, and that’s how you start to deflate the arms race between payers and providers," Kadakia said.

In the current financial environment, health systems need solutions that can improve their financial position quickly, noted Mike Spadafore, managing director of Valtruis. "We’re backing Midstream because it’s built first-of-its-kind infrastructure to turn complex financial data into action. Where enterprise healthcare technology can take years to demonstrate value, Midstream delivers within the quarter," he said.

AI is intensifying an ongoing financial battle between health systems and insurers, and data shows that this AI "arms race" is driving up short-term healthcare costs. The Blue Cross Blue Shield Association estimates hospitals’ AI coding tools added nearly $1 billion in costs over two years, and insurers are answering with AI of their own.

"Patients, employers and taxpayers pay for that arms race. The next decade should be judged by a simpler test: does the technology bring total cost down? That’s the standard we hold ourselves to," Kadakia said.

#5674. Scientists discover how pancreatic cancer rewrites its DNA to escape treatment

Scientists have uncovered new details about how pancreatic cancer constantly changes its genetic makeup, allowing it to become more aggressive, spread throughout the body, and resist treatment. By examining nearly half a million individual cancer cells, researchers identified genetic changes that could reveal new ways to fight one of the deadliest forms of cancer.

The study, conducted by scientists at NYU Langone Health and its Perlmutter Cancer Center, focused on pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, a particularly difficult cancer to treat. Nearly 85 percent of patients die within five years of being diagnosed.

Although researchers have already linked more than half a dozen genes to the disease, much remains unknown about how pancreatic cancer develops and adapts. By examining tumor cells individually rather than studying them in large groups, the team gained a clearer understanding of how different populations of cancer cells change their DNA as the disease progresses.

How Pancreatic Cancer Evolves To Escape Treatment

The researchers discovered that pancreatic tumors contain a variety of distinct cell populations known as clones. Each clone consists of cancer cells with similar genetic characteristics, but their behavior can differ dramatically.

Some clones develop changes that help them withstand cancer treatments, while others become better equipped to invade surrounding tissues and spread to other parts of the body. These findings suggest that the cancer's ability to continually reorganize its genetic material plays a central role in both treatment resistance and metastasis.

Previous studies generally divided pancreatic cancer cells into two main categories: classical (less aggressive) and basal (more aggressive). However, because those studies examined large collections of cells together, scientists could not fully explain how cancer cells move from one category to the other.

The latest findings help explain this process. Genetic changes occurring within individual tumors allow cancer cells to shift between these two states, potentially making the disease more dangerous as it develops.

Scientists Identify a Gene That Could Make Pancreatic Cancer Less Aggressive

Published on October 13 in Nature Genetics, the study identified several genetic changes associated with pancreatic cancer progression. One particularly important finding involved MYC, a gene that showed heightened activity in some of the most aggressive cancer cell populations.

In additional laboratory experiments, the researchers blocked MYC activity in aggressive basal pancreatic cancer cells. Remarkably, the cells shifted back toward the less aggressive classical state.

The change also made the cancer cells more exposed to immune cells, suggesting they could become easier for the immune system to recognize and attack. Although further research is needed, the results point to MYC as a promising target for future pancreatic cancer treatments.

"Our study provides the most granular view to date of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, revealing how ongoing genetic reshaping drives tumor evolution over the course of disease," said study lead investigator Despoina Kalfakakou, PhD, a postdoctoral research fellow at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and Perlmutter Cancer Center. "These findings suggest that targeting the mechanisms underlying tumor evolution, including MYC, may help restrain the cancer's rapid progression."

"Our research also suggests that single-cell clonal analysis offers a better approach to understanding complex cancers, like pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, as it develops over time, by mapping how tumors evolve and adapt at each stage of disease progression," said study co-senior investigator Aristotelis Tsirigos, PhD, a professor in the Departments of Medicine and Pathology at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and a member of Perlmutter Cancer Center.

"More broadly, our study results highlight the critical role of clonal diversity, genetic plasticity, and interactions with the tumor's microenvironment in shaping human pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma biology," said Dr. Tsirigos, who is also co-director of the Division of Precision Medicine and director of NYU Langone's Applied Bioinformatics Laboratories.

Why Pancreatic Cancer Can Evade the Immune System

The investigation also provided important clues about pancreatic cancer's ability to hide from the immune system, a characteristic that may help explain why the disease often responds poorly to immunotherapy.

Researchers discovered that certain cancer cell clones showed increased activity of the TIGIT gene, which is associated with proteins that help tumors escape immune detection.

At the same time, these clones exhibited reduced activity of the PD1 gene. This combination may help explain why immunotherapies designed to target PD1 have shown limited effectiveness against pancreatic cancer.

Understanding these differences between cancer cell populations could help scientists develop treatments that interfere with the specific mechanisms tumors use to avoid immune attack.

According to Dr. Tsirigos, clinical trials investigating drugs that inhibit MYC or TIGIT are already underway for pancreatic ductal carcinoma and other cancers. He said the latest findings underscore the need for larger studies examining the different states cancer cells can adopt and how treatments might be tailored to target them.

Nearly Half a Million Cancer Cells Reveal Hidden Tumor Diversity

To investigate how pancreatic cancer changes over time, the scientists examined gene activity (using transcriptomics) in 443,451 individual cells collected from 62 tumors belonging to 56 men and women diagnosed with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

Six of these patients also provided tumor samples both before and after chemotherapy, allowing researchers to examine changes associated with treatment.

Unlike traditional approaches that measure changes in gene activity across large groups of cells, the new analysis examined individual cells. This provided a much more detailed picture of the different cancer cell populations living within the same tumor.

The results showed that individual tumors contained approximately two to 11 distinct clones, consisting of varying combinations of classical and basal cancer cells.

By tracing the genetic origins of these clones and comparing patterns of gene activity, the researchers connected differences in DNA copy numbers with the types of cells present in each tumor.

This approach allowed them to identify which genes, including MYC and TIGIT, were particularly active at different points during cancer progression.

Together, the findings provide a more detailed understanding of how pancreatic tumors evolve, resist treatment, and spread. They also suggest that interfering with the genetic mechanisms driving these changes could offer new opportunities to combat a disease that remains exceptionally difficult to treat.

The research was supported by the Sky Foundation and National Institutes of Health grants P30CA016087 and R01CA245005.

In addition to Drs. Kalfakakou and Tsirigos, the NYU Langone research team included Daniel Cameron, MS; Emily Kawaler, PhD; Ziaohong Jing, PhD; Cristina H. Hajdu, MD; Dylan Tamayo, MS; Yoona Shim; Amanda Ackermann, MD, PhD; Daniel Weissinger; Rosmel Hernandez, PhD; Matthew Beier, MD; Dacia Dimartino, PhD; Peter Meyn; Kalina Rice, MS; Shanmugapriya Selvaraj, MS; Cynthia A. Loomis, MD, PhD; Adriana Heguy, PhD; Amanda W. Lund, PhD; and Igor Dolgalev, PhD.

Additional contributors from Oregon Health and Science University were co-investigators Motoyuki Tsuda, MD, PhD; Hayley Zimny; and Rosalie Sears, PhD.

Researchers from the University of California San Diego included Lidong Wang, PhD; Qi Su, PhD; Sungsik Kim, PhD; Hannah Carter, PhD; Theodore Welling, MD; and co-senior study investigator Diane Simeone, MD.

#5672. STAT+: Coming readout of Kymera eczema trial is a high-stakes moment in a bid to rival Dupixent

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

West Coast Biotech & Life Sciences Reporter

Jonathan Wosen is STAT’s West Coast biotech & life sciences reporter. You can reach Jonathan on Signal at jwosen.27.

Over the past decade, Sanofi and Regeneron’s Dupixent has become the top-selling drug in immunology, bringing in tens of billions in revenue while transforming outcomes for the 1.4 million patients currently on the therapy for conditions including eczema, asthma, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. But investors and doctors are intensely following an experimental therapy positioned to rival the pharma blockbuster, with results from a key study fast approaching.

Massachusetts biotech Kymera Therapeutics plans to announce data from a mid-stage clinical trial of its lead asset, KT-621, in eczema before the end of the year. Market analysts for the investment bank Jefferies, using common shorthand for immunology and inflammatory disorders, have called the upcoming results “one of the most impactful I&I readouts this year.”

Success (or failure) could have major consequences for Kymera, its growing list of competitors, and the millions of people who live with eczema in the United States. The results could also bolster or dampen the biotech’s aspirations to treat a broader class of immunological diseases with its drug, including chronic spontaneous urticaria and asthma. Analysts forecast that the drug’s sales could reach nearly $4 billion by 2035, including more than $3 billion in eczema revenue, according to Visible Alpha.

#5671. Athenahealth launches tool to bring patient health records into Anthropic's Claude

Athenahealth launches tool to bring patient health records into Anthropic's Claude" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Electronic health record company athenahealth is opening up patient health records to outside AI assistants, starting with Anthropic’s Claude, through a new connection designed to give patients personalized answers based on their clinical data.

The new server solution, athenaPatient MCP, uses the Model Context Protocol to connect Claude directly with the athenaOne platform. Patients authenticate using their athenahealth patient portal credentials and decide what information Claude can access, according to the EHR company. Credentials are not shared with Claude.

Paul Brient, athenahealth's chief product and operations officer, said that information is encrypted in transit, patients control what information is shared, and they can revoke access at any time. "Once the connection is established and patients approve what types of data they would like to share, the rest is between Claude and the patient," he told Fierce Healthcare in an interview.

Brient noted that AI can meaningfully reduce complexity and help patients play a more active role in their care. "At its core, this is about helping patients get value from their own healthcare data," he noted.

Athenahealth is committed to responsible AI integration, company executives said.

Patients are turning to generative AI, like Claude and OpenAI's ChatGPT, to interpret lab results, medication instructions and other medical information. More than a third of U.S. adults (34%) have used AI assistants for health-related purposes, including looking up symptoms to understanding a diagnosis, according to an August Pew Research Center survey. This trend reflects a growing expectation for immediate, conversational health guidance, but also introduces new governance challenges, athenahealth executives noted.

"Claude is the first connection we’ve enabled for athenaPatient MCP, but it's not intended to be the only one," Brient said. "Anthropic has been a strong launch collaborator because of its approach to responsible AI development. But our strategy isn't built around a specific AI model. The AI landscape is moving incredibly quickly, with new models and tools coming to market seemingly every week. We designed athenaPatient MCP with that reality in mind and built it on a Model Context Protocol (MCP) that has become an industry norm for AI interoperability."

Claude Pro and Max users in the U.S. can add the athenaPatient MCP connector within their Claude settings. Patients can then ask Claude questions about their health information using natural language. With a patient’s permission, Claude can reference information such as lab results, medications, vitals, health conditions, diagnostic reports, immunizations, visit history, allergies, procedures and care plans to generate personalized answers based on their clinical data, instead of generic or incomplete information, athenahealth executives said.

"Patients often have questions about their health records between visits, from what a lab result means to what to ask at their next appointment," Syed Mohiuddin, head of healthcare at Anthropic, said in a statement. "athenahealth is giving patients a way to bring their own records into Claude when they choose to, so they can explore those questions and feel more confident and prepared in conversations with their care team."

Athenahealth's EHR is a cloud-based, open platform, Brient noted, and the company's objective is to "create a secure way for patients to use their health information with the AI assistants they choose," he said.

The company plans to expand access to other models, but Brient did not provide any details about additional integrations.

The company built athenaPatient MCP to connect to general-purpose AI assistants rather than build those generative AI capabilities entirely within athenaPatient.

"It's not our job to decide which AI assistant patients should use. Patients are increasingly using AI tools in their daily lives, and I expect that trend to continue. If we've learned anything over the last few years, it's that people will gravitate toward the experiences that work best for them. Healthcare shouldn't be isolated from that reality," Brient said.

"At its core, this is about giving patients access to their health information in the places where they want them—safely, of course. Our patient-facing connector is consistent with our broader interoperability capabilities. Consumers increasingly expect their personal data to integrate into the digital tools they use. Healthcare shouldn't be an exception," he said.

Some providers have raised concerns that as patients increasingly use AI chatbots to interpret health records and lab results, it will drive an uptick in follow-up messages to physicians. Brient noted that giving patients an easier way to connect their health records to AI tools helps patients better understand the information their providers have given them and have more informed questions.

"One of the realities of healthcare is that patients often leave an appointment with more information than they can reasonably absorb in the moment. Lab results often arrive after the patient has seen their doctor. Questions come up after the visit. Medication instructions get forgotten. That's not a criticism of patients or clinicians. It's just reality," he said.

"When patients have a stronger understanding of their healthcare situation, conversations with their care teams tend to be more productive. From the clinician perspective, we were equally focused on what this should not do. We did not want to create additional work for clinicians. A recurring theme across our product strategy is reducing work while improving outcomes. The best healthcare technology helps patients become more engaged without creating more administrative burden for clinicians," Brient noted.

Athenahealth provides EHR software, revenue cycle management and patient engagement solutions to small and independent provider practices. A year ago, the company unveiled new AI features for ambulatory providers as part of a larger upgrade to an "AI-native" athenaOne platform. This summer, the company rolled out more than 80 new AI features for RCM operations on its AI-native athenaOne platform.

Athenahealth executives describe the launch of athenaPatient MCP and the connection to Claude as just the first step, suggesting a broader strategy of allowing patients to use AI tools with their health records.

"The immediate focus is helping patients securely access and understand their health information through the AI assistants they choose to use. Looking further ahead, I think it's reasonable to expect both the number of AI assistants and the capabilities available through them to expand. One of the reasons we're excited about MCP is that it creates a standardized way to provide context to AI systems. Context is what makes AI particularly useful. Without context, AI can provide general information. With context, it can provide a more detailed, personalized set of information and is less likely to lead you astray," Brient said.

Major EHR companies are moving forward with AI integrations to connect patient data with AI tools OpenAI's ChatGPT for Healthcare now integrates with Epic's EHR to enable authorized clinicians to access and summarize patient information from medical records within ChatGPT or directly in supported Epic workflows. That integration can now pull together clinical notes, lab results, medications and specialist documentation, the company said in a blog post.

Oracle’s AI-powered patient portal allows patients to chat directly with their electronic health record using a conversational interface built on OpenAI frontier models.

In healthcare, MCP creates a common framework for connecting AI agents to clinical systems and data.

"I think it's still early, but this is an important trend to watch," Brient said. "One of the challenges with AI is that intelligence without context isn't particularly useful. In healthcare, context must be accurate, permissioned, secure, and current. That's a much harder problem than simply connecting a chat to a data source."

What makes MCP interesting, he noted, is that it provides a framework for connecting AI systems with the context they need while preserving appropriate controls and governance.

"Whether MCP ultimately becomes the interoperability layer for AI in healthcare remains to be seen, but I think the demand for this type of interoperability is only going to increase. Patients and providers are already using AI. The question is whether healthcare data can participate in those experiences safely and effectively," he said, adding, "I feel good about where the industry is headed, and I believe standards like MCP can play an important role in getting us there. But we're still in the early innings, and much work remains. Our goal is straightforward: reduce friction, maintain trust, and help patients and providers benefit from advances in AI without compromising security or control."

#5670. Popular cannabis sleep gummies may have a hidden dark side

Cannabinol (CBN) has become a popular ingredient in sleep supplements, often promoted as a natural, gentle way to relax and get a better night's rest. However, new research from the University of Connecticut suggests that this widely available cannabis compound may have risks that consumers should know about.

Scientists found that repeated exposure to CBN caused mice to develop signs of physical dependence. The findings, published in the November issue of the journal Drug and Alcohol Dependence, raise questions about the safety of using CBN regularly, particularly over long periods.

"CBN is everywhere right now. Gummies, tinctures, capsules, and it's marketed as a safe, herbal sleep supplement," says Steven Kinsey, professor in UConn's Elisabeth DeLuca School of Nursing. "Our findings suggest consumers should be aware repeated use may carry risks."

Popular Sleep Aid Shows Effects Similar to THC

CBN is a naturally occurring compound in cannabis, along with THC (tetrahydrocannabinol) and CBD (cannabidiol). Although CBN is generally considered less psychoactive than THC, the researchers discovered that it affects some of the same biological systems and can produce several key signs associated with drug dependence.

In the experiments, mice received CBN twice a day for three consecutive days. As treatment continued, the animals became less responsive to the compound, indicating that they had developed tolerance. When CBN was withdrawn, the mice also displayed physical symptoms resembling withdrawal, including head twitching and paw fluttering. These movements are comparable to the shaking that people can experience during drug withdrawal.

Another experiment revealed a surprising connection between CBN and THC. Mice previously trained to recognize and respond to THC's psychoactive effects reacted similarly when given CBN. This suggests that the two compounds produce overlapping subjective effects, at least in mice.

Together, the results indicate that CBN, despite its reputation as a milder cannabis compound, interacts with some of the same receptor systems that contribute to THC dependence.

Scientists Raise Concerns About CBN Sleep Supplements

The findings are particularly relevant because CBN products have become increasingly common, even though scientists still have limited information about their long-term effects.

The lead author of the study, Olivia Vanegas '26 Ph.D., notes "The marketing of minor cannabinoids is pretty wild right now. There are so many therapeutic claims about these drugs, but we really don't know much about their potential risks, especially with repeated use."

CBN is now widely promoted as a sleep aid, yet important questions remain unanswered. Researchers do not fully understand how CBN affects sleep quality or whether taking it repeatedly at doses commonly found in supplements could lead to addiction in humans.

There is also a historical reason for caution. Over the past century, several medications initially promoted as helpful sleep treatments were eventually found to carry serious risks of dependence and habit formation.

Potential Benefits Come With Unanswered Safety Questions

The researchers also identified potentially useful properties of CBN. The compound demonstrated anti-inflammatory effects, including at lower doses that did not produce psychoactive effects.

However, the experiments revealed another possible concern. During a simulated bacterial challenge, CBN reduced the body's ability to defend itself. This weakening of immune protection could make it easier for an infection to develop, similar to how bacteria can enter through a cut on the foot and cause illness.

These findings suggest that CBN may have medical applications, but scientists need a clearer understanding of its benefits, potential side effects, and appropriate doses before determining how it can be used safely.

Importantly, the experiments were conducted in mice, so the findings do not establish that CBN causes dependence or withdrawal in people. Additional studies are needed to understand how the compound affects humans, especially when taken frequently, at higher doses, or over extended periods.

"CBN may still have therapeutic value," he says. "But until we know more about dosing and long-term effects, the message for consumers is simple: buyer beware."

Materials provided by University of Connecticut. Original written by Kim Krieger. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5668. Brigham and Women's nurses set Nov. 12 date for open-ended strike

Brigham and Women's nurses set Nov. 12 date for open-ended strike" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Union nurses at Brigham and Women's Hospital are set to strike in the coming weeks after failed contract negotiations, in what could be the largest open-ended nurse strike in Massachusetts history.

Brigham and Women's Hospital said in a statement it received notice from the Massachusetts Nurses Association (MNA) on Nov. 1 about an open-ended strike beginning Thursday, Nov. 12 at 7 a.m.

"While we had hoped to avoid another strike, we are prepared to continue providing safe, high-quality care throughout any work stoppage, building on our experience and extensive contingency planning," the statement read. "We deeply value and respect our Brigham nurses and remain committed to reaching a fair and responsible agreement. Our latest offer provides market-leading compensation and competitive benefits while recognizing our responsibility to our patients, our entire workforce and the long-term financial sustainability of Brigham and Women’s Hospital."

Negotiations with MNA are set to resume Nov. 9, the hospital said.

MNA said in a statement negotiations will focus on "securing a fair contract that meets the needs of the nurses, their patients and the community members they serve." Nurses are seeking the following terms as part of a fair contract, per the union:

"We are ready to strike but are equally prepared to negotiate a fair contract that protects patient care, respects nurses, and averts the strike," said Kelly Morgan, chair of the union's bargaining committee for the hospital. “Brigham nurses are resolved to fight for as long as it takes for patient safety and the professional respect we deserve.”

Union nurses at Brigham and Women's Hospital voted to reject management's "last, best and final offer" on updated contracts, potentially steering the dispute back toward what could be the largest open-ended nurse strike in Massachusetts history.

The Massachusetts Nurses Association had previously scheduled the strike for Oct. 14, but postponed to give its members a chance to vote on the proposal from Mass General Brigham, the hospital's parent system. The union said it has requested to resume contract negotiations this week, with the hospital responding in its own public statement this it "is prepared to maintain uninterrupted care and respond to any steps the union may take."

MGB's rejected offer would have retained the hospital's existing nursing wage progression system of annual 5% step increases until 20 years tenure, with the addition of two additional 2.5% increases at the top of the prior structure. The union has said it is seeking limits on the use of temporary nurses, more affordable health insurance benefits and “a meaningful cost-of-living wage increase” that includes a differential for nurses floating between units.

“This vote shows the resolve of Brigham nurses, who are fighting for patient safety and for the professional respect we deserve," Kelly Morgan, chair of the union's bargaining committee for the hospital, said in a weekend release. "It’s [time for] MGB to return to the table ready to negotiate in good faith to reach a fair agreement that recognizes the value of Brigham nurses and the expertise they offer for the care of some of the region’s most complex patients every day.”

Brigham and Women's Hospital said it was "disappointed" by the rejection, and that its proposal "reflected the hospital’s commitment to investing in our nurses while supporting long-term sustainability, including meaningful compensation and benefit enhancements that kept Brigham nursing pay among the highest in the market."

Notably, the announcement of the member vote's outcome coincided with news that MGB has begun a new round of layoffs affecting both clinical and operational programs. The unspecified number of cuts reflect a financial need to further adjust operating MGB's structure even after roughly 1,500 people were laid off in 2024, the system said.

Nurses at Brigham and Women’s Hospital have lifted their notice of an Oct. 14 strike after their union and Mass General Brigham management made progress toward a potential contract deal late Saturday night, the sides said in statements.

The 4,000-member open-ended strike would be the largest in state history if launched, and follows months of contract negotiations between the health system and the Massachusetts Nurses Association (see that coverage below).

A formal deal has yet to be struck, though the union said it agreed to call off its 10-day strike notice "given the complexity of the agreement and the impact of a potential strike on our nurses and the community." The proposal is being presented to members for a vote, which might yield a new 10-day notice if rejected.

Brigham and Women's Hospital, in a Sunday statement, said its "last, best and final offer ... reflects significant movement on several of the union's priorities while maintaining a responsible approach to supporting nurses, patients and the long-term strength of the hospital."

It added that the offer retains the hospital's existing nursing wage progression system of annual 5% step increases until 20 years tenure, with the addition of two additional 2.5% increases at the top of the prior structure. The withdrawn notice also saved the hospital from having to implement its contingency staffing plan of hiring temporary nurses.

"We are thankful the MNA has pulled its indefinite strike notice and will allow its members to vote on the hospital's final offer," the hospital said. The union's statement did not specify the timing of that vote.

Editor's note: On Oct. 2, the Massachusetts Nurses Association announced an Oct. 14, 7:00 a.m. start time for their strike if no deal is reached.

Nurses at Brigham and Women’s Hospital have voted to authorize an open-ended, 4,000-member strike that could become the largest nurses’ strike in Massachusetts history.

The Massachusetts Nurses Association announced the 93% in favor vote that was held Thursday evening. No date has been set yet by the union, which is legally required to give employer Mass General Brigham (MGB) 10 days' notice.

“Brigham nurses have made clear that we are prepared to stay on strike for as long as it takes to win a contract that protects our patients and respects the nurses who care for them,” Kelly Morgan, a labor and delivery nurse and chair of the Brigham and Women’s Hospital MNA Bargaining Committee, said in the union’s announcement. “An open-ended strike is a serious step that will undoubtedly create a healthcare crisis in Massachusetts. MGB can prevent the strike by returning to the table and negotiating the contract our nurses need to keep providing world-class care.”

Contract negotiations between the sides have been ongoing since last November, with the prior agreement expiring on March 31. In July, the nurses (plus an additional 450 home care clinicians) conducted a one-day awareness strike that was also a record breaker for the state and the first at Brigham and Women’s, a flagship hospital and founding member of the nonprofit system.

Demonstrations have continued in the weeks since, including a rally held earlier this week outside of an MGB-hosted World Medical Innovation Forum, where bargaining members painted a contrast between executives’ conversations with investors on AI and the demands of their clinical workforce.

The hospital, in statements given to press, said “we remain committed to bargaining in good faith and have put forward a fair and responsible proposal that maintains Brigham nurses’ market-leading compensation, preserves meaningful wage growth and competitive benefits, and balances those investments with the long-term financial sustainability of our system,” the hospital said in a statement given to press.

The hospital has previously said it has found agreements with the union on several issues. However, the union has previously said that talks stalled in mid-August and reiterated Thursday that it still is seeking limits on the use of temporary nurses, more affordable health insurance benefits and “a meaningful cost-of-living wage increase” that includes a differential for nurses floating between units.

MGB is the largest private employer in Massachusetts with roughly 85,000 workers and $22.8 billion in annual revenue, making it among the country’s largest nonprofit health systems. Financial results released last month outlined a $15 million operating income (0.1% operating margin) across nine months of its ongoing fiscal year, up from a $44 million operating loss (-0.3% operating margin), though its nine-month bottom line including nonoperating gains like investment returns was $1.9 billion. Early last year saw the organization undertake the largest layoffs in its history, when it cut about 1,500 workers.

The union has pointed to MGB’s bottom line (nearly $2.4 billion across fiscal 2025), substantial total assets ($35.8 billion) and the compensation of executives (almost $9.2 million for CEO Anne Klibanski, M.D.) in its calls for stronger contracts.

#5667. This mysterious mushroom makes people see hundreds of tiny humans

People living thousands of miles apart have reported an extraordinarily strange experience after eating certain wild mushrooms. They begin seeing tiny human figures that appear to move through the real world, walking around objects, climbing over surfaces, and interacting with their surroundings.

These visions are known as Lilliputian hallucinations, named after the miniature inhabitants of "Gulliver's Travels," who stand just 6 inches tall. For decades, researchers suspected that cultural beliefs and folklore might explain why people in different regions described such similar experiences.

Now, a new study provides evidence that the phenomenon has a biological explanation.

Researchers at the University of Utah (U) used DNA sequencing to identify Lanmaoa asiatica as the mushroom responsible for these unusual hallucinations in Southwest China and the northern Philippines. Surprisingly, their investigation found no evidence of any known psychoactive mushroom compounds, including psilocybin.

The findings suggest that the mushroom may produce an entirely unfamiliar hallucinogenic substance. Identifying that chemical could help scientists better understand neurological disorders, unusual visual experiences, and the processes through which the brain creates our perception of reality.

The research was conducted by Colin Domnauer, a doctoral student at the U, and Bryn Dentinger, a mycologist affiliated with the university and the Natural History Museum of Utah. Their findings were published in the journal Mycologia.

In an interview with @theU, Domnauer explained how researchers traced the mushroom's identity, what makes its effects so unusual, and why the discovery could have implications far beyond the study of fungi.

A Century-Old Mystery of Tiny Human Hallucinations

The scientific mystery dates back to 1934, when Western researchers learned that people in Papua New Guinea sometimes experienced vivid visions of miniature humans after eating wild mushrooms. The bizarre effect became known as "mushroom madness."

During the 1950s and 1960s, anthropologists and mushroom specialists traveled to Papua New Guinea to investigate. Their work pointed toward several possible species belonging to the Boletaceae (bolete) family.

However, chemical testing failed to reveal any substances that could explain the hallucinations. Samples were even examined by Albert Hofmann, the scientist who first isolated psilocybin and discovered LSD. He, too, was unable to identify an active ingredient.

With no chemical explanation available, some researchers began questioning whether the mushrooms were responsible at all. They suggested that the visions might instead arise from cultural expectations or traditional beliefs. By the end of the 1960s, scientific investigation of the phenomenon had largely stopped.

The mystery resurfaced during the 1990s, when people in Yunnan, Southwest China, reported similar hallucinations after eating bolete mushrooms. Although the precise species remained uncertain, researchers suspected a recently described mushroom called Lanmaoa asiatica.

Scientists Identify the Mushroom Behind the Strange Visions

Another important clue appeared in 2024, when Domnauer learned of comparable experiences among an Indigenous community in the remote Northern Cordillera region of the Philippines.

Community members described a wild edible mushroom called "Sedesdem" that could sometimes cause people to see miniature human figures. Similar mushrooms were known locally as "Nonda" in Papua New Guinea and "Jian shou qing" in Yunnan.

These mushrooms have an important place in local food traditions, but consuming them without thoroughly cooking them can trigger the unusual hallucinations.

The Philippine accounts represented a third independent report of wild mushrooms causing remarkably similar visions of tiny people.

To investigate, Domnauer traveled to Yunnan and the Philippines, interviewed local residents, and collected specimens of L. asiatica along with other mushrooms belonging to the Lanmaoa genus.

The fieldwork included the first scientific survey of fungi in the northern Philippines. Researchers then analyzed DNA from the collected mushrooms to establish their identities and evolutionary relationships.

The results revealed that the mushrooms called Jian shou qing in China and Sedesdem in the Philippines were both L. asiatica.

This was an unexpected finding because scientists had previously believed the species occurred only in China.

Dentinger also visited Papua New Guinea in hopes of collecting specimens from the location where the mystery originally began. Unfortunately, unusually dry weather made it impossible to obtain samples for genetic comparison.

Although the Papua New Guinea mushroom remains unverified, the evidence from China and the Philippines provides a compelling connection. Three geographically separated cultures have described the same highly specific hallucinations, and DNA testing has linked two of those cases to a single mushroom species.

That consistency strongly suggests a shared chemical and neurological explanation rather than unrelated cultural influences.

Hallucinations of Tiny Humans That Seem Remarkably Real

What makes these hallucinations especially unusual is their striking similarity across different accounts.

People typically describe seeing dozens or even hundreds of miniature figures, generally measuring between 3 and 30 centimeters tall. The figures appear with extraordinary clarity, often seeming as solid and convincing as actual people.

According to Domnauer, approximately 90% of those experiencing the visions describe figures resembling elves, clowns, or other fairy-like characters, often wearing brightly colored clothing.

Even more surprising is the way these imaginary figures seem to behave.

Rather than floating through walls or ignoring their surroundings, they appear to follow familiar physical rules. They walk around obstacles, move across ordinary objects, and sometimes tumble from the edges of tables.

Domnauer recalled one particularly unusual account involving someone eating soup. The person reported seeing tiny humans leap from a spoon into the bowl, where they began swimming. When the person took another spoonful, the miniature figures reportedly remained visible inside their mouth.

Such detailed interactions distinguish these visions from many other forms of drug-induced hallucination.

A Mysterious Psychedelic Compound Unlike Any Known Drug

Scientists also investigated whether L. asiatica contains any of the chemicals already known to cause psychedelic experiences.

Using both chemical testing and genetic analysis, the researchers searched for established psychoactive compounds found in other mushroom species.

The absence of familiar hallucinogens was particularly intriguing because the mushroom's effects differ so dramatically from those associated with known psychedelic drugs.

Researchers now suspect that L. asiatica produces an unidentified psychoactive substance responsible for the tiny human hallucinations.

The compound has not yet been isolated or chemically identified, so its exact nature and mechanism remain unknown.

Discovering it could open an entirely new avenue of research into how certain chemicals alter visual perception.

What the Mushroom Could Reveal About the Human Brain

Although L. asiatica provides an unusually consistent trigger for Lilliputian hallucinations, the phenomenon is not limited to mushroom consumption.

Stories involving miniature humanlike beings appear throughout folklore around the world. Similar hallucinations have also been documented in people experiencing alcohol withdrawal, dementia, macular degeneration, and other neurological conditions.

These connections suggest that the visions may arise from a fundamental feature of the way the human brain processes visual information.

However, scientists still do not fully understand the neurological mechanisms responsible for these experiences or how best to treat them when they occur in medical settings.

This is where the mysterious mushroom could become especially valuable.

Unlike the neurological and medical conditions in which Lilliputian hallucinations occur relatively rarely, L. asiatica can produce the phenomenon in a more consistent and recognizable way.

If researchers can isolate the chemical responsible, they may gain a useful tool for investigating the brain circuits and processes that create these unusually detailed visual experiences.

Such research could eventually improve scientific understanding of hallucinations associated with neurological diseases.

The research team's next major objective is to isolate and identify the suspected psychedelic compound.

DNA Sequencing Reveals Four Previously Unknown Mushroom Species

The investigation also produced important discoveries about fungal biodiversity.

Rather than studying L. asiatica alone, Domnauer and Dentinger conducted the first comprehensive genomic analysis of the Lanmaoa genus.

They examined 53 mushroom specimens collected from natural habitats and preserved in fungarium collections around the world.

Genetic sequencing revealed 17 species within the group, including four species previously unknown to science.

Remarkably, two of those newly identified species had already been preserved in existing collections in the United States. Their distinct identities had gone unrecognized until researchers examined their DNA.

The analysis also indicated that L. asiatica is the only species in the genus currently known to produce psychoactive effects.

Scientists are now working to reconstruct the group's evolutionary history. They hope to determine how the unusual chemical trait developed and whether closely related mushrooms might produce comparable substances.

The findings also demonstrate the scientific value of museum collections. Specimens preserved for years can contain biological discoveries that become apparent only when newer analytical techniques are applied.

For Domnauer, the hidden diversity found in these collections is a reminder that many species and potentially important biological characteristics remain undiscovered, even among organisms that scientists have already collected.

Exploring Fungi Could Lead to New Medicines and Discoveries

The broader implications extend well beyond unusual hallucinations.

Fungi remain one of the least thoroughly explored groups of organisms, and researchers believe their chemical diversity could provide valuable clues about biology, medicine, and the nervous system.

One of the most famous examples is penicillin, the antibiotic originally obtained from a fungus that transformed the treatment of bacterial infections and became one of the most consequential medical discoveries of the last century.

Scientists hope continued exploration of fungal biodiversity could reveal other medically useful compounds and previously unknown biological processes.

The mysterious effects of L. asiatica illustrate just how much remains to be learned about the fungal kingdom. A mushroom long consumed by communities in Asia may contain a substance capable of revealing new information about the human brain and how it creates conscious experience.

The research received funding from the National Science Foundation (award #DEB-2114785).

#5666. A STAT reporter on covering MRT as an experimental fertility treatment

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Amanda Erickson is a news editor at STAT.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.

Good morning! We’ve got something a little different for you today – an amazing new story from Megan Molteni, and also a peek at the story behind the story.

And speaking of peeks — I’d recommend this new episode of Commons Healthcare, which examines STAT’s investigative prowess and features interviews with Executive Editor Rick Berke and the late, inimitable Helen Branswell.

Heidy Willis was struggling to get pregnant. And after several rounds of failed IVF, she was willing to try anything.

So Willis flew to Albania for a process known as mitochondrial replacement therapy, or MRT. Willis’ genetic material was inserted into another woman’s egg cells. The idea is that the donor’s healthy mitochondria power the embryo into a healthy fetus and, eventually, a baby.

MRT is not legal in the U.S. But medical tourism agencies charge thousands of dollars to connect women to clinics around the world. Many of these companies target women over 40, even though there’s scant evidence the procedure can help unwind age-related infertility.

“You’re paying for the privilege of being a guinea pig,” a John Hopkins bioethicist told STAT’s Megan Molteni.

Megan has spent the last eight months doggedly investigating the companies connecting women to MRT treatments, talking to dozens of patients, employees and researchers. Some of her findings are, quite frankly, shocking. There’s a coda to Willis’s story, for example, that made me gasp out loud.

Set aside some time today or this week to dive into the story. And below, Megan took the time to answer some of my questions about this remarkable piece of journalism.

How did the idea for this story come about?

Back in 2019, I’d reported on the results of a small pilot study of MRT for infertility and since then have continued to cover developments.

In February of this year, I was contacted by a couple in the U.K. who wanted to tell me about an experience they had with a reproductive tourism company called IFG that was marketing MRT as a sort of miracle treatment for age-related infertility. The woman in this couple was a doctor in her 40s and she’d been taken in by the hope that was being offered for her to have a genetically related child of her own, despite there being scant evidence that it improves the odds of pregnancy for older women.

Ultimately, she didn’t go through with MRT because of some bad experiences she had leading up to it. But she was in touch with a number of other women who were actively in the process and she helped me get connected to them to hear more about their stories.

What was the biggest reporting challenge?

Reproductive tourism is the business of breaking procreation into distinct components that can be routed around regulations and assembled at the end to result in a baby. It is, by design, a complex chain of events often facilitated by multiple companies across multiple jurisdictions to circumvent local laws and so is a pretty opaque process.

With MRT, you’re adding even more layers of scientific and legal maneuvering to make it possible. So getting inside required actually going to the places that patients were going, including a clinic in Albania, where the laws are more amenable to technologies like MRT.

What was the most surprising thing you learned?

One of the things that was most surprising was that we were able to get our hands on this long-awaited data from a clinic in Ukraine that had been at one time the most prolific provider of MRT, before the full-scale Russian invasion of 2022.

I had been aware of them for years, thanks to reporting by NPR and this Netflix documentary.

Scientists I know in this space have been awaiting this publication of data, but with the war breaking out, things had gone rather silent. I reached out to their former embryologist, Pavlo Mazur, to ask him what he thought about these commercial clinics offering MRT for age-related infertility, not really expecting to hear back.

Instead, that started months of conversations. He had data he wanted in the world but hadn’t been able to publish, for some reasons that make a lot of sense, and for some others that have to do with biases against science coming out of countries like Ukraine without a long history of evidence-based medicine and well-regulated biomedical research. Their results are the strongest refutation of the idea that MRT can be a silver bullet remedy for age-related infertility.

No matter what happens tomorrow, health care policy could be in for a shakeup. That’s the message from more than two dozen policymakers, lobbyists, and experts STAT’s Daniel Payne spoke with.

Of course, control of Congress will shape what happens next. But some of Daniel’s sources said the anger with the health care status quo runs deep. One health policy consultant said they’re telling insurance leaders that they predict “significant” changes to the fundamentals of American health care, and that they should “be afraid.”

If you prefer your election predictions via video, check out our new “STATus Report”. And if you haven’t yet checked out our midterms page, do it today! Who knows what it will hold after tomorrow!

Did Daniel’s story about the stakes of tomorrow’s election get your heart racing? It turns out, you’re not alone.

As STAT’s Liz Cooney reports, “studies have found a significantly higher chance of arrhythmias in the weeks just before and after elections, and an increased rate of hospitalizations for heart attacks right after voting day.”

The issue is stress. A deluge of news can raise your adrenaline and amp up your sympathetic nervous system, which can in turn alter the heart’s electrical activity. This makes abnormal rhythms more likely in someone already prone to them. Interested to learn about what researchers found when they looked at heart health around the 2020 and 2016 elections? Read more.

Years ago, maternal fetal medicine doctor Elyce Cardonick met two pregnant women, both suffering from ovarian cancer. The women became friends, meeting up with their newborns and comparing wigs after hair loss.

One of those mothers is thriving, alongside her 28-year-old twins. The other didn’t live to see her child turn three.

Why did one die and the other survive? Read this new First Opinion for answers.
